Two separate problems are stacking up. Each one alone can cause a large slowdown on a Mac, but I haven't measured either on your setup.

**1. Your container runs x86 code on an ARM chip.** Because the image uses `--platform linux/amd64`, every Node and npm process is translated from x86 to ARM. Docker's setting "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon" is **off by default**, so it probably isn't using Apple's Rosetta translator. It most likely falls back to a slower emulator called QEMU. Docker says Rosetta makes x86 emulation "nearly on par with native", but that's Docker's own claim.

**2. node_modules sits on a bind mount.** On a Mac, Docker runs inside a small Linux virtual machine. Every file read or write in a bind mount has to cross between macOS and that VM. node_modules is tens of thousands of small files, so npm install and the dev server's file watching pay that cost constantly. Your Linux colleagues' containers read the disk directly, so they don't.

**What to do, in order of impact:**

1. **Move node_modules into a named volume.** Keep bind-mounting the source code, but add a volume on top: `- node_modules:/app/node_modules`. The files then live inside the VM. This also stops Linux-built packages from mixing with Mac ones on your disk.
2. **Turn on Rosetta.** In Settings, set the VM manager to Apple Virtualization framework, leave file sharing on VirtioFS (the default), and tick the Rosetta box. Run `softwareupdate --install-rosetta` first. One bug report says the box quietly unticks itself if Rosetta isn't installed.
3. **Stop running everything as x86.** Build a native ARM image and handle only the x86-only dependency on its own, for example in a separate amd64 sidecar container. Ask the vendor for an ARM build too. This matters beyond speed: Apple has said Rosetta is fully available only through macOS 27, which you're on now. Whether Docker's use of it continues in macOS 28 isn't confirmed.
4. **If it's still slow,** try Docker's synchronized file shares. They keep a cached copy of your files inside the VM. Add node_modules to `.syncignore`. Its documentation page doesn't say which Docker subscriptions include it.

Sources:
- https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/
- https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/
- https://www.docker.com/?p=47759
- https://github.com/docker/for-mac/issues/7243
- https://www.jeffgeerling.com/blog/2022/new-docker-mac-virtiofs-file-sync-4x-faster/
- https://engineered.at/articles/docker-on-macos-is-still-slow
- https://techearl.com/docker-bind-mounts-slow-mac-windows
- https://www.macrumors.com/2025/06/10/apple-to-phase-out-rosetta-2/
- https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/787530

No, not on 3.13t. Free-threading only becomes officially supported in 3.14t. If you want no-GIL in production, the path is to move your platform pin to 3.14.

**Why 3.13t is a bad bet**
- **Still experimental.** Python's own 3.13 docs say to "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit." That hit is about 40% on pyperformance, because 3.13t turns off the specializing interpreter. 3.13t also has known crash risks, such as sharing iterators or frame objects between threads, and some objects are kept in memory forever, which raises memory use. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
- **Upstream has moved to 3.14t.** PEP 779 was accepted in June 2025 and dropped the "experimental" label for 3.14's free-threaded build, but it stays optional rather than the default. In 3.14 the single-threaded penalty is roughly 5–10%. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ · https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html
- **The tooling is dropping 3.13t.** manylinux removed 3.13t from its build images on 7 May 2026, and PyTorch dropped 3.13t and told users to move to 3.14t. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- **Your three dependencies have no current Linux x86-64 builds for 3.13t, but all have them for 3.14t:**
  - NumPy 2.5.4: https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files
  - pydantic-core 2.50.4: https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files
  - lxml 6.1.3: https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files

  pydantic-core did add 3.13t support back in 2.29.0 (https://newreleases.io/project/pypi/pydantic-core/release/2.29.0). Staying on 3.13t would freeze you on old versions or force you to build from source. If a package isn't marked as free-threading-safe, Python quietly turns the GIL back on with only a warning.

**What to do**
1. **Get 3.14t approved on your platform.** Without that, there's no supported no-GIL option for you.
2. **Benchmark your real workload on 3.14t** against normal 3.14, both with one thread and with many. Check `sys._is_gil_enabled()` at runtime and treat the GIL re-enable warning as an error in CI, so a single non-ready package can't silently switch the GIL back on.
3. **Audit your own thread safety.** The built-in list, dict and set types use internal locks, but Python doesn't guarantee that. Protect shared state with explicit locks, and don't share iterators, lxml trees or parsers between threads. I didn't find lxml documentation on how thread-safe it is under free-threading, so check that yourself.
4. **Run a canary rollout** that can fall back to the normal GIL build.
5. **Until 3.14t is approved,** run the CPU-bound work in a `ProcessPoolExecutor` on standard 3.13. Where it applies, NumPy code that releases the GIL already runs in parallel with plain threads.

Other source used: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-779-criteria-for-supported-status-for-free-threaded-python/84319

**Bottom line:** No. On 3.13t this isn't production-ready for you, and the ecosystem is now moving away from 3.13t. If free-threading matters, the realistic target is CPython 3.14t, which means changing your platform's 3.13 pin.

**Findings**

1. **3.13t is officially experimental.** The CPython 3.13 docs say to "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit," about 40% on pyperformance, mainly because the specializing interpreter is turned off. They also list ways to crash it: frames accessed from other threads, `sys._current_frames()`, and iterators shared between threads. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
2. **"Officially supported" starts with 3.14.** PEP 779 is Final and was accepted on 16 June 2025: 3.13 is phase I (experimental) and 3.14 is phase II (supported but optional). https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ The 3.14 What's New says the PEP 703 work is complete, the specializing interpreter is back on, and the single-thread penalty is about 5–10%. https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html
3. **The build ecosystem has dropped 3.13t.** pypa/manylinux removed cp313t from its images on 2026-05-07 and treats 3.14t as the stable free-threaded target. Because of that, PyTorch is dropping 3.13t wheels. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
4. **None of your three dependencies ships cp313t wheels in its current release, but all three ship cp314t manylinux x86-64 wheels:**
   - NumPy 2.5.4 (2026-10-10). https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files NumPy calls its free-threading support experimental (it started in 2.1 with CPython 3.13). Writing to a shared array while another thread reads it gives races, and resizing it can crash the process, so you'd need your own locking. https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/thread_safety.html
   - pydantic-core 2.50.4 (2026-11-05). https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files Pydantic 2.11 added "experimental" free-threading support. https://pydantic.dev/articles/pydantic-v2-11-release
   - lxml 6.1.3 (2026-09-02). https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files
5. **On 3.13t you'd be building from source, and the GIL may come back on its own.** CPython re-enables the GIL when it imports an extension that isn't marked free-thread-safe, and prints a warning. Any dependency that falls back like this cancels the benefit. (3.13 howto, above)

**Recommendation:** Don't ship on 3.13t. Make the case for moving the platform to 3.14t, then:
- benchmark the real workload against GIL 3.14
- run with `PYTHON_GIL=0` unset and watch for GIL re-enable warnings
- stress-test the threading code, especially any shared NumPy arrays and lxml trees
- keep a fallback path using GIL-enabled 3.14 or multiprocessing

**What I'm unsure of**
- The PyPI pages were cut off at about 100k characters each. The cp313 wheels I could see were all the normal GIL builds, but older releases might still have cp313t wheels that you could pin to.
- The py-free-threading tracker lists lxml at 7.0.0, which doesn't match 6.1.3 already shipping cp314t wheels, so the tracker may be out of date. https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking/
- I didn't find an official lxml statement on how thread-safe it is when free-threaded. Sharing parsed trees across threads is untested territory.
- I didn't confirm whether other libraries the service uses support free-threading.

**Report to coordinator (press, forums, issue trackers, community)**

**Bottom line:** Not on 3.13t. That build has lost ecosystem support. The free-threaded build the ecosystem now supports is 3.14t, and all three of our dependencies ship wheels for it.

**Findings**

1. **manylinux removed 3.13t.** On 2026-05-07, pypa/manylinux took CPython 3.13t out of its Docker images. Its maintainers called 3.13t experimental and 3.14t "the stable, non-experimental free-threaded variant". As a result, PyTorch dropped 3.13t from its nightlies and from the 2.13 release (announced 2026-05-14, tracking issue pytorch/pytorch#182949). Most projects build their Linux wheels on manylinux, so this affects them too.
   https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386

2. **None of our three dependencies ships 3.13t wheels in its current release. All three ship cp314t manylinux x86-64 wheels.** I checked the PyPI file lists:
   - **NumPy 2.5.4** (2026-10-10): cp314t yes, cp313t no. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files
   - **pydantic-core 2.50.4** (2026-11-05): cp314t yes, cp313t no. It did ship 3.13t wheels from 2.29.0 onward (PR #1628, Feb 2025), so older pins would still have them. https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files and https://newreleases.io/project/pypi/pydantic-core/release/2.29.0
   - **lxml 6.1.3** (2026-09-02): cp314t and cp315t yes, cp313t no. https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files
   
   On 3.13t we would have to pin old releases or build from source, and miss future security fixes. lxml is the biggest worry here because it parses untrusted XML.

3. **3.13t is slow on single-threaded code.** Community write-ups put the penalty at about 40% on pyperformance, because the specializing interpreter is turned off in 3.13t. For 3.14t they report roughly 5–10%. These numbers come from blogs, not official benchmarks.
   https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html, https://dev.to/dmaxdev/python-314-free-threading-real-benchmarks-real-breakage-real-code-3m5, https://www.buildmvpfast.com/blog/free-threaded-python-3-14-should-you-switch-2026

4. **Hidden risks with C extensions.** If an extension hasn't declared itself free-threading safe, importing it silently turns the GIL back on. Extensions can also crash in multithreaded code in ways the GIL used to prevent. lxml is a C wrapper around libxml2, and I found no changelog entry from lxml about its thread safety under free-threading.
   https://labs.quansight.org/blog/free-threaded-one-year-recap, https://py-free-threading.github.io/ci/

5. **Opinion on production use is split.** Some say stay on the GIL build for user-facing traffic. Others say free-threading is usable for selected workloads if you keep a rollback path.
   https://velobot-wiki.pages.dev/article/software/free-threaded-python-adoption-playbook/

**Recommendation from my angle:** Don't move to 3.13t. Either ask the platform team to allow 3.14t, or keep the GIL build and use multiprocessing for the CPU-bound work. If we do pilot 3.14t:
- Set `PYTHON_GIL=0` or check at runtime that the GIL is really off.
- Load-test lxml with many threads.
- Benchmark our real workload.

**What I'm unsure of**
- I couldn't tell which NumPy and lxml release was the last to ship cp313t. pydantic-core's first 3.13t release was 2.29.0, but I don't know its last.
- I found no official statement from lxml on how thread-safe it is under free-threading.
- The performance numbers come from blogs and haven't been checked against official benchmarks.
- One search summary claimed NumPy 2.5 still covers 3.13t. The PyPI file list shows no cp313t wheels, so I went with the file list.

**Report to coordinator (independent measurements, critiques, counter-evidence)**

**Short answer:** No. 3.13t is not production-ready for this stack, and the free-threaded ecosystem has moved on to 3.14t. The team should run their service on standard 3.13 for now and try free-threading on 3.14t.

**Findings**

1. **CPython itself calls 3.13t experimental and slow on one thread.** The 3.13 docs say: "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit," about **40% on pyperformance**. The main cause is that the specializing interpreter is turned off in 3.13t. Some objects are also made immortal, which can raise memory use, and the docs list unsafe uses of frames and iterators. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
2. **Supported status starts at 3.14t, not 3.13t.** PEP 779 (Final, accepted 16 June 2025) makes 3.14t "officially supported but still optional." Its targets are at most 15% slower and at most 20% more memory than the normal build, and it reports about 10% / 15–20% at the time. 3.13t stays in the experimental phase. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/
3. **Build tooling has dropped 3.13t.** pypa/manylinux removed cp313t from its images on 2026-05-07, calling it "experimental," and PyTorch dropped 3.13t wheels as a result. Expect other C-extension projects to stop shipping 3.13t wheels too. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
4. **NumPy:** the latest release, 2.5.4 (Oct 10, 2026), has free-threaded wheels only for **cp314t and cp315t. There is no cp313t.** https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files
5. **lxml:** the latest release, 6.1.3 (Sep 2, 2026), also has free-threaded wheels only for **cp314t and cp315t**. The 7.0.0a1 changelog says free-threading support is "experimental" and starts at 3.14t. https://pypi.org/project/lxml/ , https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a1/
6. **pydantic-core** added 3.13t support in 2.29.0 by declaring it doesn't need the GIL (`gil_used=false`). A search summary says 2.34.1 still ships cp313t wheels, but I didn't open the file list to confirm. https://newreleases.io/project/pypi/pydantic-core/release/2.29.0
7. **One unready extension brings the GIL back.** If an imported extension doesn't declare free-threading support, the interpreter turns the GIL back on for the whole process. `PYTHON_GIL=0` overrides that, but risks crashes. Even if lxml and NumPy were built from source for 3.13t, one undeclared module would remove the benefit. https://pyo3.rs/v0.23.2/free-threading , https://discuss.python.org/t/how-to-get-an-extension-module-working-w-free-threading/63653
8. **Independent benchmarks don't agree on 3.13t's single-thread cost.** Reports range from about 17% to 40% slower. CodSpeed found 3.13t threads beat the alternatives at 8 threads but called the build "not ready for production." https://codspeed.io/blog/state-of-python-3-13-performance-free-threading , https://buttondown.com/ckae930413/archive/python-gil-vs-free-threading-313t-cpu-benchmark/

**Recommendation from my angle:** Don't deploy 3.13t. Ask the platform team to allow 3.14 and test on 3.14t. Run the real workload single-threaded and at N threads, measure memory too, and check at startup that `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is False. Until then, use multiprocessing on standard 3.13.

**What I'm unsure of**
- Whether pydantic-core's newest release still ships cp313t wheels (finding 6 is unconfirmed).
- Whether older NumPy versions (2.1–2.3) had cp313t wheels you could pin to. If they did, they are now unmaintained.
- How lxml behaves on 3.14t in practice (it is labelled experimental).
- I found no independent production case studies for this exact stack.

**Report: primary and official sources**

**Findings**

1. **Where the "91%" comes from.** It is AHA conference Abstract P192, presented in March 2024 by senior author Victor Zhong (Shanghai Jiao Tong). It had not been peer-reviewed. The data are NHANES 2003–2018 (about 20,000 US adults) linked to death records through 2019. People eating in under 8 hours had HR 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03) for cardiovascular death, compared with a 12–16 h window. All-cause mortality was not raised. Zhong said this "does not mean that time-restricted eating caused cardiovascular death." Sources: https://www.news-medical.net/news/20240318/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-schedule-may-increase-heart-disease-mortality.aspx and https://mdedge.com/content/intermittent-fasting-linked-higher-cvd-death-risk

2. **The peer-reviewed version.** Chen…Manson, Tucker, Zhong, *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome* 2025; 19(7):103278, doi 10.1016/j.dsx.2025.103278. It covers 19,831 adults with a median follow-up of 8.1 years. The reference group was changed to 12–14 h, and the estimate went up to HR 2.35 (95% CI 1.39–3.98) for CV death. All-cause and cancer mortality were still not significant. The authors write that it is unclear whether the risk comes from short eating duration itself or from residual confounding. Sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/ and https://medicaldialogues.in/amp/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915

3. **Main weaknesses.**
   - The eating window was taken from two 24-hour dietary recalls at a single point in time. That says nothing about a deliberate 16:8 habit kept for years.
   - The design is observational, so illness before death could itself shorten eating windows (reverse causation).
   - The <8 h group reportedly had more smokers.
   - The <8 h group was small: about 414 people and 31 deaths, against 11,831 people and 423 deaths in the reference group. I took these counts from a secondary source and could not check them against the paper.
   - Sources: https://peterattiamd.com/time-restricted-eating-and-ascvd/ and https://www.sciencefocus.com/news/intermittent-fasting-cardiovascular-risk-2. A collective rebuttal from 34 experts is at https://cms.ahs.uic.edu/inside-ahs/wp-content/uploads/sites/12/2024/04/Collective-Reponse-to-AHA-press-release-on-TRE.pdf, but the page would not load for me.

4. **A separate NHANES analysis.** Mao…Farsijani, *Aging Cell* 2025; 24(11):e70230, with 33,052 adults. It found a U-shaped curve: risk was lowest at about 11–12 h, and both ≤8 h and ≥15 h windows had higher mortality. It shares the same measurement weakness. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40944446/

5. **Randomized trials.** These are small and short (about 12 weeks), and none measures mortality.
   - Time-restricted eating lowers systolic blood pressure modestly, probably through weight loss (10 RCTs): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9644535/
   - Without calorie restriction, it has little effect on lipids (11 RCTs): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12672340/
   - It gives no extra benefit over plain calorie restriction: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37488260/
   - None of these trials signalled harm. I only read abstracts and snippets.

**Overall view:** The evidence is weak to moderate. It is one observational dataset, the exposure measure is poor, the high-risk group is small, the confidence intervals are wide, and all-cause mortality showed no effect. None of this shows that deliberate 16:8 eating harms a healthy 45-year-old. Still, the signal has now held up through peer review and appeared in a second NHANES paper, so it shouldn't be dismissed outright.

**What I'm unsure of**
- I could not get the full text of the 2025 paper, so the event counts, covariates (for example whether calories and diet quality were adjusted for) and the sensitivity analyses are unverified.
- I found no official AHA or other guideline position on time-restricted eating published after this study.
- I did not see any trial that measured cardiovascular events.

**Report to the coordinator (press, forums and community angle)**

**What the claim is**
- The 91% figure (HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.20–3.03) comes from a poster at the AHA Lifestyle meeting in March 2024. It was promoted by an AHA press release before peer review. The data were about 20,000 NHANES adults (2003–2018). Eating windows were inferred from two 24-hour dietary recalls; participants were never asked whether they practised TRE. https://www.heart.org/en/news/2024/03/18/time-restricted-eating-may-raise-cardiovascular-death-risk-in-the-long-term ; https://www.statnews.com/2024/03/19/intermittent-fasting-study-heart-risk/
- It was later published as Chen…Zhong, *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome* 2025 (PMID 40849219, n=19,831, median follow-up 8.1 years). For eating windows under 8 hours, CV death HR was 2.35 (1.39–3.98) against a 12–14 hour reference. There was no link to all-cause or cancer death. The authors say residual confounding is possible. https://medicaldialogues.in/amp/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915

**The main criticisms**
- **Tiny exposed group.** It had about 414 people and 31 deaths, against 11,831 people and 423 deaths in the reference group. Attia's site quotes an "absolute increase of 3.9%". My arithmetic suggests that is the crude, unadjusted gap (7.5% vs 3.6%). https://peterattiamd.com/time-restricted-eating-and-ascvd/
- **Sicker, different people.** Roughly 38% of CV deaths in the short-window group were in people who already had disease, vs 15% in the reference group (same source).
- **Open letter from 34 TRE and epidemiology researchers** (Panda, Varady, Peterson, Taub and others). Points:
  - The short-window group was about 2% of the sample.
  - It had 60% more smokers and many more Black participants (23.2% vs 6.6%).
  - Under-8-hour windows on a recall often reflect incomplete food records.
  - Shift work and sleep were not accounted for.
  - One or two days of short eating is not the same as practising TRE.
  - The letter cites more than 100 trials showing no serious harm. The authors of the letter have an interest in TRE research.
  https://blog.mycircadianclock.org/debunking-misleading-claims-the-truth-behind-the-headlines-on-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-risk/
- **UK experts (McConway, Mellor, Sanders).** They said the abstract left out tobacco, alcohol, activity, poverty and antisocial working hours. Krumholz (Yale) called it "exploratory", a call for more research rather than a reason for alarm. https://gulfnews.com/special-reports/latest-intermittent-fasting-study-kicks-up-storm-what-experts-say-1.1710937118699 ; https://fortune.com/well/2024/03/18/how-healthy-intermittent-fasting-heart-disease-study-91-percent-risk/
- **Author response (Zhong).** He says the association held after adjusting for these factors, and accepts that causation cannot be shown.

**Bottom line from this angle**
Press and expert commentary overwhelmingly treat this as a weak, hypothesis-generating signal. It is observational, has a small exposed group, measures exposure poorly and is likely confounded. It is not evidence that a deliberate 16:8 routine harms a healthy 45-year-old. Nothing I found recommends that healthy people stop TRE because of it. A sensible step for the user is checking blood pressure, lipids and glucose with a doctor.

**What I'm unsure of**
- I couldn't read the full 2025 paper; PubMed and ScienceDirect were blocked. So I haven't confirmed the group size, death counts or covariates in the published version, and the 414/31 figures come from the 2024 poster.
- The two estimates (1.91 and 2.35) use different reference groups (12–16 hours vs 12–14 hours).
- I didn't search forums such as Reddit in depth.
- I found no RCT that measured cardiovascular death outcomes. The trial evidence covers risk factors only, and the other researchers should cover it.

Status: I've finished researching my angle (critiques and independent evidence). Here's my report to the coordinator.

**Researcher 3 report: independent measurements, critiques and counter-evidence**

**What the claim is based on**
- The "91%" figure (HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.20–3.03) came from a March 2024 AHA conference abstract, not a peer-reviewed paper. It used NHANES 2003–2018 data on about 20,000 US adults with a median 8 years of follow-up. Only **414 people (about 2%) ate in under 8 hours, and 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes.** There was no link with all-cause or cancer death. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- The peer-reviewed version (Chen/Zhong, *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome*, 2025) compared people eating in under 8 hours with people eating over 12–14 hours. It reported HR 2.35 (95% CI 1.39–3.98), which is where the "135%" headlines come from. All-cause and cancer mortality were still not associated. The authors say residual confounding may explain the result. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1871402125000955 ; https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915

**Main critiques**
- **Exposure measurement:** eating window came from two 24-hour dietary recalls taken at baseline. That is not intentional, sustained time-restricted eating (TRE), and NHANES does not ask about fasting on purpose.
- **Confounding and reverse causation:** the short-window group smoked more, had higher BMI, less lean mass and a different racial mix. Sick people also tend to eat less often. Donald Lloyd-Jones (a past AHA president): "It wasn't their eating time… It was what they brought to the table." (TCTMD link above)
- **Process:** 34 researchers wrote to the AHA objecting to the press release about an unvetted poster. (TCTMD; the letter PDF at cms.ahs.uic.edu would not load for me.)
- **Wide CIs from few events:** an all-cause signal is absent, which is odd if the effect were real. Coverage also notes subgroup results were inconsistent. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/intermittent-fasting-linked-to-higher-risk-of-death-from-heart-disease-preliminary-study-finds-180983993/

**Counter-evidence and other data**
- **Same data, different analysis:** Aging Cell 2025 (NHANES, n=33,052) found a U-shaped curve with the lowest risk at about 11–12 hours. Windows of 8 hours or less carried higher risk, mainly in older adults. This is **the same data source, so it is not independent replication.** https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/acel.70230
- **Null independent cohort:** Communications Medicine 2025, a Manchester cohort of older UK adults, found no mortality link with eating-window length. https://www.nature.com/articles/s43856-025-01035-x
- **NutriNet-Santé** (France, 103k people, repeated food records): later meals were linked to higher cardiovascular risk, and a longer overnight fast to lower stroke risk. This does not suggest harm from fasting. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10721609/
- **RCTs (surrogate markers only, short-term):** a 2025 meta-analysis of 22 RCTs (n≈1,004) found no significant TRE effect on blood pressure or LDL. A 2025 meta-analysis of 13 RCTs in women found no lean-mass loss. No RCT has measured cardiovascular deaths. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full

**Bottom line from my angle:** the evidence for harm is weak. It is observational, the exposure was measured crudely, it rests on few events and has obvious confounding, and no independent cohort has replicated it. Evidence of benefit beyond weight loss is also weak. Neither side has hard-outcome RCTs.

**What I'm unsure of**
- I couldn't access the full published paper, so I don't know its exact sample in the under-8-hour group, the number of deaths or the covariates.
- I didn't verify the Manchester cohort's size or methods.
- I found no UK Biobank analysis.
- I don't know whether the subgroup results in the published version differ from the abstract.

# Free-threaded Python for your service: not on 3.13t

**Short answer:** 3.13t is not production-ready for your stack. If free-threading matters to you, the real target is **3.14t**, and that means changing your platform's 3.13 pin.

## Why not 3.13t

- **Officially experimental.** CPython's own docs say to "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit." That hit is about 40% on pyperformance, because the specializing interpreter is turned off. The docs also list known crash cases, such as iterators shared between threads. Independent benchmarks put the penalty at 17–40%. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html, https://codspeed.io/blog/state-of-python-3-13-performance-free-threading
- **Support starts at 3.14.** PEP 779 makes 3.14t "officially supported but optional," with roughly a 5–10% single-thread cost. 3.13t stays experimental. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/, https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html
- **The ecosystem has dropped it.** manylinux removed cp313t on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch and others followed. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- **Your dependencies have no cp313t wheels.** The current releases of NumPy 2.5.4, pydantic-core 2.50.4 and lxml 6.1.3 all ship cp314t wheels for manylinux x86-64, but none for cp313t. On 3.13t you would have to build from source or pin old, unmaintained versions. That is risky for lxml in particular, because it parses untrusted XML. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files, https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files, https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files
- **One unready extension undoes the benefit.** Importing any extension that isn't marked free-thread-safe silently turns the GIL back on. https://pyo3.rs/v0.23.2/free-threading

## Caveats, even on 3.14t

- **Support is still labelled experimental.** NumPy, pydantic and lxml all describe their free-threading support that way. https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/thread_safety.html, https://pydantic.dev/articles/pydantic-v2-11-release, https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a1/
- **NumPy does no locking for you.** Writing to a shared array while another thread reads it is a race, and resizing it can crash the process, so you need your own locks.
- **lxml thread safety is unknown.** I found no official statement on sharing parsed trees across threads.

## What to do

1. **Now:** stay on the standard 3.13 build and use multiprocessing for the CPU-bound work.
2. **Ask the platform team to allow 3.14.** Then pilot 3.14t:
   - Leave `PYTHON_GIL` unset. Forcing `PYTHON_GIL=0` risks crashes.
   - At startup, assert that `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is False, and treat any GIL re-enable warning as a failure.
   - Benchmark your real workload single-threaded and at N threads against GIL-enabled 3.14. Measure memory as well as speed.
   - Stress-test shared NumPy arrays and lxml usage under heavy concurrency.
   - Check that your other dependencies support free-threading too.
3. **Keep a rollback path** to GIL-enabled 3.14 plus multiprocessing.

**Short answer:** This study alone isn't a good reason to stop. The "91%" figure comes from weak evidence. Since 16:8 is working for your weight, keeping it is reasonable. A slightly wider window, such as 10 hours, would also be reasonable if you'd rather be cautious.

**Where the number comes from**
- The "91% higher risk of cardiovascular death" was first presented as a conference abstract at an American Heart Association meeting in March 2024. It hadn't been peer-reviewed. ([NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/heart-health/intermittent-fasting-risk-cardiovascular-death-rcna143853))
- The peer-reviewed version came out in 2025. It followed 19,831 US adults from a national nutrition survey for a median of about 8 years. People eating within less than 8 hours had a higher risk of cardiovascular death than those eating over 12–14 hours: HR 2.35, 95% CI 1.39–3.98. They had **no higher risk of death from any cause** or from cancer. The authors say confounding by other factors might explain the link. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/); [Medical Dialogues](https://medicaldialogues.in/amp/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915))

**Why the evidence is weak**
- **Two days of data:** Eating windows came from just two 24-hour food recalls. Nobody was asked whether they were deliberately fasting, so the study wasn't really looking at people doing 16:8 for years. ([NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/heart-health/intermittent-fasting-risk-cardiovascular-death-rcna143853))
- **Observational design:** It shows an association, not cause and effect. Short eating windows often go with skipped breakfasts, irregular work, smoking, illness or poor diet. Diet quality and calories weren't accounted for.
- **Imprecise estimate:** The confidence interval is wide, so the true effect could be anywhere in a large range. The headline figure also changed between the abstract and the paper (91% vs. 135%).
- **Caution from the author:** The lead researcher said it's too early to make recommendations from this study. ([NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/heart-health/intermittent-fasting-risk-cardiovascular-death-rcna143853))

**What randomized trials show**
- Trials of time-restricted eating show modest weight loss and possibly lower systolic blood pressure, with no sign of harm to risk factors. ([meta-analysis](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9644535/))
- In a 12-month trial, adding time restriction to calorie restriction gave no extra benefit. That suggests most of the benefit comes from eating less. ([NEJM trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35443107/))
- No trial has run long enough to measure deaths, so long-term safety is still unproven either way.

**Practical steps**
1. Get a yearly check of blood pressure, cholesterol (LDL) and blood sugar. Those numbers tell you more about your own risk than this study does.
2. Keep your diet quality high and eat enough protein. Add strength training, since one suggested explanation for the finding was lower muscle mass.
3. Tell your doctor about the regimen, especially if your health changes.

This is general information, not personal medical advice.

**Short answer:** This study is not a good reason to stop. The evidence behind the "91%" claim is weak and doesn't really describe what you're doing.

**Where the number comes from**
- It was a March 2024 American Heart Association (AHA) conference poster that had not been peer-reviewed. It used US national survey data (NHANES) on about 20,000 adults.
- People who ate within less than 8 hours had a hazard ratio of 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03) for cardiovascular death, compared with people eating over 12–16 hours. Death from any cause was **not** higher. The senior author said this does not show causation. https://www.heart.org/en/news/2024/03/18/time-restricted-eating-may-raise-cardiovascular-death-risk-in-the-long-term
- The peer-reviewed version (2025) compared against a 12–14 hour group and reported HR 2.35 (1.39–3.98). All-cause mortality was still not raised, and the authors flag possible residual confounding. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/

**Why it's weak**
- **Eating window was measured badly.** It was inferred from two single-day food recalls. Nobody was asked whether they deliberately practised time-restricted eating (TRE), so a one-day snapshot stands in for your year-long 16:8 habit. Short recalled windows may also just be incomplete records.
- **Very small group.** In the poster, about 414 people (~2%) ate in under 8 hours, and 31 of them died. My researchers couldn't check the published paper's counts. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- **Confounding.** The short-window group smoked more and had more existing disease. Illness can also shorten eating windows. https://peterattiamd.com/time-restricted-eating-and-ascvd/
- **Expert pushback.** 34 researchers objected, and Yale's Krumholz called it "exploratory." https://fortune.com/well/2024/03/18/how-healthy-intermittent-fasting-heart-disease-study-91-percent-risk/

**Other evidence**
- A second NHANES analysis found the lowest risk at about 11–12 h. It uses the same data and the same flaw, so it isn't independent confirmation. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/acel.70230
- A UK cohort found no link with mortality. https://www.nature.com/articles/s43856-025-01035-x
- Short trials show no harm to blood pressure or LDL cholesterol. They also show no benefit beyond weight loss, and none measured deaths. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full

**For you:** If 16:8 helps you control your weight, the weight control itself benefits your heart. This study gives no solid reason to drop it. It's also not proven to be better than ordinary calorie restriction (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37488260/), so a 10–12 hour window is a fine choice if you prefer it. A sensible step is to check your blood pressure, lipids and glucose with your doctor and decide based on those numbers.

**Decision: Don't run production on 3.13t.** For CPU-bound work, keep standard GIL 3.13 with multiprocessing. Ask the platform team to unpin 3.14 so you can pilot 3.14t. Don't ship 3.14t until that pilot passes on your own workload.

**Why 3.13t is ruled out**

- CPython calls 3.13t experimental. Its docs say to "expect some bugs" and a single-threaded slowdown of about 40%, and they list known ways to crash it. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
- PEP 779 puts 3.13t in the experimental phase. Supported free-threading starts with 3.14t, where the single-thread cost drops to about 5–10%. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ and https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html
- pypa/manylinux removed cp313t from its images on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch dropped 3.13t wheels as a result. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- None of your three dependencies ships cp313t wheels in its current release. All three ship cp314t x86-64 wheels:
  - NumPy 2.5.4: https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files
  - pydantic-core 2.50.4: https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files
  - lxml 6.1.3: https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files
- Staying on 3.13t would mean building from source or pinning old releases. Old pins would miss security fixes, which matters most for lxml if it parses untrusted XML.
- If any extension isn't marked free-thread-safe, CPython turns the GIL back on for the whole process, which removes the benefit. https://pyo3.rs/v0.23.2/free-threading

**3.14t is promising but not proven for you**

- NumPy and pydantic both call their free-threading support experimental.
  - https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/thread_safety.html
  - https://pydantic.dev/articles/pydantic-v2-11-release
- Writing to a shared NumPy array while another thread uses it can race, and resizing it can crash, so you would need your own locks.
- No one found an lxml statement on thread safety under free-threading. The lxml 7.0.0a1 notes call its support experimental. https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a1/

```text
Decision: No 3.13t. Run GIL 3.13 with multiprocessing now, and pilot 3.14t after the platform pin changes.
Rests on: CPython's own docs and PEP 779 (3.13t is experimental); PyPI file lists checked by three researchers (no cp313t wheels for NumPy, pydantic-core or lxml; cp314t wheels for all three).
Not verified: whether your service on 3.14t actually runs with the GIL off, is faster than multiprocessing, and is stable with lxml and NumPy under threads.
Next check: On 3.14t, install your locked dependencies, start the service and assert sys._is_gil_enabled() is False. Then benchmark the real workload with 1 thread and N threads (throughput and memory) against GIL 3.14 with multiprocessing.
```

**Decision: No, this study gives you no reason to stop your 16:8 routine.** The evidence behind the "91%" headline is weak, and it does not measure what you are doing.

**Where the number comes from**
- It was an unreviewed AHA conference poster from March 2024, based on about 20,000 US adults in NHANES. People eating within 8 hours had a hazard ratio of 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03) for cardiovascular death. https://www.news-medical.net/news/20240318/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-schedule-may-increase-heart-disease-mortality.aspx
- The peer-reviewed version (*Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome*, 2025) used a different comparison group and reported a hazard ratio of 2.35. All-cause and cancer deaths were not raised. The authors say the result may come from residual confounding. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/

**Why it doesn't apply to you**
- **It didn't measure deliberate fasting.** Each person's "eating window" came from two single-day food recalls. Nobody was asked whether they practise time-restricted eating, so a year of planned 16:8 eating was never studied. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- **The group was tiny and different.** About 414 people (2% of the sample) ate within 8 hours, and 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes. That group smoked more, had more prior disease, and differed in other ways. Illness can also shorten eating windows rather than the other way round. https://peterattiamd.com/time-restricted-eating-and-ascvd/
- **Other cohorts don't confirm it.** A UK cohort found no link between eating window and mortality. https://www.nature.com/articles/s43856-025-01035-x A large French cohort linked a longer overnight fast to lower stroke risk. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10721609/ A second NHANES analysis that also flagged windows of 8 hours or less uses the same data and the same crude measure, so it is not independent support. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40944446/
- **Trials show no harm signal.** Randomised trials are short and only measure risk factors, not deaths. They find little change in blood pressure or LDL. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full
- **Experts dismissed it.** 34 researchers objected to the press release, and a past AHA president attributed the result to who the participants were, not when they ate (TCTMD link above).

**How strong is the evidence?** For harm to someone like you, it is weak: one observational dataset, a poor exposure measure, few deaths, and no all-cause effect. For benefit beyond weight loss, it is also weak. 16:8 is a reasonable weight-control tool, not proven heart protection.

**Not verified:** none of us could read the full 2025 paper, so its exact counts and adjustments are unchecked. They would not change this decision.

**Next check:** none needed.

I found two separate causes that stack on each other. Both are documented by Docker or Microsoft (VS Code docs), and Docker's own docs give a fix for each.

**1. CPU emulation, since the image is forced to amd64 on an Arm Mac**
- Docker's multi-platform build docs say "Emulation with QEMU can be much slower than native builds." The worst cases are CPU-heavy work like compiling and decompressing, which is what npm install does. https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/
- Docker Desktop has a "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon" setting. The current settings docs list its default as **Disabled**, and it only works with the Apple Virtualization framework VMM. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/
- The VMM page says the newer Docker VMM option doesn't support Rosetta, "so amd64 emulation is slow." https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/
- Fixes, in order of value:
  - Build the image natively as arm64 and keep only the one x86-only dependency on amd64, in a separate container or service.
  - Otherwise, turn on Rosetta with the Apple Virtualization framework VMM.

**2. Bind mount I/O, especially node_modules (tens of thousands of small files)**
- The VS Code docs explain that on macOS the containers run in a VM, and bind mounts from the Mac's disk are slower than the container's own filesystem. They recommend a **named volume for node_modules**, or cloning the repo into a container volume, and give a `devcontainer.json` snippet: `"mounts": ["source=${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}-node_modules,target=${containerWorkspaceFolder}/node_modules,type=volume"]`. https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance
- VirtioFS is the default file sharing method on Mac. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/
- Docker's **Synchronized file shares** feature keeps a cache of the host files on an ext4 filesystem inside the VM. It needs Docker Desktop 4.27 or later and a paid Pro, Team or Business plan. Docker says it suits repos with 100,000 or more files. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/
- Docker's blog claims file operations are "2–10x faster" with it. That's Docker's own marketing number, not an independent benchmark. https://www.docker.com/blog/announcing-synchronized-file-shares/
- The memory limit defaults to 50% of host RAM. The settings page lists no default for the CPU limit, so it's worth checking.

**What I couldn't confirm**
- A search snippet attributed to Docker's known-issues page said inotify (file-change notifications) doesn't work under QEMU emulation, which would break dev server hot reload. That text isn't on the current page, so treat it as unconfirmed or outdated. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/troubleshoot-and-support/troubleshoot/known-issues/
- An older GitHub issue reports a Next.js npm build hanging at 100% CPU with Rosetta on, and Docker staff suggested turning Rosetta off as a workaround. It's from around Docker Desktop 4.24/4.25 and may be fixed now. https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384
- I found no official numbers on how much each cause contributes. Emulation could plausibly be the bigger one, but nothing I found measures it. A quick test would separate them:
  - Run `npm install` in a native arm64 container.
  - Run it in the amd64 container with node_modules on a named volume.
- The Rosetta default may vary by Docker Desktop version. The docs say Disabled, but check the actual setting on the machine.

**Recommendation:** use a native arm64 base image with the x86 dependency isolated, put node_modules on a named volume, and turn on Rosetta if any amd64 part has to stay.

**Report: press, forums, issue trackers (9 of 12 lookups used)**

**Findings**

1. **The bind-mounted `node_modules` is the main cause of slow I/O.** Containers on a Mac run inside a Linux VM, and every file operation on a bind mount has to cross the VM boundary. `npm install` and module resolution touch tens of thousands of small files, which is the worst case for this. One 2025 test measured npm install as 3.5× slower on a bind mount than on a named volume. The standard fix is to keep the source as a bind mount and put `node_modules` in a named or anonymous volume, then run `npm install` inside the container. Named volumes live in the VM's own filesystem, so they avoid the crossing.
   - https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem
   - https://eastondev.com/blog/en/posts/dev/20251217-docker-mount-comparison/
   - https://techearl.com/docker-bind-mounts-slow-mac-windows

2. **The file-sharing backend matters, and VirtioFS is the right one.** VirtioFS measured 2–4× faster than gRPC FUSE on Apple Silicon. It is reportedly the default in recent 4.x versions, but the user should check Settings → General.
   - https://www.jeffgeerling.com/blog/2022/new-docker-mac-virtiofs-file-sync-4x-faster/
   - https://dev.to/dkechag/improving-docker-file-performance-on-macos-537k

3. **amd64 emulation adds a CPU penalty that Linux colleagues never pay.** Rosetta went GA in Docker Desktop 4.25 and is on by default on macOS 14.1+. Without it, Docker uses QEMU. Blog figures, which nobody has verified, put QEMU at 5–10× slower and Rosetta at 2–3×. The issue tracker also reports Node and Vite hanging or pinning a CPU under Rosetta, possibly because of AVX handling. Disabling Rosetta avoids the hang but runs slower. One commenter fixed their case by switching to `platform: linux/arm64` with arm64 rollup binaries.
   - https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384
   - https://github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946
   - https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/
   - https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-16-docker-mac-apple-silicon/view

   **Implication:** building the whole image as amd64 for one x86-only dependency puts Node, npm and the dev server under emulation. Options are a native arm64 image that runs only that one dependency as amd64 (a separate service or sidecar), or checking whether an arm64 build of the dependency now exists.

4. **The dev server's file watching can add more cost.** If `CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING` or `WATCHPACK_POLLING` is set, polling a bind mount burns CPU. With VirtioFS, native watch events reportedly work, so polling is unnecessary.
   - https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt.js/issues/27617
   - https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-08-how-to-use-docker-desktop-file-sharing-settings/view

5. **Alternatives:**
   - Docker's Synchronized File Shares (4.27+, paid plans only) keeps a synced ext4 copy of the files inside the VM: https://docs.docker.com/desktop/synchronized-file-sharing
   - Mutagen or Compose `watch`
   - OrbStack, which reports its own yarn install at about 77% of native speed. That is a vendor benchmark.

**What I'm unsure of**
- None of these sources isolates how much of the 5–10× comes from emulation versus file I/O. Testing two things separately would settle it: moving `node_modules` to a volume, and a native arm64 build.
- I don't know if Docker 4.26+ fully fixed the Rosetta/Node hangs. That claim is secondhand.
- I couldn't confirm the exact release where VirtioFS became the default.
- Most speed figures come from blogs or vendors, not controlled benchmarks.

**Report to coordinator: independent measurements, critiques and counter-evidence**

**Findings**

1. **The bind mount alone probably doesn't explain a 5–10× gap.** The best independent benchmark I found is Mainardi's 2025 test (M4 Pro, Docker Desktop 4.37.1, native arm64 images, `npm install`, mean of 3 runs). With the whole project bind-mounted, Docker Desktop VZ+VirtioFS took 9.53s, against 3.37s on the host: about 2.8×. Putting `node_modules` in a named volume brought it to 3.61s. Synchronized file shares (paid) gave 3.88s, and OrbStack with a bind mount gave 4.22s. https://www.paolomainardi.com/posts/docker-performance-macos-2025/
   - Critique: this tests only `npm install`, on one small React app. His Linux comparison box used BTRFS and was slower than the Mac. Sync shares threw "Permission denied" errors on `node_modules` during heavy churn.
2. **x86 emulation probably adds a second multiplier, but measurements vary widely.**
   - VPSMAC (M4): sysbench was 36% slower under Rosetta amd64 than native arm64. https://vpsmac.com/en/blog/docker-on-m4-mac-linux-container-performance-analysis.html
   - Older personal test: Rosetta about 20% slower than native, QEMU about 85% slower. https://patrickwthomas.net/macos-docker/
   - A single-run report shows amd64 about 5–6× slower on a CPU loop. https://github.com/orbstack/orbstack/issues/2744
   - So roughly 1.2–6× from emulation, times about 2.8× from the bind mount, would be consistent with the 5–10× you see. That's my inference, not a measured result.
3. **Rosetta can make things worse, not just slower.** There are reports of amd64 builds hanging or taking hours with "Use Rosetta" on (one: about 33,600s vs 37s) and npm/Next builds pinning one CPU at 100%. Docker staff suspected Rosetta mishandles AVX. https://github.com/docker/for-mac/issues/7075 · https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384 · https://github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946
4. **Possible macOS 27 regression.** One unconfirmed report says amd64/Rosetta got slower after upgrading to macOS 27.0.1, with no maintainer response yet (issue #2744 above). The machine I'm running on reports Darwin 27, so this may apply here.
5. **The dev server has a separate cost.** inotify events don't cross the macOS↔VM boundary reliably, so watchers fall back to polling (`CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING`/`WATCHPACK_POLLING`), which is expensive on bind mounts. https://www.github.com/docker/for-mac/issues/7274 · https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/36774
6. **Docker's "2–10× faster" claim for synchronized file shares is a vendor claim** with no published method; the independent figure is the 3.88s in item 1. https://www.docker.com/blog/announcing-synchronized-file-shares/

**What I'm unsure of**
- I found no rigorous benchmark of Node under Docker Desktop Rosetta vs arm64. The figures above are sysbench runs or anecdotes.
- I can't tell whether this setup is actually using Rosetta or QEMU. Both can be registered in `binfmt_misc`.
- I don't know if the problem dependency could run as a separate amd64 service while the main container runs arm64. That would remove emulation from npm and the dev server.

**Suggested test for the user:** time `npm ci` and a cold dev-server start in four setups (amd64 vs arm64, with and without a named volume for `node_modules`), each with Rosetta on and off. That separates the two causes.

# Why your dev container is slow on the Mac, and what to do

Two separate penalties multiply together. Your Linux colleagues pay neither of them.

**1. CPU emulation: Node and npm run as x86 code on an Arm chip.** Because of `--platform linux/amd64`, everything in the container is emulated, not just the one dependency. With QEMU, Docker says it "can be much slower" for CPU-heavy work like npm installs (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/). With Rosetta the penalty is smaller. Independent tests put it at roughly 20–36% (https://vpsmac.com/en/blog/docker-on-m4-mac-linux-container-performance-analysis.html, https://patrickwthomas.net/macos-docker/). Sources disagree on whether Rosetta is on by default (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/ vs https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/), so check Settings yourself. Rosetta needs the Apple Virtualization framework VMM; Docker VMM doesn't support it (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/). Rosetta has also caused Node builds to hang or pin a CPU (https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384, https://github.com/docker/for-mac/issues/7075). On macOS 27 there is an unconfirmed report that it got slower (https://github.com/orbstack/orbstack/issues/2744).

**No, it isn't safe.** The SQLite docs rule out this setup: WAL mode doesn't work across machines, and even without WAL, SQLite on NFS is a known way to corrupt a database.

**Why WAL fails here**
- The WAL docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." WAL keeps a "wal-index" in shared memory, made by memory-mapping a `-shm` file. "Processes on separate host machines obviously cannot share memory with each other." With three servers, each would have a different view of the WAL, which can lead to stale reads or corruption. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- The only way to run WAL without shared memory is `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, which allows a single process. That defeats the point of sharing the database.

**Why NFS is risky in any mode**
- SQLite depends on file locks and fsync ordering. "Some filesystems contain bugs in their locking logic… This is especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular… database corruption might result." https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- SQLite isn't tested over networks, and use over one is "at the user's risk… Rely upon it at your (and your customers') peril." https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- Rollback-journal mode reduces the risk but doesn't remove it. You also lose concurrent reads during writes, and every lock costs a network round trip.

**Load**
Twenty writes per second is easy for SQLite on a local disk. Over NFS, latency on each lock and sync makes contention and `SQLITE_BUSY` errors more likely. SQLite's guidance is to avoid it "where the same database will be accessed directly… and simultaneously from many computers over a network." It also says a site busy enough to need several servers should consider a client/server database. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

**What to do instead (best first)**
1. **Use PostgreSQL or MySQL.** This is the standard fix for several app servers sharing one database, and the SQLite docs recommend it.
2. **Run a single database owner.** Keep SQLite in WAL mode on local disk on one host, and have the other servers send requests to it through a small API or proxy. This is the pattern useovernet.html suggests. The trade-off is that the host becomes a single point of failure.
3. **Use a replicated SQLite system** such as rqlite, LiteFS or Turso/libSQL, if you want to stay with SQLite. I didn't research these within this budget, so check them yourself.

If you ignore this advice anyway, at least use rollback mode, not WAL, plus backups and regular `PRAGMA integrity_check` runs. Corruption is still possible.

Sources:
- https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html

# Unsafe code on crates.io: the figure to cite

**Cite: about 19% of crates.io crates directly contain `unsafe` code** (Rust Foundation, May 2024). Present it as "roughly one in five," not as a precise value. Confidence is moderate for the ~20% range and low for anything more exact.

## Main source

**Rust Foundation, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild," 21 May 2024.** It reports that 24,362 of about 127,000 crates "with significant code" use the `unsafe` keyword, stated as 19.11%. It also reports that 34.35% of crates make a direct call into a crate that uses `unsafe`.
https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/
The researchers also gave a `/news/` path for this post; check which URL resolves before publishing.

Auditors are likely to raise these points:
- **Undefined denominator.** "Significant code" is never defined, and about 18,000 of roughly 145,000 crates were excluded.
- **Arithmetic doesn't match.** 24,362 / 127,000 = 19.18%, not 19.11%, so the published denominator is rounded.
- **Not reproducible.** No dataset or method has been published, only the tool: https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter
- **Not peer-reviewed, and about 2.5 years old.** I found no census from 2025 or 2026.

## Independent check

**Cui, Sun, Xu & Zhou, ICSE 2024.** They found 21,506 of 103,516 crates using `unsafe` (snapshot 2023-01-30), which is about 20.8%. This was measured with a source-level scan, which is a different method from the Foundation's.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04785
Another researcher found the same numbers in a later preprint by the same group (https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06251v1). Confirm the count appears in the ICSE version before citing it as peer-reviewed.

**Older context (2020):** Evans et al., ICSE 2020, report `unsafe` in "less than 30%" of libraries.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752

## Two warnings for a supply-chain assessment

1. **Direct use understates exposure.** About 34% of crates call directly into unsafe-using crates. Evans et al. found that more than half of libraries can't be fully checked by the compiler once dependencies are counted. Popular crates use `unsafe` much more often than the registry as a whole. State clearly whether your figure means direct use or dependency exposure.
2. **`unsafe` does not mean vulnerable.** Most uses are FFI (calls into C/C++) or SIMD, and the Foundation says so itself.

Don't cite the apparent decline from 29% to 19% as a trend. The studies use different methods and different sets of crates.

**Suggested wording:** "Approximately 19–21% of crates.io crates directly use `unsafe` (Rust Foundation, 2024; Cui et al., ICSE 2024). A larger share, over a third, depends directly on crates that do."

**Short answer: no, it isn't safe.** SQLite's own documentation says WAL mode cannot work across hosts, and it warns separately that SQLite on NFS risks corruption.

**Findings:**

1. **WAL doesn't work over a network filesystem.** The WAL page says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." The reason is that WAL keeps a shared-memory index (the `-shm` file, accessed with mmap), and processes on different machines can't share memory. This alone rules out the plan as proposed. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html (sections 1 and 2.2)

2. **The FAQ names NFS directly.** "fcntl() file locking is broken on many NFS implementations. You should avoid putting SQLite database files on NFS if multiple processes might try to access the file at the same time." https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html (Q5)

3. **The corruption guide names NFS too.** Buggy locking is "especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular… database corruption might result." It also warns that connections using different locking protocols can't see each other's locks. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html (sections 2.1 and 2.4)

4. **The network-use page** says SQLite "is not tested in across-a-network scenarios… use of a remote database is done at the user's risk." For clients on several machines it offers three options:
   - (a) a client/server database such as PostgreSQL;
   - (b) WAL mode with all reads and writes on the machine that holds the file, behind a proxy that relays requests from the other servers;
   - (c) rollback-journal mode, which allows many readers or one writer, never both at once. It still depends on network locks working correctly.

   https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html

5. **The "when to use" page** advises avoiding a database "accessed directly… and simultaneously from many computers over a network." It adds that for a site "so busy that it requires multiple servers, consider… client/server." https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

6. **The Linux NFS man page** says NFS "is not designed to support true cluster file system cache coherence." Clients only get close-to-open consistency, which can leave them reading stale cached data. NFSv4 does build locking into the protocol, but the page says nothing about whether mmap is coherent across clients. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html

**What I'm unsure of:**
- I couldn't tell from these sources what actually happens when WAL is turned on over NFSv4 from several clients. It might fail outright, or it might seem to work and quietly corrupt data. The docs only say it "does not work." That would need testing, or a look at what other researchers find.
- I don't know whether NFSv4's built-in locking is reliable enough for rollback mode (option c) on the user's particular server. The docs say reliability "var[ies] among implementations and installations."
- I found no official guidance on throughput. 20 writes/sec is low for SQLite on local disk, but round trips over NFS could add a lot of latency to every transaction and lock.
- I didn't check replication tools like LiteFS or rqlite, or SQLite's own server-based projects. Those aren't part of the core SQLite documentation.

**Bottom line:** Don't put a WAL-mode SQLite database on NFS with writers on three hosts. The options SQLite's docs back are PostgreSQL (or another client/server database), or a single host that owns the SQLite file with the other servers sending requests to it.
