5. **User reports.** On the sqlite-users list, one user reported corruption on NFS with only a single process accessing the file: https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg29235.html. Another thread argues there's no hope of safety on NFS older than v4, and that problems can appear when NFS client daemons restart: https://lists.fedoraproject.org/pipermail/devel/2007-October/111891.html. Xojo forum users say concurrent multi-user writes over a share eventually corrupt the database: https://forum.xojo.com/t/multi-user-access-to-sqlite-on-network-drive/18271?page=2. Storj's FAQ says NFS and SMB are incompatible with SQLite: https://storj.dev/node/faq/how-to-fix-a-database-disk-image-is-malformed

6. **Performance.** A SQLite forum post reports Fossil running 10–15x slower over NFS because of locking. That matters at 20 writes/s from three hosts. Source: https://sqlite.org/forum/info/2fda3a1987ae6f60be177d070e2f0bc07bdd91071022edf4ce3cc8beda8a6d27?t=c

**Where I'm unsure**
- Nobody has published a test of rollback-journal mode on Linux NFSv4 with three writers. Its safety depends on the server and on mount options such as `lock`/`nolock` and attribute caching. I found no source that says it is safe.
- I couldn't read the Red Hat solution note (https://access.redhat.com/solutions/120733) because it's paywalled. The search snippet mentions `nolock`, which would be dangerous here, so please don't rely on it.
- Some sources are weak: the OneUptime and macmyths blogs are secondary and I only saw them in search results, and many forum posts are old (2007–2008). The GitHub corruption reports I found (diskcache #345, Optuna) never confirmed NFS as the cause.

**Suggestion for the coordinator:** Use Postgres or MySQL. If SQLite is a requirement, give one host ownership of the file and have the others send writes to it, or look at rqlite or LiteFS. Other researchers should check those last two.

**Report to coordinator (angle: independent measurements, critiques and counter-evidence)**

**Short answer: no. WAL mode on a shared NFS mount, with writes coming from three hosts, is a configuration SQLite says does not work. A rollback journal over NFS is still a risk that SQLite does not test.**

**Findings**

1. **WAL does not work across hosts.** SQLite's WAL docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." The reason is that the wal-index is shared memory, an mmapped `-shm` file, and processes on different machines cannot share it. This is how the design works, not an occasional bug. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
2. **SQLite's guidance on network use** says network filesystems "do not support the ability to do simultaneous reads and writes while at the same time keeping the database consistent." SQLite is "not tested in across-a-network scenarios," and failures are "not frequent or repeatable," so a passing test proves little. It recommends three options: (1) a client/server database such as PostgreSQL, (2) WAL on one host behind a proxy, or (3) rollback mode, accepted at your own risk. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
3. **Locking bugs:** "some filesystems contain bugs in their locking logic… This is especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular." Version 3.51.0 (Nov 2025) added more defenses for WAL with multiple processes, but the docs say they are "not a cure-all." https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
4. **An independent vendor hit the same problem.** OpenAI's Codex docs say Linux hosts sharing a home over NFS "can corrupt a SQLite database if they open it in WAL mode at the same time." On NFS, Codex now forces DELETE (rollback) journal mode instead. https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/network-file-systems
5. **Older technical critique (2008):** Brian Smith argued that because SQLite's fcntl locks are only a convention, NFS cache coherency is not guaranteed and "it is never safe to use SQLite on NFS in a read-write situation." This is old, and NFSv4 clients have improved since. https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg31765.html
6. **Someone who tried to make it work:** a user on AWS EFS (NFS) wanting several hosts to share one database was warned off by forum regulars. They then tried GFS2 and OCFS2: GFS2 didn't work and OCFS2 hung the servers. They were considering RDS. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/89c52cdf66?t=h&hist
7. **Counter-evidence (anecdotal):** one forum poster runs "countless SQLite databases hosted on nfs" over NFSv4, with up to a dozen readers and writers on different machines, and reports "very few problems." They don't say which journal mode they use, give failure rates, or say how they check for corruption. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/341635c1ffeb30fc?raw

**What I'm unsure of**
- I found no controlled study or measured corruption rate for multi-host SQLite on NFSv4. All the evidence is design reasoning, vendor docs and anecdotes.
- I couldn't tell whether 20 writes/s in rollback mode over NFSv4 would perform acceptably. The forum poster mentions limits on concurrency, and each commit takes an exclusive lock over the network.
- I couldn't confirm which NFS server and client versions, or which mount options (e.g. `nocto`, `local_lock`), make fcntl locking reliable. The setup would need its own cross-host lock and fault-injection tests.
- Several search hits were low-quality SEO or AI-generated blogs, and I left them out.

**Bottom line from my angle:** WAL in this setup is disqualified. Rollback mode is possible but untested by SQLite and relies on correct NFS locking. The independent sources favor PostgreSQL, or a single SQLite host that the other servers reach through a service.

answer.text:
# No. It isn't safe as planned, and WAL makes it worse.

**WAL mode cannot work across hosts.** SQLite's documentation says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." WAL keeps its index in a memory-mapped `-shm` file, and processes on three different servers can't share that memory. This is how WAL is designed, so mount tuning won't fix it. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

**NFS locking itself is a known source of corruption.** SQLite warns that fcntl locking "is broken on many NFS implementations" and that NFS locking bugs can corrupt the database. https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html (Q5), https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html. The Linux NFS man page adds that NFS gives only close-to-open consistency, not cluster-level cache coherence. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html

**This has happened in production.** OpenAI's Codex docs report that WAL over shared NFS corrupted SQLite databases. Codex now detects NFS and forces rollback-journal mode. https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/environments/network-file-systems (our researchers found this page at two slightly different paths). GoToSocial refuses to support SQLite on networked storage for the same reason. https://docs.gotosocial.org/en/latest/advanced/sqlite-networked-storage/

**Rollback-journal mode isn't a safe fallback.** It only allows many readers or one writer at a time. SQLite doesn't test it across a network, and its safety depends entirely on your NFS server getting locking right. Failures are "not frequent or repeatable," so passing tests prove little. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html. Every lock also costs a network round trip. One report measured a 10–15x slowdown over NFS. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/c04bf5be0e. Some people say they run SQLite on NFSv4 with "very few problems," but they don't report journal mode or how they check for corruption. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/341635c1ffeb30fc?raw

**What to do instead**, in order of preference:

1. **Use PostgreSQL or MySQL.** SQLite itself recommends a client/server database for multi-server sites. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html. 20 writes/s is trivial for either.
2. **Keep SQLite on one host's local disk** in WAL mode, and have the other two servers send reads and writes to it through a small service. SQLite endorses this setup. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
3. **Look at rqlite or LiteFS** if you want SQLite with replication. Our researchers didn't evaluate these, so check them yourself.

Whatever you choose, don't put the database on NFS with writers on three hosts.

**Decision: cite "about one in five crates on crates.io (19–21%) contain `unsafe` code directly."** Two independent registry-wide counts support it:

- **19.11%**, from the Rust Foundation (May 2024): 24,362 of about 127,000 crates "with significant code".
- **20.8%**, from Cui et al., ICSE 2024, peer-reviewed: 21,506 of 103,516 crates, snapshot 2023-01-30.

Different teams using different methods (compiled call-graph analysis versus source scanning) landed within two points of each other. You can be confident in the ~20% range. Don't present the second decimal place as reproducible.

For supply-chain exposure, also cite the Foundation's second figure: **a further 34.35% of crates directly call into a crate that uses `unsafe`.** The direct-use share understates dependency risk.

When you cite these figures, state the following up front so auditors don't find it themselves:
- "Significant code" is undefined. About 18,000 crates were excluded from the denominator.
- 24,362 / 127,000 = 19.18%, so the published denominator is rounded.
- The Foundation's data and queries are unpublished (the Painter tool is public, but no results are), and its figure comes from a blog post, not peer review.
- Cui et al. include 3,614 yanked crates. Excluding them gives about 21.5%.
- The data is from 2023–24. No 2025–26 census exists. The share has been falling as the registry grows.
- `unsafe` is not the same as vulnerable. Much of it is FFI or SIMD.

Don't cite the 2020 figures (Evans ~29%, Astrauskas ~25%). Nobody read them in the primary papers, and they would add nothing auditors can check.

```text
Decision: Cite ~20% (19.11% Rust Foundation 2024; 20.8% Cui et al. ICSE 2024), plus 34.35% via direct dependency calls
Rests on: Two independent whole-registry measurements of crates.io, agreeing within 2 points
Not verified: Nothing that would change the decision. No count newer than May 2024 exists.
Next check: None needed. Before submitting, open the Foundation URL below; one researcher reached it at /news/ instead of /media/.
```

**Sources**
- Rust Foundation, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild" (2024): https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/
- Painter tool: https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter
- Cui et al., ICSE 2024: https://arxiv.org/html/2308.04785 · https://conf.researchr.org/details/icse-2024/icse-2024-research-track/136/Is-unsafe-an-Achilles-Heel-A-Comprehensive-Study-of-Safety-Requirements-in-Unsafe-R

```text
Decision: Don't put the SQLite database on the NFS mount with all three
servers writing to it. Use PostgreSQL (or another client/server database).
If you must keep SQLite, have one server own the file on its local disk
and let the other two send their reads and writes to it through a service.

Rests on: WAL mode cannot work across hosts. SQLite's own docs say so.
The WAL index is a shared-memory (-shm, mmapped) file, and processes on
different machines cannot share memory. This is how WAL is designed, so
it is not a bug a test could rule out. OpenAI's Codex team saw corruption
in production when Linux hosts opened the same SQLite file in WAL mode
over NFS, and Codex now forces rollback mode on NFS. SQLite's network
guidance lists only two supported paths: client/server, or a single host
behind a proxy.

Not verified: whether rollback-journal mode would be safe and fast
enough on your NFSv4 server. SQLite doesn't test it, it depends on fcntl
locking being correct, and it adds a network round trip to every lock.
Forum reports say it runs 10–15x slower. Nobody tested it on your setup,
but it doesn't change the decision. It is only a fallback, and it is
still at your own risk.

Next check: none needed.
```

At 20 writes/s, a single Postgres instance, or one SQLite owner with a small write API, is well within capacity.

**Sources**
- SQLite WAL docs, "does not work over a network filesystem": https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- SQLite on network use, the three options: https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- SQLite FAQ Q5, NFS locking: https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html
- How to corrupt SQLite, NFS locking bugs: https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- When to use SQLite, many hosts means client/server: https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
- Codex NFS corruption and forced rollback mode: https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/environments/network-file-systems
- Linux NFS man page, no cluster cache coherence: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html
- SQLite forum on EFS/NFSv4, lock round-trip cost: https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/c04bf5be0e
- Fossil 10–15x slower over NFS: https://sqlite.org/forum/info/2fda3a1987ae6f60be177d070e2f0bc07bdd91071022edf4ce3cc8beda8a6d27?t=c
- GoToSocial, same conclusion: https://docs.gotosocial.org/en/latest/advanced/sqlite-networked-storage/

Probably not. The claim comes from one observational study with serious flaws, and it doesn't show that your 16:8 routine is dangerous.

**Where "91%" comes from**
- It was a March 2024 American Heart Association conference abstract based on US national survey data (NHANES), covering about 20,000 adults followed for a median of 8 years. People whose recorded eating fit in under 8 hours had a 91% higher rate of cardiovascular death than those eating over 12–16 hours. It was promoted with a press release before any peer review ([NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/heart-health/intermittent-fasting-risk-cardiovascular-death-rcna143853), [Smithsonian](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/intermittent-fasting-linked-to-higher-risk-of-death-from-heart-disease-preliminary-study-finds-180983993/)).
- A version was published in 2025 in *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome*. It reports a hazard ratio of 2.35 for cardiovascular death and no link to death from all causes or cancer ([Medical Dialogues](https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915)).

**Why the evidence is weak**
- **It doesn't measure fasting habits.** Eating windows came from just two days of food recall, which were assumed to hold for years. A short window on two days isn't a deliberate, consistent routine like yours.
- **The group was small.** About 2% of participants were in it (roughly 414 people), so a chance result is more likely.
- **The groups weren't comparable.** The short-window group had about 60% more smokers, and sleep, shift work and diet quality weren't properly accounted for.
- The lead author says the study shows a link, not that eating windows cause heart deaths. 34 researchers in the field publicly criticized how it was promoted ([expert letter](https://blog.mycircadianclock.org/?p=13102), [Becker's](https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/cardiology/experts-cast-doubt-on-link-between-intermittent-fasting-heart-disease)).
- Another analysis of the same survey data found the lowest death risk at 11–12 hours of eating per day ([News-Medical](https://www.news-medical.net/news/20250915/Daily-meal-timing-influences-longevity-risk-in-adults-study-reveals.aspx)). These datasets give conflicting signals.

**What trials show**
- Randomized trials find time-restricted eating safe in the short term, with weight loss about equal to ordinary calorie cutting ([2025 meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12479299/)).
- Long-term outcomes like heart attacks and deaths haven't been tested. Researchers raise possible concerns about muscle loss and late eating ([Frontiers 2025](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1524125/full)).

**What this means for you**
- If 16:8 keeps your weight under control, this study isn't a good reason to stop. It's a low-quality warning sign, not proof of harm.
- To be careful:
  - Eat earlier in the day rather than late.
  - Get enough protein and do strength training to protect muscle.
  - Eat good-quality food and don't smoke.
  - Check your blood pressure, lipids and glucose with your doctor.
- Your weight control matters more than the exact window. Widening to 10 hours would cost you little if that helps you worry less.

This is general information, not medical advice.

**Report to coordinator: official and primary sources**

**What the official investigations agree on**

1. **ENTSO-E Expert Panel final report, 20 March 2026.** No single cause. The panel names "oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive power control, differences in voltage regulation practices, rapid output reductions and generator disconnections in Spain, and uneven stabilisation capabilities." Together these led to "fast voltage increases and cascading generation disconnections," meaning an overvoltage collapse.
   - Press release: https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/
   - Report page: https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/ (the factual report of 3 October 2025 is also here)

2. **Spanish government Committee report, 17 June 2025.** The origin was "multifactorial," with three elements:
   - **Weak voltage control.** Too little dynamic voltage control capacity: only 10 synchronous plants able to regulate voltage were scheduled, the lowest of the year. Some plants paid to regulate voltage did not respond properly, and one produced reactive power when it should have absorbed it.
   - **Oscillations.** A 0.6 Hz oscillation at 12:03 started at one installation on the peninsula. A 0.2 Hz inter-area oscillation followed at 12:19. The operator's damping measures raised voltage.
   - **Disconnections.** Generators tripped between 12:32:57 and 12:33:18, and some appear to have tripped before the regulatory 380–435 kV limits were reached.
   - A cyberattack was ruled out.
   - Sources: https://www.miteco.gob.es/en/prensa/ultimas-noticias/2025/junio/se-presenta-el-informe-del-comite-de-analisis-de-la-crisis-elect.html and the full non-confidential report: https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/consejodeministros/resumenes/Documents/2025/Informe-no-confidencial-Comite-de-analisis-28A.pdf

3. **CNMC (Spanish regulator).** It also found a "multifactorial" origin ending in an overvoltage collapse. On 17 April 2026 it opened about 20 sanction proceedings: one "very serious" against Red Eléctrica (REE) as system operator, and serious ones against Iberdrola, Endesa, Naturgy, Repsol and others. It opened 15 more on 24 April 2026. The CNMC says these suspected breaches do **not by themselves constitute the cause** of the blackout, and the proceedings do not prejudge the outcome. They last 9–18 months, so they are still open.
   - https://www.cnmc.es/prensa/incoacion-incidente-electrico-28A-20260417
   - https://www.cnmc.es/prensa/incoaciones-incidente-electrico-28A-2
   - Recommendations report, 19 March 2026: https://www.cnmc.es/prensa/informe-incidente-electrico-20260319

4. **ERSE (Portuguese regulator), May 2026.** Classed the blackout as an "exceptional event" that started in Spain. It found Portugal's TSO (REN) acted diligently during restoration. https://www.erse.pt/communication/press-releases/erse-classifica-apagao-iberico-de-28-de-abril-de-2025-como-evento-excecional/

**What is still contested**

- **Who is responsible.** REE's June 2025 report blames generators for not meeting voltage control obligations under P.O. 7.4. The utilities' association Aelec blames REE's scheduling. REE says the CNMC proceedings do not show its conduct caused the blackout. Sources: https://www.ree.es/sites/default/files/2025-06/NP_RedElectrica_InformeOS_180625.pdf (I could not extract its text), https://www.vozpopuli.com/economia/energia/las-electricas-denuncian-que-redeia-provoco-el-apagon-al-programar-mal-la-energia.html
- **Which plant caused the 0.6 Hz oscillation, and how much it mattered.** Neither the government nor the ENTSO-E press release names the source plant. The exact causal role of the oscillations is unclear.
- **Some trips are unexplained.** Data gaps stopped the panel from finding the cause of some disconnections. Some owners did not record trip events.
- **Renewables and inertia.** ENTSO-E officials say voltage control, not renewables, was the problem, and low inertia is not treated as a root cause. Public debate continues.

**What I'm unsure of**

- I could not parse the ENTSO-E final report PDF or the briefing slides. Some details come from a secondary summary, not the report: the 0.63 Hz figure, missing or poorly tuned stabilisers, renewables held at a fixed power factor, and synchronous units missing reactive power targets in 75% or more of hourly samples. Summary: https://sciencemediacentre.es/en/final-blackout-report-european-operators-confirms-event-was-caused-multiple-factors-recommends
- The number of recommendations (21 or 22) and the page count (440 or 472) conflict between secondary sources.
- Check all of the above against Chapters 4 and 9 of the ENTSO-E final report before quoting.

**Report to coordinator (angle: press, forums, issue trackers)**

**What is established**
1. **ENTSO-E Expert Panel final report (20 Mar 2026, 472 pp.).** It finds no single cause. The blackout was an overvoltage cascade: a plant tripped on overvoltage, which removed reactive absorption, which pushed voltage higher and tripped more plants. Press accounts of the report give this sequence:
   - 12:03–12:08 CEST: a 0.63 Hz forced oscillation driven by converters in southern Spain.
   - 12:19–12:22: the 0.2 Hz inter-area mode. Damping it (less export, lines reconnected) raised voltages.
   - From 12:32:57: Granada transformer (355 MW), Badajoz (727 MW), then about 928 MW of wind and solar. Over 2.5 GW was lost in about 78 s, the system lost synchronism at 12:33:19, and the last tie to France, the HVDC link, opened at 12:33:24.
   - Contributing factors: too little or too slow reactive power control; synchronous units meeting their reactive set points less than 75% of the time; shunt reactors switched by hand; renewables in fixed power-factor mode; protection settings below grid-code limits; Spain allowing up to 435 kV; defence plans built for frequency events, not overvoltage.
   - The panel says the oscillations "did not directly cause" the blackout.

   Sources: https://www.powermag.com/anatomy-of-a-blackout-findings-from-the-spain-portugal-grid-collapse-final-report/ ; https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/03/23/entso-e-report-finds-systemic-failures-behind-2025-iberian-blackout/ ; ENTSO-E press deck: https://eepublicdownloads.blob.core.windows.net/public-cdn-container/clean-documents/Publications/2025/iberian-blackout/260318_Final%20report_press%20briefing%20PPT_Final.pdf
2. **Spanish Government committee (17 Jun 2025).** It found a multifactorial overvoltage event and ruled out a cyberattack. It blamed both REE (not enough voltage control scheduled) and generators (did not absorb reactive power, or tripped "apparently unduly"). https://www.elsaltodiario.com/energia/informe-apagon-senala-red-electrica-empresas-culpables
3. **Portugal (ERSE, 26 May 2026).** ERSE classed it as an "exceptional event", so customers get no automatic compensation. It says REN acted correctly during restoration. https://www.erse.pt/communication/press-releases/erse-classifica-apagao-iberico-de-28-de-abril-de-2025-como-evento-excecional/

**What is contested**
- **Who is to blame.** REE's own report says generators breached the voltage-control rules (P.O. 7.4) and that the blackout would not have happened otherwise. It says the ENTSO-E report shows "no cause attributable" to REE. The utilities' association Aelec, in a study by Compass Lexecon and INESC TEC, says REE scheduled too little voltage control and had warnings, for example on 22 Apr. https://www.energias-renovables.com/panorama/demoledor-informe-de-ree-20250621 ; https://www.vozpopuli.com/economia/energia/las-electricas-denuncian-que-redeia-provoco-el-apagon-al-programar-mal-la-energia.html ; https://forbes.es/economia/893544/ree-considera-que-el-informe-de-los-expertos-europeos-ratifica-que-no-fue-responsable-del-apagon/
- **Whether the ENTSO-E report is reliable.** Aelec cites "imprecisions or omissions" in it. Endesa's CEO alleged a conflict of interest because REE sat on the panel, and threatened legal action (≈20 Apr 2026). https://forbes.es/economia/813220/las-electricas-preocupadas-ante-las-imprecisiones-u-omisiones-detectadas-en-el-informe-de-entso-e/ ; https://www.energias-renovables.com/panorama/endesa-denuncia-carencias-en-el-informe-europeo-20260421
- **Regulator and courts.** On 17 Apr 2026 the CNMC (Spain's energy regulator) opened a "very serious" case against REE and cases against Almaraz-Trillo, Iberdrola, Endesa, Naturgy and others. It says opening a case "does not by itself attribute cause". REE asked for its case to be closed. Iberdrola has sued Redeia for unfair competition. The Senate committee, controlled by the PP, blames the Government, REE and the CNMC. https://www.elespanol.com/invertia/empresas/energia/20260417/competencia-abre-varios-expedientes-sancionadores-apagon/1003744210707_0.html ; https://rtvc.es/un-ano-del-historico-apagon-28-abril-2026/

**What I'm unsure of**
- I could not open the ENTSO-E primary report. The timestamps and MW figures above come from press summaries and need checking against the report.
- I found no CNMC rulings dated after May 2026.
- The press does not name the plant behind the 0.63 Hz oscillation. REE says an internal control fault at one plant is "probable"; this is unverified.
- The ENTSO-E report leaves some things unexplained, which is useful to flag in the brief: about 208 MW of distributed generation that tripped "for unknown reasons", and rooftop PV that the TSO could not see.
- Media disagree on how many CNMC cases there are (19, 35 or about 50).
- I found no useful forum or issue-tracker material. Everything above is from press and trade media.

Searching is done (12 calls). Here is the report to the coordinator.

## Angle: independent measurements, critiques and counter-evidence

**Official findings and their limits**
- **ENTSO-E's Expert Panel final report (20 Mar 2026, about 470 pp.)** finds no single cause. It names "systemic failures in voltage control, reactive power management, and regulatory frameworks," with responsibility spread across Red Eléctrica (REE), conventional and renewable generators, and the regulatory framework.
  - Some conventional units delivered less than 75% of the reactive power REE requested.
  - Many renewable plants ran fixed power factor, and some had overvoltage protection set below the regulatory limits.
  - Sequence: 727 MW tripped in Badajoz by 12:33:16, then 928 MW more within two seconds, voltages above 435 kV, and loss of synchronism at 12:33:19.
  - The report says data gaps (no fault records from some owners, no data on generators under 1 MW) **meant it could not find the cause of some disconnections**. It calls itself "not an attribution of liability." https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/03/23/entso-e-report-finds-systemic-failures-behind-2025-iberian-blackout/
- **Oscillations:** ENTSO-E found a forced local 0.64 Hz oscillation, plus a 0.21 Hz inter-area mode. They did not directly cause the blackout, but the steps taken to damp them raised voltage. Limited PMU coverage meant the minutes before the collapse could not be fully reconstructed. https://www.powermag.com/anatomy-of-a-blackout-findings-from-the-spain-portugal-grid-collapse-final-report/ ; https://www.erse.pt/communication/press-releases/investigation-by-the-entso-e-expert-group-into-the-iberian-blackout-of-28-april-2025-assessment-of-the-investigation-following-the-meeting-on-15-july-2025/

- **Spanish government committee (17 June 2025):** the cause was a cascade of overvoltage, because the system did not have enough voltage-control capacity. Three points:

**Report to coordinator: primary and official sources**

**Findings**

1. **Where the headline comes from.** The "91%" figure is from an American Heart Association (AHA) press release about a conference poster (Abstract P192, EPI|Lifestyle, March 2024). The study used about 20,000 US adults from the NHANES survey (2003–2018), with a median follow-up of 8 years. People eating within a window of **less than 8 hours** had HR 1.91 for cardiovascular death compared with those eating across 12–16 hours. There was **no link with death from all causes or from cancer**. The release says the results were preliminary and not peer-reviewed. The senior author, Victor Zhong, is quoted saying it "does not mean that time-restricted eating caused cardiovascular death." Limitations it lists: eating windows came from only **two days of self-reported food recall**, and diet quality wasn't reported. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death
2. **How small the exposed group was.** Only **414 people (about 2%)** were in the under-8-hour group, with **31 cardiovascular deaths**. That group had more smokers, higher BMI and a different racial mix. AHA-affiliated cardiologists Lloyd-Jones and Taub called the result confounded and "not ready for prime-time." A letter signed by 34 researchers criticised the press release. Zhong said the result needs replication and that no dietary advice should rest on this study alone. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
3. **The peer-reviewed version.** It was later published as Chen…Zhong, *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome* 2025, DOI 10.1016/j.dsx.2025.103278. Secondary coverage says it reports **HR 2.35** (a "135% higher" risk) against a 12–14 hour reference, and again finds no link with all-cause or cancer death. https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915
4. **Randomized trials of time-restricted eating.** These measure risk factors only, not deaths. A meta-analysis of 11 trials (653 participants) without calorie restriction found it lowered blood pressure and improved glucose, with no effect on lipids: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12672340/. A meta-analysis of 8 trials (579 participants) combining it with calorie restriction found less weight and fat loss than diet alone, but said long-term heart effects are unknown: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10630127/. No randomized trial has looked at cardiovascular deaths.

**Assessment from this angle:** the evidence for the claim is weak. It is one observational study that can't show cause, with very few deaths in the exposed group, eating habits measured from two days of recall, and likely confounding. The authors themselves say it shouldn't guide advice. "Under 8 hours" on two recall days, often probably from irregular schedules or skipped meals, is not the same as a planned 16:8 routine. For a healthy 45-year-old, this doesn't establish a reason to stop. Diet quality, lipids and blood pressure are better things to check.

**What I'm unsure of**
- I couldn't open the published paper (ScienceDirect returned 403 and PubMed needed cookies). So I haven't checked the HR 2.35 confidence interval, the covariates adjusted for, or the group sizes myself. Those figures come from secondary coverage.
- I believe Liu et al., NEJM 2022 found time-restricted eating plus calorie restriction no better than calorie restriction alone, but that is from memory. My search didn't confirm it.
- I didn't find whether replication cohorts or an AHA scientific statement have appeared since 2025. A U-shaped NHANES result (lowest risk at about 11–12 hours) exists, but I didn't confirm its authors: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12763438/

**What the claim is**

2. Only **414 of 20,078** people were in the under-8-hour group, about 2%. The whole cohort had 840 cardiovascular deaths. I couldn't find how many of those were in the 414 group. https://mdlinx.com/article/could-intermittent-fasting-lead-to-a-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death-recent-research-suggests-so/6qjE2w4ivtLdgy62kbUlva

- The PubMed pages wouldn't load, so the 2025 figures (HR 2.35, 12–14 h reference) come from secondary coverage.

**Findings**

1. **Where the number comes from.** It began as an American Heart Association conference poster in 2024 (Zhong et al.) using NHANES, a US national survey: 20,078 adults followed for a median of 8 years. People eating within 8 hours or less had a hazard ratio of 1.91 for cardiovascular death (95% CI 1.20–3.03). There was no link to all-cause or cancer death. Only 414 people (about 2%) were in that group, and 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality

3. **Main criticisms:**

   - Reverse causation is likely: illness reduces appetite and leads to skipped meals.
   - Donald Lloyd-Jones, a past AHA president, called the result "not ready for prime-time." Pam Taub called the press coverage "absurd."
   - 34 researchers who study time-restricted eating (TRE) wrote to the AHA objecting to the press release.

   Sources: TCTMD link above; https://www.mdedge.com/content/intermittent-fasting-linked-higher-cvd-death-risk
4. **Partial replication in the same data.** An *Aging Cell* 2025 paper (33,052 NHANES adults, 1,277 cardiovascular deaths) found a U-shaped curve with the lowest risk at 11–12 hours. Windows of 8 hours or less were linked to at least 30% higher all-cause mortality and over 50% higher cardiovascular mortality, mainly in older adults, men and White participants. It has the same measurement and confounding problems and isn't an independent dataset. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40944446/
5. **Randomized trials of TRE.** None measure deaths. A 2025 meta-analysis (22 trials, 1,004 people) found modest drops in weight and fasting glucose, higher HDL, and no significant change in blood pressure or LDL. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9644535/

**What I'm unsure of**

- I couldn't read either full paper. I don't have the confidence interval for the published HR 2.35 or the cardiovascular hazard ratios from the *Aging Cell* study.
- I found no letter to the editor responding to the 2025 journal paper.
- No randomized trial with hard outcomes like heart attacks or deaths exists, so a small real harm can't be ruled out.
- The deliberate-practice point: none of these studies separate people who fast on purpose from people who eat little because they're ill or poor.

**For the coordinator's synthesis:** the evidence is weak (an association, not causation). Reasonable steps for this person are to check whether the 16:8 window is actually helping their weight, keep protein intake adequate, and get standard checks of blood pressure and lipids.

# Should you stop 16:8 over the "91% higher heart death" headline?

**Short answer:** No, not on the strength of this evidence. It is a weak observational signal, not a demonstrated risk. It is still a reasonable prompt to check that 16:8 is actually helping you.

## Where the 91% comes from

The figure comes from a 2024 American Heart Association conference poster. It was not peer-reviewed at the time. The study used NHANES, a US survey of about 20,000 adults followed for a median of 8 years.

- People eating within a window of **under 8 hours** had HR 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03) for cardiovascular death, compared with a 12–16 hour window.
- There was no link with all-cause or cancer death.
- The senior author said the study does not show that time-restricted eating caused the deaths.

https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death

A peer-reviewed version appeared in 2025 (Chen et al., *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome*), reporting HR 2.35 against a 12–14 hour window. I'm relying on secondary coverage for that figure: https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915

## Why the evidence is weak

- **Small group:** only 414 people (about 2%) were in the short-window group, with 31 cardiovascular deaths. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- **Thin measurement:** eating windows came from two days of food recall, then were assumed to hold for years.
- **Confounding:** the short-window group had more smokers and higher BMI.
- **Reverse causation:** illness or poverty can make people eat less. That is not the same as choosing 16:8.
- **Expert pushback:** a former AHA president called the result "not ready for prime-time," and 34 researchers objected to the press release. Spiegelhalter said it shouldn't have been publicised. https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/

A second NHANES analysis found a U-shaped curve, with the lowest risk at 11–12 hours. Its cardiovascular signal was mainly in older adults and was not significant in younger adults after full adjustment. It uses the same data and has the same flaws. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40944446/

No randomized trial has measured deaths, so a small real harm can't be fully ruled out.

## What's worth doing instead

- **Check it's working.** In one 16:8 trial, weight loss was no better than control, and much of the weight lost was muscle. Eat enough protein and do resistance training. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32986097/
- **Get routine checks** of blood pressure and lipids. Trials show modest effects of time-restricted eating on risk factors, not on outcomes. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full
- **Consider a gentler window** of around 10–12 hours if it suits you as well. Shorter isn't proven better.

**No, this headline gives you no reason to stop.** The evidence behind it is weak: one observational signal that can't show cause, and it was measured in people who are not like you.

**Where "91%" comes from**
- It started as a 2024 American Heart Association conference poster, released before peer review. The study used about 20,000 US adults from the NHANES survey. Those eating within a window under 8 hours had a hazard ratio of 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03) for cardiovascular death. There was no link with all-cause or cancer death. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death
- Only 414 people (2%) were in that group, and 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes. The group had more smokers and higher BMI. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- Eating windows came from just two days of food recall. Nobody asked whether people ate that way on purpose. A short window often meant illness, poverty or skipped meals, not a planned 16:8 like yours.
- The senior author said it "does not mean" that time-restricted eating caused the deaths. Experts, including a past AHA president and 34 researchers, criticised the press release. https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/
- A later peer-reviewed version reported HR 2.35, with the same design limits. https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915
- A second analysis of the same dataset found a U-shaped curve. It was not significant in younger adults after full adjustment. https://news-medical.net/news/20250915/Daily-meal-timing-influences-longevity-risk-in-adults-study-reveals.aspx
- Randomized trials show neutral-to-modestly-favourable effects on risk factors. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full

**Separate from the headline:** in one 16:8 trial, much of the weight lost was muscle. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32986097/ Whether 16:8 is still worth it for your weight is your call on its own merits.

Rests on: Authors and independent experts agree the study cannot show cause.

You have two problems that make each other worse. Every process in the container, including `node` and `npm` themselves, runs as emulated x86 code. And all of the many small file operations in `node_modules` go through the slow Mac-to-Linux file sharing layer. Your Linux colleagues have neither problem: they run natively and their bind mounts are plain local disk access.

**1. Emulated amd64 (`--platform linux/amd64`)**
- An Apple Silicon Mac can't run x86 binaries directly. Docker Desktop translates them with QEMU, or with Rosetta, which is faster. Docker says Rosetta gives "near-native" speed, but that's a vendor claim. Independent users report native arm64 images are still much faster.
- Docker's settings page says the Rosetta option is off by default. Docker's 4.25 announcement says it's on by default on macOS 14.1+. Check it yourself: Settings → General → "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon". This needs the Apple Virtualization framework VMM. Docker VMM doesn't support Rosetta, so amd64 emulation there "is slow".
- **Best fix:** build the image as native arm64 and emulate only the one x86 dependency. First check whether it now ships arm64 builds. If not, you could run it as a separate amd64 service or install just that binary.

**2. `node_modules` on a bind mount**
- Bind-mounted files stay on the macOS side and cross into the Linux VM for every file operation. Named volumes live inside the VM and are much faster. npm install and file watching on tens of thousands of files is close to the worst case for this.
- **Fix:** keep the source code bind-mounted, but put `node_modules` in a named volume, e.g. `- node_modules:/app/node_modules` in Compose.
- Make sure file sharing is set to VirtioFS (the documented default) and not gRPC FUSE.
- For large repos, Docker Desktop's "Synchronized file shares" keeps a synced copy of the files inside the VM. Its docs give no benchmarks, and I couldn't confirm from the docs which paid plans include it.
- An alternative runtime, OrbStack, says its bind mounts are faster. That's the vendor's own benchmark.

**Order to try:** confirm Rosetta is on, move `node_modules` to a named volume, then work toward a native arm64 image. Together these should close most of the gap. I haven't measured that myself.

**Sources**
- https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/
- https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/
- https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/
- https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/
- https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-16-docker-mac-apple-silicon/view
- https://blog.nashcom.de/nashcomblog.nsf/dx/tips-running-domino-container-images-on-apple-silicon.htm
- https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem
- https://techearl.com/docker-bind-mounts-slow-mac-windows

# No, 3.13t isn't production-ready for this stack

Two things rule it out:

- **CPython calls 3.13t experimental.** The docs say to "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit." That hit is about 40% on pyperformance, though independent workloads measured 6–20%. 3.13t also never frees classes, modules, functions or code objects once a second thread starts, so memory grows. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html, https://static-frame.readthedocs.io/en/latest/articles/freethread.html, https://codspeed.io/blog/state-of-python-3-13-performance-free-threading
- **The ecosystem has dropped 3.13t.** manylinux removed it from its build images on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch followed. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
  - None of your dependencies' current releases ships cp313t wheels: NumPy 2.5.4, pydantic-core 2.50.4 and lxml 6.1.3. All three ship cp314t wheels. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files, https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files, https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files
  - Staying on 3.13t would mean pinning old releases that get no security fixes, or building from source.

3.14 is the supported free-threaded target under PEP 779, with about 8% overhead on Linux x86-64. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/, https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html

**lxml is a risk even on 3.14t.** One researcher reports that lxml 6.x turns the GIL back on when imported. Proper free-threading support appears only in 7.0.0a1, an experimental alpha. https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289, https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a1/

NumPy (2.1+) and pydantic-core (2.29+) are listed as supporting free-threading. That means they don't crash; it doesn't mean shared objects are safe to write from several threads without your own locks. https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking/

## What to do

1. **Keep production on standard 3.13 for now.** If you need CPU parallelism today, a process pool (`multiprocessing` / `ProcessPoolExecutor`) is the low-risk route.
2. **Ask the platform team to allow 3.14t** and run a pilot there.
3. **Check the GIL at startup.** After all imports, assert `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is `False`. If lxml re-enables it, you lose the whole gain without any error.
4. **Contain lxml** until 7.0 is final: keep its calls on one thread, behind a lock, or in a worker process. Don't force `PYTHON_GIL=0` around it.
5. **Benchmark your own workload** against the GIL build, both single-threaded and multi-threaded, before switching.

## Caveats

- The PyPI file lists were only partly read, so a stray cp313t wheel can't be fully ruled out.
- The lxml GIL behaviour is reported by one researcher; step 3 will confirm it either way.
- No published production case studies of 3.13t were found.

**No, this isn't safe. The WAL part of your plan won't work at all.**

**1. WAL doesn't work across machines.** WAL mode keeps a shared-memory index in an mmapped `-shm` file. Every process that uses the database has to share that memory. The SQLite docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem… processes on separate host machines obviously cannot share memory with each other." Three servers on an NFS mount can't share that memory, so you risk corruption, not just slow performance.
https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

**2. NFS locking itself is a corruption risk.** Even without WAL, SQLite relies on file locks to coordinate writers. The docs say locking bugs are "especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular," and that "database corruption might result." They also say "there is nothing SQLite can do to prevent it." Your tests may pass and still miss the problem. SQLite isn't tested over a network, so this setup is "at the user's risk."
https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html

**3. Even "working" rollback mode is a poor fit.** The SQLite docs list rollback-journal mode over the network as a way to reduce the risk. In that mode, writers block readers, and NFS delay makes each lock last longer. At 20 writes/sec across three hosts you'd likely see `SQLITE_BUSY` contention, and you'd still depend on NFS locks behaving correctly. Their rule of thumb is to avoid SQLite when the same database is "accessed directly… and simultaneously from many computers over a network."
https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

**What to do instead** (the SQLite docs suggest the first two):
- **Use a client/server database.** The docs name PostgreSQL as "an excellent choice." For three app servers writing at the same time, this is my recommendation.
- **Keep SQLite on one machine behind a service.** Put the database in WAL mode on a single host's local disk. Have only processes on that host touch the file, and send the other servers' reads and writes to them over the network, through a small API or proxy. At 20 writes/sec, one SQLite writer can easily keep up.
- Replicated SQLite systems such as rqlite or LiteFS also exist. I didn't research them here, so check them yourself before relying on them.

Sources:
- https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

**Decision:** Don't run 3.13t in production. To get CPU parallelism now, use a process pool (`multiprocessing` / `ProcessPoolExecutor`) on your standard 3.13 build. If you still want no-GIL, ask the platform team to allow 3.14 and pilot 3.14t off the production path.

**Rests on:** All three researchers independently found the following.

- CPython calls 3.13t experimental. It warns of bugs, about 40% single-thread slowdown, and memory growth from immortalized objects. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
- PEP 779 grants "supported" status only from 3.14. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/
- manylinux dropped 3.13t on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch followed. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- Current releases of all three of your dependencies ship cp314t and cp315t wheels for Linux x86-64, but no cp313t:
  - NumPy 2.5.4: https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files
  - pydantic-core 2.50.4: https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files
  - lxml 6.1.3: https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files

So staying on 3.13t would mean pinning old NumPy and pydantic-core with no security fixes. lxml may have no 3.13t wheel at all.

lxml is also the blocker on 3.14t. Per one researcher, lxml 6.x turns the GIL back on at import, and that switches it on for the whole process. Forcing `PYTHON_GIL=0` risks crashes. Real free-threading support exists only in lxml 7.0.0a1, an alpha. https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289, https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a1/

Overhead on 3.14t is about 8% on Linux x86-64. https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/free-threading-python.html

**Not verified:**
- Whether 3.14t actually speeds up *your* workload. Nobody benchmarked your service.
- Whether the GIL stays off on 3.14t once all three libraries are imported.
- Whether pydantic and NumPy objects shared across your threads are safe without your own locks. "Supported" on the tracker means "doesn't crash." https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking/

**Next check:** On a 3.14t build, import NumPy, pydantic and lxml, then print `sys._is_gil_enabled()`.
- If it prints `True`, lxml has re-enabled the GIL. In that case, run lxml in separate processes or wait for lxml 7.0 final.
- If it prints `False`, benchmark your real workload on 3.14t against 3.13 with a process pool. Move to production only if 3.14t wins and passes load tests.

answer.text:
## Two causes stack, and Linux laptops have neither

**1. Everything runs under x86 emulation.** `--platform linux/amd64` emulates all of Node, npm and your build tools, not only the one dependency. Rosetta is much faster than QEMU, but it is only available with the Apple Virtualization framework VMM. The sources disagree on whether it is on by default. Docker's current settings page lists it as "Disabled" ([settings](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/)), while the 4.25 announcement says it is enabled on macOS 14.1+ ([4.25 post](https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/)). On "default settings" you may be running on QEMU, which is far slower ([Docker multi-platform docs](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/)). Rosetta also has known problems: no AVX, hangs, and 100% CPU ([roadmap #384](https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384)). npm install on node:20 under emulation has a specific hang bug ([docker-node #1946](https://github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946)).

**2. `node_modules` on a bind mount.** Each file operation crosses the macOS-to-VM sharing layer (VirtioFS). npm install and file watching do huge amounts of small-file I/O, which is the worst case for that layer. GOV.UK measured a compile dropping from about 19s to about 4s after moving `node_modules` to a named volume ([GOV.UK ADR](https://docs.publishing.service.gov.uk/repos/govuk-docker/adr/0003-use-docker-volumes-for-improved-macos-performance.html)). Other reports put npm install at roughly 3.5× slower on a bind mount ([benchmark](https://eastondev.com/blog/en/posts/dev/20251217-docker-mount-comparison/)).

No source splits your 5–10× between the two causes. A plausible estimate is about 3–5× from the mount, with the rest from emulation.

## What to do, in order

1. **Today:** In Settings > General, select the Apple Virtualization framework and turn on Rosetta.
2. **Today:** Mount a named volume over `node_modules` and keep the source bind-mounted ([VS Code guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance)). The cost is that the IDE can't see `node_modules` on the host. "Clone Repository in Container Volume" goes further.
3. **Measure:** Time `npm ci` with the mount vs the volume, and with Rosetta on vs off. This shows which cause dominates for you.
4. **Real fix:** Build the image native arm64 and isolate the x86-only dependency. Check for an arm64 release first, and if there isn't one, run it in an amd64 sidecar. Apple is phasing out Rosetta after macOS 27 ([MacRumors](https://www.macrumors.com/2025/06/10/apple-to-phase-out-rosetta-2/)), so an amd64-only setup is a long-term risk.
5. **Upgrade off Node 20.** It reached end-of-life on 2026-04-30.
6. **If it's still slow:** Try Synchronized File Shares, which needs a paid plan ([docs](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/)), or OrbStack. OrbStack's speed claims are vendor-only ([OrbStack](https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem)).

## Recommended figure

**Cite about 19% (roughly 1 in 5) of crates on crates.io that contain significant code use the `unsafe` keyword directly.** Source: Rust Foundation, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild," May 2024. The post says: "Of those 127,000 crates, 24,362 make use of the `unsafe` keyword, which is 19.11% of all crates." It also reports that **34.35% call directly into another crate that uses `unsafe`**. For supply-chain risk, that second number may matter more.
https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/

## Confidence

**High confidence in "about 20–25%". Low confidence in any decimal.** Independent studies using different methods land close together:

| Source | Snapshot | Crates | Share with unsafe |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rust Foundation (Painter tool) | May 2024 | ~127,000 | 19.11% |
| Cui et al., Fudan (arXiv 2412.06251) | 2023-01-30 | 103,516 | 21,506 crates, which I calculate as ≈20.8% |
| Astrauskas et al., OOPSLA 2020 | ~2020 | 31,000+ | ~25% (75% use none) |
| Evans et al., ICSE 2020 | ~2019 | ~15,000 | 29% ("less than 30%" in the abstract) |

https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06251v2 · https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752v1 · https://alastairreid.github.io/RelatedWork/papers/astrauskas:oopsla:2020 · https://alastairreid.github.io/RelatedWork/papers/evans:icse:2020

## Caveats to disclose

- **No peer review.** The Rust Foundation figure is from a blog post. It doesn't define "significant code" or publish Painter's method.
- **Small arithmetic gap.** 24,362 ÷ 127,000 = 19.18%, not 19.11%. The 127,000 is probably rounded, so cite "≈19%".
- **The data is old.** It's from May 2024, about 2.5 years ago, and the registry has grown since. I found no newer measurement of this metric.
- **Different definitions.** The studies count different things: the keyword itself, unsafe blocks, or unsafe functions. Don't present them as a time series.
- **Popular crates are higher.** Evans found over 50% among the most-downloaded crates.
- **Don't confuse with advisory failures.** A January 2026 blog post reports 24.2% of crates failing cargo-deny's "unsound" advisory check. That measures known advisories, not unsafe usage (https://mr-leshiy-blog.web.app/blog/crates_io_analysis/).

## What I couldn't verify

I couldn't extract text from the Evans or Astrauskas PDFs, so those rows come from the arXiv abstract and secondary summaries. Before auditors check them, confirm both against the primary papers (Astrauskas: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3428204).

**Decision:** Do two cheap, reversible fixes now. Decide whether to rework the image after timing the result.

1. **Move `node_modules` off the bind mount into a named volume.** Keep the source bind-mounted. On a Mac, every file operation on a bind mount crosses the macOS-to-VM file-sharing layer, and npm install and file watching are mostly small-file I/O. Others measured large gains from this change: GOV.UK went from about 19s to about 4s, and one team went from 18m44s to 3m51s. The downside is that the host IDE no longer sees `node_modules`.
   - https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance
   - https://docs.publishing.service.gov.uk/repos/govuk-docker/adr/0003-use-docker-volumes-for-improved-macos-performance.html
   - https://blog.stackademic.com/my-docker-bind-mount-made-npm-install-take-47-minutes-the-vm-was-fine-c0718f513603
2. **Turn on Rosetta.** In Settings, set the VMM to Apple Virtualization framework, then enable "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation". `--platform linux/amd64` emulates all of Node, not just the one dependency. Docker's settings page lists Rosetta as disabled by default, which would leave you on QEMU, the much slower path. Docker's 4.25 post says the opposite, so check your own setting.
   - https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/
   - https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/
   - https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/

**Rests on:** Docker's documentation and several independent reports, all from other people's machines. Each cause alone is reported at roughly 3–5× (bind mount) or worse (QEMU), so together they fit your 5–10×. Nobody has measured how the slowdown splits between them on your setup.

**Not verified:**
- How much slowdown remains after these two fixes.
- Whether your x86-only binary uses AVX. Rosetta doesn't support AVX, and Node 20 npm installs have hung under amd64 emulation.
   - https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384
   - https://github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946

These are what would justify the bigger change: build a native arm64 image and run the x86-only dependency in a separate amd64 sidecar, or use a newer release of it that ships arm64 binaries. This is also a longer-term hedge, since Apple is phasing out Rosetta 2 after macOS 27.
   - https://www.macrumors.com/2025/06/10/apple-to-phase-out-rosetta-2/

**Next check:** After the two fixes, time `npm ci` on your Mac and compare it with a colleague's Linux laptop. If it is close, you're done. If it is still several times slower, emulation is the remainder, and the arm64 image plus sidecar is worth the effort.

**Separately:** Node 20 reached end-of-life on 2026-04-30, so plan to move to a supported version. If you ever need the whole tree on a fast mount, Synchronized File Shares is an option, but it requires a paid Docker plan.
   - https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/

Together with 19.11% in 2024, the share has slowly fallen as the registry grew. https://arxiv.org/html/2404.02230v3 · Ozdemir's count was 1,048 of 3,638 crates: https://cs.stanford.edu/~aozdemir/blog/unsafe-rust-syntax/
5. **Critiques:**
   - A count of crates says nothing about how much unsafe code each one has or whether it's justified. Much of it is FFI; the windows bindings crate has the most uses.
   - The figure for direct use understates exposure: 34% to over 50% of crates rely on unsafe code through their dependencies.
   - Sources: https://developers.slashdot.org/story/24/05/25/2250236/rust-foundation-reports-20-of-rust-crates-use-unsafe-keyword
   - I found no rigorous statistical rebuttal.

**What I'm unsure of**

- I couldn't confirm the exact figures in Evans' paper (29.4%, and 38% transitive-only) from the paper itself. Its PDF wouldn't parse, so those numbers come only from secondary sources.
- The studies define "contains unsafe" differently: the keyword anywhere, or unsafe blocks or functions specifically. They also differ on whether crates that don't build are included.
- I found no measurement from 2025 or 2026. A January 2026 blog post (Pozhylenkov, 196,923 crates) reports that 24% of crates fail RustSec "unsound" advisory checks. That measures something else and shouldn't stand in for the share of crates using unsafe. https://mr-leshiy-blog.web.app/blog/crates_io_analysis/

# Share of crates.io crates containing unsafe code

**Figure to cite:** About **1 in 5 crates (19.11%)** use the `unsafe` keyword directly. This is 24,362 of the roughly 127,000 crates the Rust Foundation classed as having "significant code," as of May 2024.
https://rustfoundation.org/news/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/

Always state the denominator. The post calls this a share "of all crates," but against all ~145,000 crates it would be about 16.8%. The 19.11% only works against the "significant code" subset, and the post never defines that term. Auditors will probably notice this.

**Corroborating sources (same order of magnitude):**
- **Cui et al. (2023 snapshot):** 21,506 of 103,516 crates, about 20.8%, found by regex matching. https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06251
- **Astrauskas et al., OOPSLA 2020:** about 31,867 crates. Roughly 20% have unsafe blocks and about 13% declare unsafe functions. A later survey gives the total as 23.6%. https://doi.org/10.1145/3428204 · survey: https://arxiv.org/html/2404.02230v3
- **Evans et al., ICSE 2020:** the abstract says "less than 30%." The 29% figure appears only in secondary sources. https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752

Together these show the share falling slowly, from about 29% in 2016–2018 to about 19–21% in 2023–24.

**Transitive exposure:** This is often the more relevant figure for supply-chain risk. 34.35% of crates directly call a crate that uses `unsafe` (same Rust Foundation post). Evans et al. report that "more than half" have `unsafe` somewhere in their call chain.

**Confidence:**
- **High** that roughly 1 in 5 crates use `unsafe` directly.
- **Low** on the exact decimal. The Foundation's method (its Painter tool, https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter) is thinly documented, has not been peer reviewed, and has not been independently replicated.
- No measurement from 2025 or 2026 exists, so the figure is about 2.5 years old.

**Caveats to state in the assessment:**
- Studies define "unsafe" differently: the keyword anywhere, unsafe blocks, unsafe function declarations, or regex hits.
- Containing `unsafe` does not make a crate vulnerable. Much of it is calls into C/C++ code.
- Do not cite the 23.6% figure as Astrauskas's own number; it comes from the later survey. None of the researchers read the full Evans or Astrauskas papers.

**Recommendation:** Cite 19.11% with its denominator and date, and give the 19–24% range as corroboration. For the strongest audit trail, also run `cargo-geiger` on your own dependency tree. Your actual exposure is a figure you can reproduce, which matters more than the ecosystem average.

**Finding: No. SQLite's own documentation says this setup is not safe. WAL mode in particular does not work across hosts.**

1. **WAL won't work across three servers.** The WAL page says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." The reason is that WAL coordinates through a shared-memory wal-index (an mmapped `-shm` file). Processes on different machines can't share that memory. The only way to run WAL without shared memory is `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, and that limits the database to a single process. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

2. **NFS locking is named specifically as a cause of corruption.** The corruption page says broken locking is "especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular… database corruption might result." It adds that every connection must use the same locking protocol. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html

3. **The FAQ says to avoid it outright:** "fcntl() file locking is broken on many NFS implementations. You should avoid putting SQLite database files on NFS if multiple processes might try to access the file at the same time." https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html (Q5)

4. **The network-use guidance:** it may "appear to work" but problems are rare and hard to reproduce. "Rely upon it at your (and your customers') peril." SQLite is "not tested in across-a-network scenarios." Its recommendations are:
   - use a client/server database such as PostgreSQL;
   - or keep the database in WAL mode on one host and send all access through a proxy or app service on that host;
   - or, if you must share the file, use rollback-journal mode, though that still carries risk.

   https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html

5. **When to use SQLite:** "avoid using SQLite in situations where the same database will be accessed directly… and simultaneously from many computers over a network." For websites: "if the website is… so busy that it requires multiple servers, then consider using an enterprise-class client/server database." The page also says SQLite allows only one writer at a time. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

6. **Related bug.** The corruption page describes a "WAL-reset bug," a race condition that can corrupt a database when several connections write or checkpoint at once. It reportedly affects versions 3.7.0 through 3.51.2. This applies even on a single host, so check your SQLite version whatever you decide. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html

**Uncertainties:**
- The docs don't mention NFSv4 specifically. NFSv4 has built-in locking with leases, which is better than v3's NLM, but SQLite still says network locking is not tested or guaranteed. The WAL shared-memory problem has nothing to do with locking, so NFS version doesn't fix it either.

- **Rust Foundation, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild" (21 May 2024):** 24,362 of about 127,000 crates "with significant code" use `unsafe`, measured with its Painter tool. https://rustfoundation.org/news/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/

- The Astrauskas OOPSLA 2020 percentages: these came only from a secondary summary.

**Not verified:** No count from 2025 or 2026 was found, so the figure is current only to May 2024. Date-stamp it ("as of May 2024"). That keeps it defensible and doesn't change what to cite.
