# No, this setup isn't safe. WAL mode across hosts is the main problem.

## Why

1. **WAL can't work across machines.** WAL coordinates through a shared-memory index, the `-shm` file, which each process memory-maps. Three servers can't share memory over NFS, so each one would see a different index. SQLite's docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." NFSv4's better locking doesn't change this, because the issue isn't locking. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
2. **NFS locking is a known cause of corruption.** SQLite singles out "network filesystems and NFS in particular." Its FAQ says to avoid NFS when several processes access the file at once. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html, https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html
3. **"It worked in testing" proves little.** SQLite says network failures are rare and hard to reproduce, and it doesn't test network setups. Richard Hipp, SQLite's author, told one user whose cross-host WAL test passed: "that just means you didn't test it enough." https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html, https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg108685.html
4. **People have hit this exact failure.** OpenAI's Codex docs report corruption when Linux hosts share a WAL database over NFS. GoToSocial doesn't support NFS at all, with or without WAL. Nextcloud users on NetApp NFS reported corruption on every restart. https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/environments/network-file-systems (one researcher cited a slightly different path for this page), https://docs.gotosocial.org/en/latest/advanced/sqlite-networked-storage/, https://help.nextcloud.com/t/storage-over-nfs-on-netapp-corrupts-database/41506

Rollback-journal mode is less risky, but it's still unsupported. Every write would also block all readers across the network, which at 20 writes/s means latency and `SQLITE_BUSY` errors.

## What to do instead

Your load of 20 writes/s is easy for SQLite on a single host. The problem is the three-server layout, not the volume. Pick one of these:

- **PostgreSQL or MySQL.** This is SQLite's own advice for sites that need several servers. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
- **One server owns the SQLite file** in WAL mode on local disk. The other two servers send reads and writes to it through an API. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- **A replication layer** such as LiteFS or rqlite. We didn't evaluate these.

## Also

SQLite's corruption page describes a "WAL-reset" race that can corrupt a database even on a single host. One researcher reported that it affects versions 3.7.0 through 3.51.2. Check your SQLite version against https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html whichever option you choose.

**Short answer:** No. For a healthy 45-year-old, this headline isn't a good reason to stop. The evidence behind it is weak.

**Where the claim comes from**
- It started as a March 2024 conference abstract presented at an American Heart Association (AHA) meeting, not a peer-reviewed paper. The study used US national survey data (NHANES, 2003–2018) for about 20,000 adults, linked to death records, with a median follow-up of 8 years. People who ate within an 8-hour window had a "91% higher" risk of cardiovascular death (HR 1.91) than people who ate over 12–16 hours. They did not have higher risk of death from all causes or from cancer.
- The full paper came out in August 2025 in *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome*. It reported HR 2.35 for an eating window under 8 hours compared with 12–14 hours. The authors themselves point to "residual confounding," meaning other differences between the groups may explain the result.

**Why the evidence is weak**
- **It shows a link, not a cause.** It can't show that the eating window caused the deaths.
- **Eating habits were measured from only two days.** Each person's window came from two 24-hour food recalls, which were then assumed to describe their eating over many years. Nobody in the study was actually following a planned 16:8 diet.
- **The numbers are small.** Only about 414 people (2%) were in the short-window group, and 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes. The 95% confidence interval runs from 1.20 to 3.03, so the true effect could be much smaller.
- **The groups differed from the start.** The short-window group had more smokers and higher body weight. Experts suggested that some people ate in short windows because of shift work or hardship, not by choice. Cardiologist Donald Lloyd-Jones said the result was "not ready for prime-time." Another expert, Pam Taub, said 34 researchers objected to how the AHA publicized it.

**The other side of the evidence**
Short randomized trials of time-restricted eating show modest improvements in weight, insulin, blood pressure and cholesterol, and few side effects. One 2025 meta-analysis found no loss of lean muscle. No trial has measured long-term heart deaths either way.

**What to do**
- If 16:8 is working for you, it's reasonable to continue.
- Focus on what you eat as well as when: plenty of protein, regular strength training to protect muscle (low muscle mass was one possible explanation the researchers raised), and no smoking.
- Get blood pressure, lipids and glucose checked as usual for your age.
- Stop and talk to a doctor if you get dizziness or palpitations, notice signs of disordered eating, or start a medication such as a diabetes drug.

**Sources**
- https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- https://www.heart.org/en/news/2024/03/18/time-restricted-eating-may-raise-cardiovascular-death-risk-in-the-long-term
- https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915
- https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1664412/full

**Decision:** Don't put the SQLite database on the NFS mount with all three servers writing to it. Use one of these instead:

- **PostgreSQL or MySQL.** This is the simplest fit for three app servers. At about 20 writes/s, load isn't a concern for either.
- **One server owns the SQLite file** on its local disk, in WAL mode. The other two servers send their reads and writes to it through an API.

**Rests on:** WAL mode depends on a shared-memory index (the mmapped `-shm` file). Processes on different machines cannot share that memory, so the three servers would each see a different index. This is a design limit, not a tuning issue, and NFSv4's improved locking doesn't change it.

- SQLite's documentation says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- SQLite's author says that cross-host WAL tests which appear to pass mean "you didn't test it enough." https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg108685.html
- OpenAI's Codex docs report this failure in practice: Linux hosts sharing a WAL database over NFS corrupted it. https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/environments/network-file-systems (one researcher cited it at …/docs/environments/network-file-systems)

Turning WAL off doesn't make it safe either:

- SQLite names NFS locking as a known cause of corruption. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html and https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html (Q5)
- SQLite says it is "not tested in across-a-network scenarios." Its own recommendation is a client/server database, or WAL on one host behind a proxy. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- Its guidance for a site busy enough to need several servers is to use a client/server database. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
- Other projects say the same and report corruption: GoToSocial calls NFS unsupported with or without WAL (https://docs.gotosocial.org/en/latest/advanced/sqlite-networked-storage/), and a Nextcloud user saw corruption on NetApp NFS (https://help.nextcloud.com/t/storage-over-nfs-on-netapp-corrupts-database/41506).

**Not verified:** Nobody tested your own NFS server or mount options. That wouldn't change the decision, because the WAL limit applies to every NFS setup. No source supports rollback-journal mode over NFSv4 at your load either.

**Next check:** None needed for the decision. If you go with the single-owner option, it may be worth a short look at LiteFS or rqlite, which are built for replicating SQLite. None of the researchers evaluated them.

**Established by official investigations**

- **The mechanism.** This was an overvoltage collapse, not a frequency or inertia event. ENTSO-E's expert panel published its final report on 20 March 2026. It found "a combination of many interacting factors": oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive-power control, differences in voltage-regulation practice, rapid output cuts and generator disconnections in Spain, and uneven stabilisation capabilities. These caused fast voltage rises and a cascade of disconnections. The panel's factual report came out on 3 October 2025. [ENTSO-E](https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/), [report page](https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/)
- **Sequence, as summarised by trade press.**
  - At 12:32:57 a transformer near Granada tripped on overvoltage (355 MW).
  - At 12:33:16, 727 MW of solar was lost near Badajoz, and 928 MW more followed.
  - In total more than 2.5 GW was lost in about 78 seconds, and synchronism with Europe was lost at 12:33:19.
  - Several synchronous generators met their reactive-power setpoint less than 75% of the time. Some generator overvoltage protection was set below the regulatory limits. Shunt reactors are switched by hand and were not reconnected in time. Spain's 400 kV voltage band is wider than its neighbours', which left little margin before generators disconnected.
  - Sources: [POWER](https://www.powermag.com/anatomy-of-a-blackout-findings-from-the-spain-portugal-grid-collapse-final-report/), [pv magazine](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/03/23/entso-e-report-finds-systemic-failures-behind-2025-iberian-blackout/)
- **Spanish government report (17 June 2025).** It also blamed overvoltage and a lack of voltage-control capacity, and ruled out a cyberattack. [Energía Estratégica](https://energiaestrategica.com/strategicenergy/en/notes/spanish-goverment-report-blackout)
- **CNMC (the Spanish regulator).** It agrees the origin was "multifactorial". [CNMC](https://cnmc.es/prensa/incoacion-incidente-electrico-28A-20260417)

**Still unresolved or contested**

1. **Who is to blame.**
   - The operator, REE, says "no cause attributable to Red Eléctrica" and points to generators' incorrect disconnections and weak voltage control. [Energías Renovables](https://www.energias-renovables.com/panorama/ree-no-fall--en-el-apag-20260320)
   - The utilities' association, Aelec, blames REE's voltage control and generation scheduling. [Euronews](https://es.euronews.com/2025/06/18/red-electrica-contradice-al-gobierno-y-culpa-a-las-electricas-por-el-apagon-masivo-del-28-)
2. **Pending sanctions.** In April 2026 the CNMC opened proceedings: one against REE for a "very serious" infringement and about 20 or more against generators for "serious" ones. It says these do not attribute the cause of the blackout to anyone. The REE case has up to 18 months to run. I found no rulings yet. [El Independiente](https://www.elindependiente.com/economia/2026/04/17/cnmc-investiga-red-electrica-apagon-multas-60-millones/)
3. **Gaps in the investigation.** The panel could not determine:
   - why some generators fell short on reactive power;
   - the exact role of the 0.63 Hz oscillation, which was driven by inverter-based generation in southern Spain;
   - why about 208 MW of distributed generation disconnected. Records for units under 1 MW were missing.
   - Source: [SMC España](https://sciencemediacentre.es/en/final-blackout-report-european-operators-confirms-event-was-caused-multiple-factors-recommends)
4. **Litigation.** Iberdrola's unfair-competition suit against REE is ongoing. A secondary source says the criminal sabotage inquiry was closed. [Inteligenia](https://www.inteligenia.info/home/informe-analitico-del-apagon-electrico-del-28-de-abril-de-2025-un-ano-despues/)

**Before you rely on this:** I didn't open the full ENTSO-E PDF or the government's own text, so the timestamps, MW figures and generator findings come from press summaries. Check them against [the primary report](https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/) before you cite them as the panel's findings.

**Report to coordinator: official and primary sources on the 28 April 2025 Iberian blackout**

**Established by official investigations**

1. **ENTSO-E Expert Panel final report (20 March 2026).** This is the main official finding. There was no single root cause. The blackout came from "many interacting factors": oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive power control, different voltage regulation practices, rapid output reductions and generator disconnections in Spain, and uneven stabilisation capability. Together these caused "fast voltage increases and cascading generation disconnections." Collapse was at 12:33 CEST.
   - Press release: https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/
   - Report hub, with the final report and the 3 Oct 2025 factual report: https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/
   - I could not read the full report PDF myself: it is over 10 MB and the fetch tool's limit is 10 MB. The details below come from secondary summaries of it.
2. **Details of the final report, from secondary summaries.** Sources: https://sciencemediacentre.es/en/final-blackout-report-european-operators-confirms-event-was-caused-multiple-factors-recommends and https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/03/23/entso-e-report-finds-systemic-failures-behind-2025-iberian-blackout/
   - There were two oscillations: a forced one at 0.63 Hz, linked to converter-based generation, and a natural inter-area one at 0.2 Hz.
   - Several synchronous plants did not follow reactive power set-points.
   - Renewables ran at a fixed power factor, so they could not regulate voltage.
   - Some overvoltage protection tripped below the regulatory thresholds.
   - Spain's allowed 400 kV voltage band is wider than its neighbours', which leaves less margin against overvoltage.
   - Voltages went above 435 kV. Spain and Portugal lost synchronism with Europe at 12:33:19.
   - ENTSO-E's Board chair said: "The problem is not renewable energy, but voltage control."
3. **Spanish Government committee (17 June 2025).** It found the cause "multifactorial", starting from an anomalous voltage oscillation. It blamed both REE's scheduling (10 thermal plants were scheduled for voltage control, but fewer were available in practice) and generators failing to deliver voltage control. It ruled out a cyberattack. https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/consejodeministros/resumenes/paginas/2025/170625-rueda-de-prensa-ministros.aspx
4. **Red Eléctrica (REE) report (18 June 2025).** REE says the root problem was overvoltage, not low inertia. In its account, plants obliged under its voltage control procedure (P.O. 7.4) did not absorb the reactive power required, and some generation disconnected while still inside the permitted voltage range. https://www.ree.es/en/press-office/news/press-release/2025/06/red-electrica-presents-report-incident-28-april-and-proposes-recommendations
5. **CNMC, the Spanish regulator (19 March 2026, file PRO/CNMC/001/26).** It gives recommendations and does not assign blame. It says regulatory tools to ensure supply existed at the time. https://www.cnmc.es/prensa/informe-incidente-electrico-20260319

**Still contested or unresolved**

- **Who is responsible.** The government blames REE's scheduling as well as the generators. REE says it complied with the rules and puts the blame on the generators. REE claims the ENTSO-E report does not question its scheduling; that is REE's own reading. CNMC sanction proceedings are reportedly open against REE and others, but I have not checked this against a primary source.
- **Gaps the panel itself named.** Data gaps meant it could not determine why some disconnections happened. It also left open the exact role of the oscillations and why some generators failed to provide reactive power.
- **How to frame renewables.** The officials quoted say renewables were not the cause, but converter-driven oscillation and distributed-generation trips are among the contributing factors.

**What I'm unsure of**

- Secondary sources disagree on the report's size: 22 or 21 recommendations, 440 or 472 pages. They also give the reactive-power shortfall two ways: "at least 75% of hourly samples" versus "<75% of required output." These should be checked in the report itself, probably Chapter 9 for the recommendations.
- I did not read the Spanish government report or Portugal's own reviews (REN, ERSE) directly.

**To the coordinator: findings on press, forums and community write-ups (12 lookups used)**

**Official findings**
1. **ENTSO-E Expert Panel final report (20 Mar 2026, 49 experts, 472 pp.).** It found many interacting factors, not one cause, and calls this the first blackout in Europe caused by overvoltage. The sequence:
   - Two oscillations: a forced oscillation of about 0.6 Hz from converters in southern Spain at 12:03, and a 0.2 Hz inter-area oscillation at 12:19.
   - The steps taken to damp them (cutting exports, reconnecting lines) raised voltages.
   - Voltage control fell short. Some conventional generators met their reactive-power target less than 75% of the time, renewables ran at a fixed power factor, and shunt reactors that are switched by hand were not reconnected in time.
   - Some generators had overvoltage trip settings below the regulatory limits. About 2.5 GW tripped in roughly 78 seconds, Iberia lost synchronism at 12:33:19, and the links to France tripped.
   - The panel president said "renewables were not the problem; voltage control was." The panel says some generator data was missing, so it could not establish why some units tripped. Press counts of its recommendations differ (17 vs 21), so check the PDF.
   - https://www.powermag.com/anatomy-of-a-blackout-findings-from-the-spain-portugal-grid-collapse-final-report/ ; https://www.ree.es/sites/default/files/2026-03/NP%20-%20FinalReport%20Expert%20Panel%2020%20marzo.pdf ; https://www.pv-tech.org/combination-of-voltage-and-oscillation-caused-iberian-blackout-says-entso-e-report/
2. **Spanish government committee (June 2025).** It blamed both Red Eléctrica (REE) and generators. Voltage control was insufficient, and one of the 10 units scheduled for it was declared unavailable on 27 April and not replaced. Plants failed to absorb reactive power or disconnected too early. https://en.ara.cat/economy/the-spanish-government-approves-the-report-the-causes-of-the-massive-power-outage_1_5414358.amp.html
3. **CNMC, the Spanish regulator (17 Apr 2026 onward).** It calls the cause multifactorial. It opened a "very serious" case against REE, the only case it describes as tied to causation, for possibly scheduling the system in a way that left it vulnerable. It also opened about 50 cases against generators, which it says do not by themselves assign blame for the blackout. All are still open (they can run 9–18 months). https://www.menorca.info/actualidad/nacional/2026/04/17/2611031/cnmc-cree-apagon-tuvo-origen-multifactorial-pero-abre-expedientes-sancionadores.html ; https://es.ara.cat/economia/energia/cnmc-abre-expedientes-sancionadores-raiz-apagon-electrico_1_5709975.html
4. **Sabotage and cyberattack ruled out.** The Audiencia Nacional (judge Calama) closed its criminal case with "not the slightest indication" of sabotage. Eight reports from INCIBE, the national cybersecurity institute, found no cyber action, and the CNI intelligence service agreed. https://www.vozpopuli.com/tribunales/la-audiencia-nacional-archiva-la-investigacion-del-apagon-al-no-existir-un-minimo-indicio-de-sabotaje-terrorista.html

**Still contested (mark as such in the brief)**
- **Who is to blame.**
  - REE's own report (June 2025) blames generators that did not control voltage, and names a PV plant in Badajoz as the source of the oscillation. https://www.pv-magazine.com/2025/06/19/iberdrolas-500-mw-nunez-de-balboa-pv-plant-blamed-by-ree-for-spain-blackout
  - Aelec, the lobby for Iberdrola, Endesa and EDP, says REE alone is responsible because it dispatched too little voltage control. https://es.ara.cat/economia/energia/electricas-atribuyen-apagon-mala-gestion-red-electrica_1_5421074.html
- **Where the 0.6 Hz oscillation came from.** Iberdrola denies that its Núñez de Balboa plant caused it. A Comillas study paid for by Iberdrola and Endesa calls it an inter-area oscillation, not a forced one; only a summary is public. A community analysis by security researcher Rubén Santamarta argues the data points to this plant, but says the root cause can't be known without plant data. https://www.reversemode.com/2025/10/what-happened-at-iberdrolas-nunez-de.html ; https://files.griddo.comillas.edu/resumen-informe-preliminar-comillas-iit-rouco-lobato-echavarren-v16_1.pdf
- **Whether the panel was impartial.** In April 2026 Iberdrola questioned this, because REE, an affected party, sat on the panel. It is also seeking REE's audio recordings and emails. https://www.energias-renovables.com/panorama/iberdrola-duda-de-la-imparcialidad-del-informe-20260421
- **Why the voltage rose.** A UPV academic notes the report does not examine the cause of the initial rise. https://sciencemediacentre.es/manuel-alcazar-informe-final-apagon

**What I'm unsure of**
- I didn't confirm whether the ENTSO-E report names the plant behind the oscillation. The press says only "southern Spain."
- I don't have the date the court closed the case.
- Nothing I found shows the CNMC cases resolved as of November 2026.
- I didn't cover Portuguese investigations (ERSE, REN).

**Report to coordinator: independent measurements, critiques and counter-evidence**

**Findings**

1. **The ENTSO-E final report (20 March 2026) says there was no single cause.** A panel of 49 experts found several factors that interacted: two oscillations, weak voltage and reactive-power control, generators disconnecting, and protection settings. Outside experts said its methods were mostly sound. They also noted that the report itself admits gaps in its records, that missing data was filled in by simulation, and that it is not a ruling on who is liable. https://sciencemediacentre.es/en/final-blackout-report-european-operators-confirms-event-was-caused-multiple-factors-recommends
2. **Details from Ars Technica's summary of the ENTSO-E report:**
   - Of 19 devices that disconnected in the last 12 seconds, only 4 behaved as required and 9 clearly did not, taking out about 1.9 GW.
   - Some protection would trip at 430 kV, at or near the alarm thresholds, so the margin was small or none.
   - The second oscillation is attributed to a "likely" inverter fault, not a confirmed one.
   - Inverter data covered only about 15% of roughly 6.5 GW of small-scale solar.
   - Tripling inertia would have damped the oscillations by only about 3%.
   
   This is secondary coverage; check it against the primary report. https://hn.jakechampion.name/reader/https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/03/final-analysis-of-2025-iberian-blackout-policies-left-spain-at-risk/
3. **Still unexplained, and should be marked as contested:**
   - Why some synchronous units missed their reactive-power targets in at least 75% of hourly samples.
   - Whether the Badajoz plant started the oscillations.
   - How much the smaller early oscillations contributed.
   - Owners of some generators that tripped before the collapse say they keep no logs of those trips. (sciencemediacentre, above; https://science.feedback.org/what-caused-iberias-blackout/)
4. **The responsibility dispute is unresolved.** The government committee (June 2025) put much of the blame on REE. REE says "Red Eléctrica did not fail" and blames generators. Aelec, the utilities group, blames REE's "poor management" and says REE did not use all available resources. One of the 10 synchronous units REE scheduled became unavailable that day and was not replaced in time. https://en.ara.cat/economy/the-power-companies-attribute-the-blackout-to-poor-management-by-red-electrica_1_5421076.html ; https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/03/23/entso-e-report-finds-systemic-failures-behind-2025-iberian-blackout/
5. **CNMC, Spain's regulator, opened about 20 sanction proceedings on 17 April 2026.** One concerns REE for a possible "very serious" infringement. The others concern Iberdrola, Endesa, Naturgy, Repsol, Ascó-Vandellós II and Bahía de Bizkaia Electricidad. CNMC says opening them does not prejudge the outcome. I found no final sanctions. https://www.pv-magazine.es/2026/04/21/la-cnmc-incoa-expedientes-sancionadores-por-el-apagon-a-ree-y-las-electricas-estas-ultimas-comienzan-su-comparecencia-en-el-congreso/
6. **Sabotage and cyberattack are officially ruled out.** In January 2026 the Audiencia Nacional (Judge Calama) closed the criminal case, finding not even a "minimal indication" of terrorist sabotage. Eight cyber reports found no harmful activity. https://www.poderjudicial.es/cgpj/es/Poder-Judicial/Noticias-Judiciales/El-juez-de-la-Audiencia-Nacional-archiva-la-investigacion-por-el-apagon-general-del-pasado-el-28-de-abril-al-no-existir--un-minimo-indicio--de-sabotaje-terrorista
7. **Critics:**
   - Reliamag argues no formal root-cause-analysis process was used, and that REE's own oscillation-damping actions may have pushed voltage up. This is an opinion piece. https://reliamag.com/topics/articles/how-spain-may-have-ignored-root-cause-failure-analysis-in-its-blackout
   - Vozpópuli cites a Senate inquiry that blames REE and the government, plus about 8,000 withheld REE recordings. It is a partisan source and I have not verified it. https://www.vozpopuli.com/economia/empresas/un-ano-del-apagon-y-8000-audios-censurados-hay-material-que-salpica-al-gobierno.html

**What I'm unsure of**
- I did not find any fully independent re-measurement, such as a PMU study that checks the official timeline. FAU (Linnert et al.) published wide-area measurements, but I couldn't check them.
- The ERSE (Portugal) assessment PDF wouldn't parse, so I have nothing from Portugal's regulator.
- Secondary sources disagree on the report's length (440 vs 472 pages) and number of recommendations (21 vs 22).
- I have not checked the status or findings of the Senate inquiry.

**Short answer:** No, not on 3.13t. Free-threading is officially supported only from **3.14t**, and none of your three dependencies currently ship 3.13t wheels. The real decision is whether your platform will move to 3.14.

**Why 3.13t is a dead end**
- PEP 703 was accepted for 3.13 explicitly as experimental. PEP 779, accepted June 2025, made the free-threaded build officially supported (still optional) only from 3.14. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ · https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-779-criteria-for-supported-status-for-free-threaded-python/84319
- manylinux removed 3.13t from its images on 7 May 2026, calling 3.14t "the stable, non-experimental free-threaded variant." PyTorch dropped 3.13t as a result. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386

**Your dependencies (checked on PyPI today)**
- **NumPy 2.5.4:** has cp314t manylinux x86-64 wheels, no cp313t. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files
- **pydantic-core 2.50.4:** has cp314t, no cp313t in the current release. It first added 3.13t support in 2.29. https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files · https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking/
- **lxml:** this is the blocker. The stable 6.1.3 has cp314t wheels, but its changelog never mentions free-threading. Real support ("Experimental support for freethreading Python… 3.14t and later") arrives only in **7.0.0a1**, an alpha. My guess, which I haven't confirmed, is that 6.x turns the GIL back on when it's imported. https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files · https://lxml.de/changes-7.0.0a1.html

If an extension that isn't marked thread-safe gets imported, CPython quietly turns the GIL back on and only prints a warning. You'd pay the single-threaded cost (about 8% on x86-64 Linux) and gain nothing. https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/free-threading-python.html

**What to do**
1. Stay on regular 3.13 in production. If you need CPU parallelism now, use `multiprocessing` or `ProcessPoolExecutor`, or move the hot loops into NumPy, which releases the GIL.
2. Ask your platform team for a 3.14 or 3.14t path. 3.13t won't get there.
3. Set up a 3.14t staging lane with NumPy, pydantic, and lxml 7.0 pre-releases. Check `sys._is_gil_enabled()` at startup and fail if it returns True. Run your test suite and benchmarks with many threads.
4. Go to production only after lxml 7.0 final is out and your benchmarks show the speedup outweighs the single-threaded cost and the higher memory use (PEP 779 cites about 15–20%).

# 28 April 2025 Iberian blackout: established cause and open disputes

**Caveat:** None of us could read the ENTSO-E final report itself, because the PDF was too large to fetch. The details in point 1 come from press summaries. Check each one against the report before you cite it in the brief.

## Established by official investigations

1. **ENTSO-E Expert Panel final report (20 Mar 2026).** There was no single root cause. Several factors interacted to cause "fast voltage increases and cascading generation disconnections":
   - two oscillations (about 0.6 Hz forced, and 0.2 Hz inter-area)
   - insufficient voltage and reactive-power control
   - renewables running at a fixed power factor
   - some protection tripping below the regulatory thresholds
   
   Iberia lost synchronism at 12:33:19. The panel describes this as Europe's first overvoltage blackout. Its chair said: "The problem is not renewable energy, but voltage control."
   - https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/

2. **Spanish Government committee (17 Jun 2025).** It found the cause multifactorial. It blamed both Red Eléctrica (REE) scheduling and generators that failed to deliver voltage control. It ruled out a cyberattack.

3. **Sabotage ruled out.** The Audiencia Nacional closed its criminal case, finding not even a "minimal indication" of sabotage.

## Contested or unresolved

- **Responsibility.**
  - REE blames generators: https://www.ree.es/en/press-office/news/press-release/2025/06/red-electrica-presents-report-incident-28-april-and-proposes-recommendations

  - https://www.energias-renovables.com/panorama/iberdrola-duda-de-la-imparcialidad-del-informe-20260421

I've finished the primary-source checks. Here is my report to the coordinator.

**Findings (primary and official sources)**

1. **The claim came from a press release about a conference abstract, not a paper.** The AHA promoted abstract P192 from its EPI|Lifestyle 2024 meeting (18 March 2024). The data were NHANES 2003–2018, about 20,000 US adults with an average age of 49, linked to death records through 2019 over a median 8 years. People eating within less than 8 hours had a 91% higher risk of cardiovascular death than people eating across 12–16 hours. The release labels this "preliminary" and not peer-reviewed. The senior author, Victor Zhong, says it "does not mean that time-restricted eating caused cardiovascular death." There was no drop in deaths from all causes. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death

2. **It was later peer-reviewed and published.** Chen M, …, Manson JE, Zhong VW, *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome* 19(7):103278, published online 22 August 2025 (n=19,831). Against a 12–14 hour window, eating in under 8 hours gave HR 2.35 (95% CI 1.39–3.98) for cardiovascular death, with no link to all-cause or cancer death. The authors write that **residual confounding** may explain the result. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/ (abstract obtained through Europe PMC)

3. **The sample is small and the measurement is weak.** Only 414 people (about 2%) were in the under-8-hour group, and only 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes. That group had 3–4 times more Black participants, more smokers and a higher BMI. Eating window was taken from just **two 24-hour dietary recalls** at enrollment. Lloyd-Jones (a former AHA president) suggests the group may include shift workers or people with irregular eating forced on them, not people deliberately doing 16:8. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality

4. **Randomized trials (short term, risk markers only) show no harm signal.** In a 2022 meta-analysis of 10 trials, time-restricted eating lowered systolic blood pressure (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9644535/). In a 2023 meta-analysis, adding it to calorie restriction gave no extra cardiometabolic benefit (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10630127/). A 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis reportedly found small LDL rises compared with whole-day fasting. I only saw a snippet of that one and did not verify it.

**Bottom line from my angle:** this is observational evidence of low strength. It measures a habitual short eating window from two days of recall in a small, higher-risk group. It does not test deliberate 16:8 in healthy people. It cannot show that 16:8 causes harm, but nothing here proves it is safe over the long term either. No randomized trial measures cardiovascular deaths.

**What I'm unsure of**
- The abstract said HR 1.91 against 12–16 hours; the published paper says 2.35 against 12–14 hours. I couldn't read the full text to see which confounders were adjusted for, or the event counts in the final version.
- I didn't fetch the full RCT meta-analyses, so I have no pooled effect sizes.
- I found no official guidance (AHA or other) addressing 16:8 for healthy adults.

**Report to coordinator (press, forums and community angle)**

**Findings**

1. **Where the "91%" comes from.** It's a 2024 AHA conference poster by Chen and Zhong (Shanghai Jiao Tong), published only as an abstract (Circulation 149 Suppl 1, P192). It used NHANES 2003–2018 data on about 20,000 adults followed for a median of 8 years. People eating within less than 8 hours had a hazard ratio of 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03) for cardiovascular death, compared with a 12–16 hour window. It found no link with death from any cause or with cancer death. The authors said it shows association, not causation, and needs replication. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death ; https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circ.149.suppl_1.P192

2. **The numbers behind it are small.** Only 414 people (about 2%) were in the under-8-hour group, and 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes. Donald Lloyd-Jones, a past AHA president, said the findings are "not ready for prime-time." His concerns:
   - eating windows came from only two 24-hour diet recalls
   - the short-window group may include shift workers or people working several jobs
   - the group had 3–4 times as many Black participants, who face higher baseline risk because of social and health inequities

   Pam Taub called the AHA headline misleading. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality

3. **34 time-restricted eating researchers wrote to the AHA** (including Panda, Varady and Ravussin). They said:
   - the short-window group had about 60% more smokers
   - sleep and shift work weren't accounted for
   - one or two short days of eating is not the same as practising TRE
   - more than 100 trials show metabolic or blood pressure benefits and no serious harms

   They have a stake: the letter is hosted on Panda's lab blog, which promotes a TRE app. https://blog.mycircadianclock.org/debunking-misleading-claims-the-truth-behind-the-headlines-on-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-risk/ ; https://nutritioninsight.com/news/scientists-dispute-study-linking-time-restricted-eating-to-poor-heart-health.html

4. **New since the headline: the full paper was peer-reviewed and published.** It appeared in *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome* in July 2025. Compared with a 12–14 hour window, it reports a larger effect (HR 2.35), which the authors say held across 14 sensitivity analyses. All-cause death still showed no association. The authors admit they can't rule out residual confounding. Some press reported this as "135% higher risk." It uses the same dataset and the same two-day recall method, so it doesn't count as independent replication. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/ ; https://medicaldialogues.in/amp/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915

5. **A separate 2025 US cohort study (Aging Cell, 33,052 people)** found a U-shaped pattern: death from any cause was lowest with 11–12 hour windows and higher below 8 hours. It also relies on recall data. https://www.news-medical.net/news/20250915/Daily-meal-timing-influences-longevity-risk-in-adults-study-reveals.aspx

**Overall view:** The evidence is weak and observational. The study didn't measure what people actually do, which is a deliberate 16:8 window held for a year. Trials show short-term benefits, but there are no long-term trials on hard outcomes like heart attacks or deaths. The signal is not proof, but it can't simply be dismissed either.

**What I'm unsure of**

- I couldn't open the 2025 paper (ScienceDirect blocked access, and PubMed showed only a cookie notice). The HR of 2.35, its confidence interval, the number of deaths and the "14 sensitivity analyses" come from search summaries and are not verified.
- The 16:8 window sits right at the study's cut-off. The poster's "under 8 hours" wording versus the press's "8 hours" is ambiguous.
- I didn't find any independent replication in another cohort that measured sustained TRE.
- I didn't get to Reddit or other forums. My budget went on the press coverage and the primary sources.

I've finished the searches and am writing up the report now.

## Report: independent measurements, critiques and counter-evidence

**1. Where the claim comes from.** The "91%" figure comes from a March 2024 American Heart Association poster abstract by Zhong et al. It used US national survey data (NHANES 2003–2018, about 20,000 adults) linked to death records. When it was publicised it had not been peer reviewed as a full paper, and critics noted that only a short abstract was available. https://gidmk.substack.com/p/is-intermittent-fasting-killing-people ; https://fortune.com/well/2024/03/18/how-healthy-intermittent-fasting-heart-disease-study-91-percent-risk/

**2. The peer-reviewed version.** It was published in 2025 as Chen…Zhong, *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome: Clinical Research & Reviews* (doi:10.1016/j.dsx.2025.103278): 19,831 adults followed for a median of 8.1 years. Eating within less than 8 hours, compared with 12–14 hours, was linked to higher cardiovascular death (HR 2.35, 95% CI 1.39–3.98). That is now reported as "135%" higher. It was not linked to death from all causes or from cancer. The authors say they cannot separate the eating window itself from confounding. The headline number shifted between versions (1.91 → 1.96 → 2.35) and the confidence interval is wide, so the estimate is unstable. https://medicaldialogues.in/amp/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915 ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/ ; https://www.nutritioninsight.com/news/scientists-dispute-study-linking-time-restricted-eating-to-poor-heart-health.html

**3. Specific critiques.** These come from an open letter by 34 time-restricted eating researchers (Varady, Peterson, Panda and others) and a later letter about the published paper. Note that these are advocates of the approach, not neutral parties.
- **Measurement:** eating windows came from only two 24-hour food recalls, then assumed to hold for years. A recorded window under 8 hours often just means the record was incomplete. This is not the same as someone deliberately doing 16:8 every day.
- **Smoking:** the short-window group had about 60% more smokers.
- **Group make-up:** Black Americans were 23.2% of that group versus 6.6% of the reference group. Shift work and sleep were not accounted for.
- **Small group:** only about 2% of participants (414 people) were in the short-window group.
- **Reverse causation:** people who are already ill may eat less often.

https://blog.mycircadianclock.org/debunking-misleading-claims-the-truth-behind-the-headlines-on-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-risk/ ; https://www.nutritioninsight.com/news/scientists-dispute-study-linking-time-restricted-eating-to-poor-heart-health.html

**4. Other observational evidence.** Another analysis of the same survey data (Mao 2025, *Aging Cell*) found a U-shaped curve, with the lowest risk at about 11–12 hours. It linked windows of 8 hours or less to roughly 30% higher death from all causes. However, it found no significant risk from short windows in younger adults after full adjustment. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12610411/

**5. Randomized trials.** Trials show neutral to modestly helpful effects on weight and blood pressure, and little effect on blood fats when calories aren't also cut. Most last 12 weeks or less, none measures heart attacks or deaths, and the longest run about a year. They therefore can't rule out long-term harm, but they show no warning sign in risk factors. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12672340/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39519533/

**Bottom line from my angle:** the evidence is weak. It is a single observational signal with poor measurement of eating habits and plausible confounding. It is not evidence that deliberate 16:8 eating causes heart deaths.

**What I'm unsure of:**
- I couldn't get the exact number of cardiovascular deaths in the short-window group, or the absolute risks.
- I couldn't read the full text of the 2025 paper or its covariate list; PubMed was blocked.
- I haven't verified the details of the Mao 2025 study myself.
- No long-term randomized trial with hard outcomes like heart attacks or deaths exists, so a small real effect can't be ruled out.

The officially supported free-threaded target is 3.14t, so moving off GIL-free Python would require changing the 3.13 pin.

**Findings**

1. **CPython calls 3.13t experimental.** The 3.13 free-threading HOWTO says to "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit." That hit is about 40% on pyperformance, mainly because the specializing interpreter is turned off in 3.13t. It also lists three limitations:
   - Functions, classes, code objects and modules are made permanently resident in memory once a second thread starts.
   - Iterators aren't safe to share between threads.
   - Reading frame objects from another thread can crash the process.

   Importing an extension that isn't marked free-threading-safe silently turns the GIL back on, with only a warning. You can check at runtime with `sys._is_gil_enabled()`. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
2. **PEP 779 (accepted 16 Jun 2025, Final):** 3.13 is "Phase I, explicitly experimental." 3.14 is "Phase II", officially supported but still optional. Its targets are at most 15% CPU slowdown (about 10% measured) and about 20% extra memory. Making free-threading the default build is left to a future PEP. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/
3. **NumPy 2.5.4 (latest):** wheels exist for cp314t (including manylinux_2_28 x86_64) but there are no cp313t wheels. https://pypi.org/pypi/numpy/2.5.4/json
4. **lxml 6.1.3 (latest):** cp314t manylinux x86_64 wheels exist, but no cp313t wheels. The community tracker lists lxml as "7.0.0", which doesn't match the 6.1.3 now on PyPI. https://pypi.org/pypi/lxml/6.1.3/json, https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking/
5. **pydantic:** the tracker lists free-threading support from pydantic 2.11 / pydantic-core 2.29 (same tracker URL). pydantic-core added 3.13t support in PR #1628 (https://data.safetycli.com/packages/pypi/pydantic-core/changelog?page=2). A later PR, #1738, is titled "Stop testing free-threaded on 3.13" (https://codspeed.io/pydantic/pydantic-core/runs/684993244e0fba92ebd9d18a).
6. **The wider ecosystem is dropping 3.13t.** PyTorch dropped 3.13t on 14 May 2026 (https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386). cibuildwheel has discussed scheduling removal of cp313t (https://discuss.python.org/t/how-to-make-cibuildwheel-support-for-cp313t-and-cp314t/105429).

**Recommendation from the primary sources:** don't deploy 3.13t to production. If you want to go GIL-free:
- Plan to move the platform to 3.14t, which is the supported phase.
- Benchmark there against your single-threaded baseline.
- At startup, assert that `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is False, so an unmarked extension can't quietly re-enable the GIL.

If you stay on 3.13, use the normal GIL build and get parallelism from multiprocessing, or from NumPy code that releases the GIL.

**What I'm unsure of**
- **Older 3.13t wheels:** I didn't confirm which was the last NumPy or lxml release with cp313t wheels. Pinning that release might work, but you'd lose future fixes.
- **pydantic-core:** I couldn't load its PyPI file list (the response was too large), so I don't know if the current release still ships cp313t wheels.

- **Unread pages:** the lxml and NumPy JSON pages were cut off before all files were read. The cp313t/cp314t sections came before the cut, so I expect those lists are complete.

**Report (press, forums, issue trackers)**

PyTorch then dropped 3.13t, calling it "experimental" and 3.14t "the stable, non-experimental free-threaded variant." https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
2. **The build tooling is dropping it too.** cibuildwheel PR #2787 (merged 2026-04-02) deprecated cp313t builds, with full removal planned about a month later. rgommers called the timeline "very rushed" but didn't argue against removing it. Several projects then dropped 3.13t, including multidict, yarl and scikit-image. https://github.com/pypa/cibuildwheel/pull/2787
3. **NumPy:** the latest release, 2.5.4 (2026-10-10), ships cp314t wheels including manylinux x86-64, but **no cp313t wheels**. On 3.13t they would have to stay pinned to an older NumPy or build from source. https://pypi.org/pypi/numpy/2.5.4/json. The community tracker lists 2.1.0 as NumPy's first free-threading-compatible version: https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking
4. **pydantic:** pydantic-core added free-threading support and 3.13t wheels in PR #1628. The tracker lists pydantic 2.11.0 and pydantic-core 2.29.0 as the first supporting versions. I couldn't confirm whether current pydantic-core still ships cp313t wheels, because the PyPI JSON was too big to fetch. https://data.safetycli.com/changelogs/pydantic-core
5. **lxml is the blocker.** Launchpad bug 2111289: the test suite segfaulted under 3.13.3t. lxml 6.0.2's cp314t wheels **turned the GIL back on at import** with a RuntimeWarning. Forcing the GIL off and using lxml from several threads would likely crash (Nathan Goldbaum's comment, not the maintainer's). The latest stable, 6.1.3 (2026-09-02), has cp314t wheels but **no cp313t wheels**. https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289 , https://pypi.org/pypi/lxml/6.1.3/json
6. **General guidance for 3.13t:** shipping wheels that turn the GIL back on is the accepted practice when thread safety isn't guaranteed. So "it installs" doesn't mean you actually run without the GIL. https://discuss.python.org/t/how-to-get-an-extension-module-working-w-free-threading/63653/25

**What this suggests they should do:** don't deploy on 3.13t. If free-threading matters, push the platform to allow 3.14t. Even on 3.14t, lxml either brings the GIL back (6.x) or is alpha (7.0), so keep lxml work on one thread or behind a lock, or put it in a process pool. Prototype and benchmark on 3.14t before committing. Check at runtime with `sys._is_gil_enabled()`.

**Unsure of**
- Whether pydantic-core's current release still has cp313t wheels.
- Whether lxml 7.0 is stable yet. The tracker shows "7.0.0" as the first supporting version, but I only confirmed the alpha.
- I didn't find independent production case studies or performance write-ups for single-threaded overhead.

**Report to coordinator (angle: independent measurements, critiques, counter-evidence)**

**Bottom line: No. 3.13t is not production-ready for this stack. The ecosystem has moved on to 3.14t and is dropping 3.13t.**

1. **CPython calls 3.13t experimental.** The 3.13 docs say to "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit": about 40% on pyperformance, mostly because the specializing interpreter is turned off. They also list immortalization memory growth, frame access that can crash, and shared iterators that can crash. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
2. **3.14t is much better.** Overhead there is about 1–8% (8% on x86-64 Linux). PEP 779 made it a supported build, but not the default. https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/free-threading-python.html ; https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-779-criteria-for-supported-status-for-free-threaded-python/84319
3. **Independent benchmarks disagree.** One third-party test measured 3.13t about 20% slower single-threaded (21.3 ms vs 17.7 ms). Other write-ups give 17–40%. The cost depends on the workload, so it has to be measured on their own service. https://static-frame.readthedocs.io/en/latest/articles/freethread.html ; https://codspeed.io/blog/state-of-python-3-13-performance-free-threading
4. **The ecosystem is dropping 3.13t.** pypa/manylinux removed cp313t from its images on 2026-05-07 because it "was an experimental free-threaded build". PyTorch stopped shipping 3.13t wheels as a result. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386

   - lxml 6.1.3: has cp314t, no cp313t. https://pypi.org/project/lxml/

The docs say an extension not marked safe turns the GIL back on at import (with a warning), which would erase the gain. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lxml/lxml/master/CHANGES.txt

**Recommendation from my angle:** Don't use 3.13t. Ask the platform team to allow 3.14t. Test on 3.14t with lxml 7.x once it is stable. **Decision:** Split. You can cite the headline cause now as official. Before you cite any technical figures, check them against the ENTSO-E final report PDF.

**Official findings you can cite now**
- **ENTSO-E Expert Panel, final report, 20 March 2026.** There was no single root cause. Oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive-power control, and cascading generator disconnections in Spain together caused "fast voltage increases." Collapse came at 12:33 CEST. It was an overvoltage event, not a lack of inertia. https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/ and https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/
- **Spanish Government, 17 June 2025.** The cause was "multifactorial." The government blamed both REE's scheduling and generators' voltage-control failures, and ruled out a cyberattack. https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/consejodeministros/resumenes/paginas/2025/170625-rueda-de-prensa-ministros.aspx
- **Audiencia Nacional, January 2026.** The court closed the criminal case, finding not "a minimal indication" of sabotage. https://www.poderjudicial.es/cgpj/es/Poder-Judicial/Noticias-Judiciales/El-juez-de-la-Audiencia-Nacional-archiva-la-investigacion-por-el-apagon-general-del-pasado-el-28-de-abril-al-no-existir--un-minimo-indicio--de-sabotaje-terrorista

**Mark as contested**
- **Who is responsible.** REE says generators failed to control voltage (https://www.ree.es/en/press-office/news/press-release/2025/06/red-electrica-presents-report-incident-28-april-and-proposes-recommendations). The utilities' association Aelec blames REE's dispatch (https://en.ara.cat/economy/the-power-companies-attribute-the-blackout-to-poor-management-by-red-electrica_1_5421076.html). The regulator CNMC has opened sanction cases against REE and generators. These were still unresolved as of our research, and CNMC says opening them does not prejudge the outcome (https://www.pv-magazine.es/2026/04/21/la-cnmc-incoa-expedientes-sancionadores-por-el-apagon-a-ree-y-las-electricas-estas-ultimas-comienzan-su-comparecencia-en-el-congreso/).
- **Where the ~0.6 Hz oscillation came from.** REE points to the Núñez de Balboa PV plant. Iberdrola denies this.
- **Why voltage rose at first, and why some units tripped.** The panel itself cites missing data.

## Short answer

Two separate slowdowns stack on top of each other, and both come from your Mac setup.

1. **Every binary in the container runs under x86 emulation.** With `--platform linux/amd64`, Node, npm and any native addons are all Intel code. Docker Desktop uses QEMU to run that code unless you turn on Rosetta, and Rosetta is **disabled by default**. Your colleagues' Linux laptops run the same image natively. ([Docker settings docs](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/))
2. **`node_modules` is on a bind mount.** On a Mac, Docker runs inside a Linux VM, so every file operation on a bind mount crosses from the VM to macOS. The default VirtioFS is faster than the older options, but it's still much slower than a native filesystem. `npm install` writes tens of thousands of small files and the dev server watches them, so this is the worst case for that boundary. One user saw a Next.js compile take 25.5 s on a Mac versus 3.1 s on Ubuntu. ([OrbStack explainer](https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem), [Docker forum](https://forums.docker.com/t/virtiofs-is-not-enabled-by-default-as-per-documentation-cannot-be-enabled-on-the-ux-and-fails-if-enabled-manually/145791))

## What to do, in order of payoff

1. **Put `node_modules` in a named volume** and bind-mount only your source code. In Compose that's `- .:/app` plus `- node_modules:/app/node_modules`, then run `npm install` inside the container. GOV.UK's team cut a build from about 31 s to about 4 s with this kind of change. One downside: your editor on the Mac won't see `node_modules`. ([GOV.UK ADR](https://docs.publishing.service.gov.uk/repos/govuk-docker/adr/0003-use-docker-volumes-for-improved-macos-performance.html), [engineered.at](https://engineered.at/articles/docker-on-macos-is-slow-and-how-to-fix-it))
2. **Turn on Rosetta:** Settings → General → "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon". This needs the Apple Virtualization framework VMM. ([Docker docs](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/), [Atomic Object](https://spin.atomicobject.com/docker-apple-silicon/))
3. **Better long-term fix: stop emulating everything.** Build the image for arm64 and isolate only the x86-only dependency, for example in a small amd64 sidecar container. Also ask the vendor whether an arm64 build exists. This matters more over time: Apple says general-purpose Rosetta is available only through macOS 27. It hasn't confirmed whether the Linux-VM version that Docker uses survives past that, and Parallels expects it to go. ([MacRumors](https://www.macrumors.com/2025/06/10/apple-to-phase-out-rosetta-2/), [Parallels KB](https://kb.parallels.com/en/129871))
4. **If the source bind mount is still slow**, try Docker's **Synchronized file shares**. It keeps a synced copy of your files inside the VM and is aimed at large repos. Check whether your Docker subscription includes it. ([Docker docs](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/))
5. Give Docker Desktop more CPU and memory, and keep VirtioFS selected as the file-sharing implementation.

Steps 1 and 2 together should remove most of the 5–10× gap. Some overhead will remain because Docker on a Mac always runs inside a VM.

# Should you stop 16:8 because of the "91% higher risk" headline?

**Short answer:** This evidence alone isn't a reason to stop. The study behind the headline is weak and didn't measure what you're doing. It also can't prove long-term safety, so ongoing monitoring is still worthwhile.

## Where the number comes from

- **The original source** was a March 2024 American Heart Association conference abstract using US survey data (NHANES), with about 20,000 adults followed for a median of 8 years. People eating within **less than** 8 hours had a 91% higher risk of cardiovascular death (HR 1.91) than those eating across 12–16 hours. It was preliminary and not peer-reviewed, and the senior author said it does not show causation. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death
- **The peer-reviewed version** was published in 2025. Compared with a 12–14 hour window, it reported HR 2.35, with a wide confidence interval of 1.39–3.98. It found no link with death from all causes or from cancer, and the authors acknowledge possible residual confounding. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/

## Why the evidence is weak

- **Small group:** Only 414 people (about 2%) were in the short-window group, with roughly 31 cardiovascular deaths.
- **Poor measurement:** Each person's eating window was estimated from just two 24-hour food recalls at enrollment. That is not the same as a deliberate, sustained 16:8 pattern like yours.
- **Confounding:** The short-window group had more smokers, higher BMI and more people facing higher baseline risk. Shift work and sleep weren't accounted for. A former AHA president called the result "not ready for prime-time." https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- **Critics with a stake:** 34 time-restricted eating researchers raised similar objections. They advocate the approach, so weigh their view accordingly. https://www.nutritioninsight.com/news/scientists-dispute-study-linking-time-restricted-eating-to-poor-heart-health.html

## Counter-evidence and limits

- **Randomized trials** show neutral to modestly positive effects on weight and blood pressure. However, they are short and none measures heart attacks or deaths. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9644535/
- **Another observational analysis** found the lowest risk at about 11–12 hour windows. It found no significant risk from short windows in younger adults after full adjustment. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12610411/

## What I'd do in your position

1. If 16:8 is working for your weight, continuing is reasonable. Losing excess weight has well-established heart benefits.
2. Check blood pressure, lipids and glucose at your routine visits. Some trial data hint at small LDL rises.
3. If you'd rather hedge, widening your window to about 10 hours probably keeps most of the benefit. Prioritise food quality and sleep either way.

# No: 3.13t isn't production-ready for this service. The free-threaded target is 3.14t.

**Why not 3.13t**

- **CPython calls it experimental.** The 3.13 docs say to "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit," about 40% on pyperformance. They also list known crashes: shared iterators, and reading frames from another thread. Third-party measurements put the slowdown at 17–40%, depending on workload. Sources: https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html, https://static-frame.readthedocs.io/en/latest/articles/freethread.html, https://codspeed.io/blog/state-of-python-3-13-performance-free-threading
- **PEP 779 makes 3.13 "Phase I, explicitly experimental."** 3.14t is the officially supported build, though still optional. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/
- **The ecosystem has dropped 3.13t.**
  - cibuildwheel deprecated cp313t builds: https://github.com/pypa/cibuildwheel/pull/2787
  - manylinux removed cp313t from its images in May 2026, and PyTorch followed: https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- **Your dependencies have dropped it too.** The current NumPy 2.5.4, lxml 6.1.3 and pydantic-core 2.50.4 ship cp314t wheels but no cp313t ones. That would leave you on stale pins or source builds. The PyPI pages were truncated, so treat this as very likely rather than certain. https://pypi.org/pypi/numpy/2.5.4/json, https://pypi.org/pypi/lxml/6.1.3/json, https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/

**lxml is the real blocker, even on 3.14t**

- lxml's test suite segfaulted on 3.13t: https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289
- lxml 6.x cp314t wheels re-enabled the GIL at import. We confirmed this for 6.0.2; 6.1.3 is unverified.
- Real free-threading support is only in 7.0.0a1, an alpha, for 3.14t and later: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lxml/lxml/master/CHANGES.txt
- An unmarked extension silently turns the GIL back on, so "it installs" doesn't mean "it runs without the GIL."

**What to do**

1. **Now:** stay on standard 3.13. Get parallelism from multiprocessing, or from NumPy operations that release the GIL.
2. **Ask the platform team to allow 3.14t.** The 3.14 docs report about 1–8% single-thread overhead, against roughly 40% on 3.13t. https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/free-threading-python.html
3. **Prototype on 3.14t.** Benchmark your own single-threaded and multi-threaded workloads against the GIL baseline.
4. **Contain lxml** until 7.x is stable: run it on one thread, behind a lock, or in a process pool.
5. **Add a guard in CI and at startup.** After all imports, assert that `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is `False`, so a silent GIL re-enable fails loudly.

The free-threading compatibility tracker is a useful way to watch dependency status: https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking/

# Should you stop 16:8 because of the "91%" headline?

**No.** This study gives you no good reason to stop. The evidence behind the claim is weak and does not describe what you are doing.

**Why the evidence is weak**

- **Not a trial.** The figure came from a 2024 conference abstract based on US survey data (NHANES, about 20,000 adults). It was later published as a peer-reviewed paper (HR 2.35 against a 12–14 h window). Both versions are observational. The authors themselves say the study does not show that time-restricted eating causes heart deaths, and that residual confounding may explain the result. Deaths from all causes were not higher.
- **Tiny, different group.** Only 414 people (about 2%) ate within less than 8 hours, and 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes. That group had more smokers, a higher BMI and more people facing higher baseline risk. Shift work and sleep were not accounted for. Former AHA president Donald Lloyd-Jones called the findings "not ready for prime-time."
- **Wrong exposure.** Eating windows came from two 24-hour food recalls. One or two short days are not a deliberate 16:8 routine kept for a year. Illness can also cause short eating windows (reverse causation). Your exact 8-hour window also sits at the edge of the study's "under 8 hours" group.
- **Trials show no warning sign.** Randomized trials of time-restricted eating show neutral to modestly helpful effects on weight and blood pressure.

Part of the criticism comes from 34 time-restricted eating researchers, who have a stake in the approach. The design flaws above stand without them.

```text
Decision: Keep doing 16:8 if it works for you; this headline is not a reason to stop.
Rests on: The signal comes from one observational dataset that measured a short eating window over two days in a small, higher-risk group, not deliberate 16:8 in healthy adults (AHA release, published paper, Lloyd-Jones). Confounding fits the data better than harm. Trials show no harm in risk markers.
Not verified: Long-term effects on heart attacks or deaths. No trial has measured these, so a small real effect can't be ruled out.
Next check: None needed.
```

Your usual check-ups (blood pressure, cholesterol) still apply, as they would for anyone.

**Sources**
- https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death
- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/
- https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- https://blog.mycircadianclock.org/debunking-misleading-claims-the-truth-behind-the-headlines-on-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-risk/
- https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9644535/
- https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12672340/

**Decision: Do not run 3.13t in production. Stay on the normal GIL build of 3.13 for now. If you want to go GIL-free, the path is 3.14t, which needs a change to the platform pin. Prototype on 3.14t before you ask for that change.**

**Rests on:**
- **CPython calls 3.13t experimental.** The docs warn of bugs and roughly a 40% single-threaded slowdown, because the specializing interpreter is off in that build. They also list known crash cases: reading frames from another thread and sharing iterators between threads. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
- **PEP 779 makes only 3.14t a supported free-threaded build.** https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/
- **Your dependencies have no current 3.13t wheels.** The latest releases of NumPy (2.5.4) and lxml (6.1.3) ship cp314t wheels but no cp313t wheels. Two researchers each read this from PyPI: https://pypi.org/pypi/numpy/2.5.4/json, https://pypi.org/pypi/lxml/6.1.3/json
- **The tooling is dropping 3.13t.** manylinux removed it, cibuildwheel deprecated it, and PyTorch dropped it, so no new 3.13t wheels are coming. https://github.com/pypa/cibuildwheel/pull/2787, https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386

Whether pydantic-core still ships cp313t wheels is unclear, but it doesn't change the answer. NumPy and lxml already rule 3.13t out.

**What waits for a test (3.14t):** Single-threaded overhead on 3.14t is about 1–8%. https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/free-threading-python.html

lxml is the weak point there:
- **lxml 6.0.2:** its cp314t wheels turned the GIL back on at import. https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289
- **lxml 7.0.0a1:** true free-threading support exists only in this alpha. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lxml/lxml/master/CHANGES.txt

If lxml turns the GIL back on, your service gets the overhead without the parallelism. A workaround is to keep lxml on one thread or in a process pool.

**Not verified:**
- Whether lxml 6.1.3 on 3.14t keeps the GIL off.
- How your service actually performs on 3.14t. Independent benchmarks vary widely, so you need your own numbers. https://codspeed.io/blog/state-of-python-3-13-performance-free-threading

None of this was observed on your setup.

**Next check:** In a 3.14t container on Linux x86-64:
1. Install current NumPy, pydantic and lxml.
2. Import all three and assert `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is False.
3. Run your CPU-bound path both single-threaded and multi-threaded, and compare against 3.13 with the GIL.

Only ask for the pin change if that shows a real gain. Keep the `_is_gil_enabled()` assertion in CI and at startup, so an extension can't quietly turn the GIL back on.

Two causes stack on each other: CPU emulation, because the image is amd64 on an arm64 Mac, and slow file I/O, because `node_modules` sits on a bind mount. Your Linux colleagues have neither problem. The emulation part comes from official docs; I'm inferring how the two combine. I used about 10 of the 12 lookups.

**Findings**

1. **The amd64 image runs under emulation.** Docker says a `linux/amd64` container can't run on an arm64 host without emulation. It also says QEMU emulation "can be much slower than native builds," especially for compile-heavy work. That covers native module builds during `npm install`, and the bundler in the dev server. Docker's fix is a multi-arch image, so each machine pulls its own variant. https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/

2. **Check whether Rosetta is on.** The setting is "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon" and needs the Apple Virtualization framework VMM. The two Docker sources disagree on the default:
   - The settings page currently says it is off by default. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/
   - The 4.25 announcement (Oct 2023, when Rosetta became GA) says it is on by default from macOS 14.1. https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/
   
   Look at Settings → General.

3. **Docker VMM breaks Rosetta.** Docker's page says VMM has no Rosetta support on Mac, so "emulation of amd64 architectures is slow." If you switched to the beta Docker VMM for faster file I/O, that cancels the fix in item 2. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/

4. **Bind mounts go through a slow file-sharing layer.** On Mac they cross VirtioFS (the default) or gRPC FUSE from macOS into the Linux VM. On Linux, Docker uses the host disk directly. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/

5. **Two official ways to speed up file access:**
   - **Named volume for `node_modules`:** VS Code's docs say to keep the source as a bind mount but put `node_modules` in a Docker named volume. If the container runs as a non-root user, add `chown` in `postCreateCommand`. https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance
   - **Synchronized file shares:** these keep an ext4 cache of the files inside the VM and are aimed at repos with 100k+ files. Docker's blog claims 2–10× faster file operations and says the feature needs Docker Desktop 4.27+ and a paid plan (Pro, Team or Business). The docs page itself doesn't mention a subscription. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/ and https://www.docker.com/blog/announcing-synchronized-file-shares/

**Recommended order**
1. Keep `node_modules` in a named volume, not on the bind mount.
2. Turn on Rosetta with the Apple Virtualization framework VMM, not Docker VMM.
3. Make arm64 the default image and isolate the x86-only dependency. Use a Rosetta-run amd64 sidecar, or an amd64 image only where that dependency is needed.
4. Consider synchronized file shares if you have a paid plan.
5. Check the memory and CPU limits. Memory defaults to 50% of the Mac's RAM.

**Uncertain**
- I couldn't settle the Rosetta default from Docker's sources (see item 2).
- I didn't confirm the subscription requirement for synchronized file shares on the docs page.
- I found no official benchmark showing how much of the 5–10× comes from emulation and how much from file I/O. Bind-mounted `node_modules` and emulation are each known to cause large slowdowns.
- I haven't checked whether Rosetta handles that particular x86 binary. A third-party Docker roadmap thread suggests problems with AVX instructions (https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384).

**What the community sources say (press, forums, issue trackers, blogs).** Two causes add up. One is emulating amd64. The other is having node_modules on a macOS bind mount. Linux hosts have neither problem, which fits a 5–10× gap.

**1. Bind-mounted node_modules is the main cost for I/O.** Bind mounts cross the boundary between macOS and the VM. Named volumes sit on ext4 inside the VM. The usual fix is to keep the source on a bind mount and put a named volume over `/app/node_modules`, then run `npm install` inside the container.
- Paolo Mainardi (Jan 2025) measured VirtioFS bind mounts at about 3× slower than native, down from 5–6×. The hybrid bind-plus-volume setup was the most consistent: https://engineered.at/articles/docker-on-macos-is-still-slow
- VS Code's guide recommends the same pattern. Caveat: delete the contents of the volume folder, not the folder itself: https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance
- Docker's paid "Synchronized file shares" feature uses an ext4 cache. The docs suggest putting node_modules in `.syncignore`: https://docs.docker.com/desktop/synchronized-file-sharing. Docker claims 2–10× gains (their own figure): https://www.docker.com/blog/announcing-synchronized-file-shares/. Mainardi saw permission errors on node_modules with it.
- OrbStack reports bind-mount `yarn install` at 77% of native speed. This is vendor data and has no Docker Desktop comparison: https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem

**2. amd64 emulation slows every CPU-bound step (npm scripts, bundler, dev server).**
- docker/roadmap#384 (still open, last activity Mar 2025): Rosetta doesn't support AVX, and some users see 100% CPU or hangs with Vite/Next.js. Docker's workaround is to turn Rosetta off, which falls back to slower QEMU, or set `EXPERIMENTAL_DOCKER_DESKTOP_FORCE_QEMU=1`. One user fixed it by switching to arm64 with `@rollup/rollup-linux-arm64-gnu`: https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384
- nodejs/docker-node#1946: `npm install` hangs on node:20 with `--platform linux/amd64` on Apple Silicon. Workarounds were moving to native arm64, upgrading Docker Desktop, or moving to Node 22. The issue was closed in May 2026 after Node 20 reached EOL on 2026-04-30: https://www.github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946
- The common recommendation is to build the image for arm64 and isolate the x86-only dependency. Options are a separate amd64 sidecar container or running just that binary under emulation.

**3. Dev-server file watching.** Inotify events over Mac bind mounts are reported as unreliable. People then turn on `CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING` or `WATCHPACK_POLLING`, which uses a lot of CPU. Under emulation that cost gets bigger. Mostly blog sources: https://dev.to/xu_xu_b2179aa8fc958d531d1/the-docker-dev-environment-trap-why-your-hot-reload-setup-fails-on-m-series-chips-and-what-38pa

**Suggested order for the coordinator:** (a) named volume for node_modules, (b) move off emulation to arm64 and handle the x86 dependency separately, (c) check that VirtioFS and Rosetta are on, not gRPC FUSE or QEMU, (d) look at Sync file shares or OrbStack.

**What I'm unsure of:**
- The default settings conflict. One source says VirtioFS has been the default since 4.22, and a forum post says it was missing on 4.37. Docker's Mac settings page lists Rosetta as "Disabled," but the admin settings reference gives it a default of true: https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings/mac/. The user should check their own Settings.
- I don't know if the x86-only dependency needs AVX. If it does, Rosetta won't work and QEMU will be very slow.
- I found no controlled benchmark that splits the 5–10× between emulation and file I/O. I also didn't look at the Docker VMM backend.
- Many of the blog sources (oneuptime, techearl) are low quality.

I've finished my angle (measurements, critiques and counter-evidence). Here is my report.

**1. The bind-mounted `node_modules` is the most likely main cause.** In one Apple Silicon test, `npm install` took 4–6 s natively. A full bind mount took 17–22 s. With `node_modules` in a named volume it took about 7 s, and on the old gRPC FUSE backend it took 57 s. CPU-bound Node under Docker ran the same as native (4.08 s vs 4.14 s), so the slowdown there was file I/O, not CPU. These are single runs on unstated hardware, and that test used native arm64 rather than emulation. https://github.com/sparkfabrik/sparkdock/issues/61
- A secondhand report puts a bind mount at 3.5× slower than a volume for npm on Mac. https://eastondev.com/blog/en/posts/dev/20251217-docker-mount-comparison/

**2. amd64 emulation adds a second multiplier, and the default emulator is the slow one.** Docker's settings page lists Rosetta emulation as **Disabled** by default and VirtioFS as the default file sharing. With "default settings", that likely means QEMU emulation. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/
- Docker VMM does not support Rosetta: "emulation of amd64 architectures is slow." https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/
- A rough guide figure says QEMU is 5–20× slower, with no method given. https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-06-docker-multi-architecture-images/view
- One measurement comparing OrbStack (Rosetta) with Docker Desktop (QEMU): 4.2 s vs 12.8 s startup for an amd64 image. https://dev.to/pickuma/orbstack-deep-review-the-macos-native-container-runtime-that-replaces-docker-desktop-25p8

**3. Counter-evidence: Rosetta has its own problems.** Node 20 on amd64 under emulation has hung during `npm install` / `yarn` / `corepack`. Docker Desktop 4.26 reportedly fixed the Rosetta freeze, but QEMU reports continued into 2025. https://www.github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946
- Other reports: Rosetta pinning a CPU at 100% (https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384), a regression after macOS 14.5 (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/755840), and `mmap` errors (https://discussions.apple.com/thread/255291840).
- Recommend upgrading Docker Desktop, then testing with Rosetta on and off. Node 20 is also end-of-life (April 2026).

**4. Dev server file watching.** Bind mounts on gRPC FUSE don't pass file-change events reliably, so watchers fall back to polling, which costs CPU and adds latency. VirtioFS or `docker compose watch` avoids the problem. These sources are blogs, not controlled tests. https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-08-how-to-use-docker-desktop-file-sharing-settings/view

**Suggested order:**
1. Put `node_modules` in a named volume and confirm VirtioFS is selected.
2. Turn on Rosetta with the Apple Virtualization VMM, not Docker VMM.
3. Better still, build the image for native arm64 and isolate the x86-only dependency (a separate amd64 sidecar, or find an arm64 build).
4. Try Synchronized File Shares (Docker Desktop 4.27+) or OrbStack.

**What I'm unsure of:**
- No source measures how much file-sharing overhead and emulation each contribute together. Timing four combinations on their machine (mount type × Rosetta on/off) would settle it.
- Whether "default settings" on their install really means QEMU. Rosetta defaults have varied by version, and some guides say it's on.
- I found no published npm benchmark for Synchronized File Shares.
- Most numbers are single, non-repeated runs from 2022–2023.
