No, this isn't safe. In this setup WAL mode itself is unsupported, not just risky. SQLite's own documentation rules it out on three separate points.

**1. WAL does not work across machines.** WAL keeps a small index in memory that every connection must share. It does this by memory-mapping a `-shm` file next to the database, and separate hosts can't share that memory. The WAL page says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." The only workaround is `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, which allows a single process to access the database. That rules out three servers.

**2. Locking over NFS can be broken, which risks corruption.** Even in the older rollback-journal mode, SQLite depends on the filesystem's locks being correct. The corruption guide says faulty locks are "especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular." If two processes write at the same time on broken locks, the database "might" be corrupted. The "when to use" page adds that "there is nothing SQLite can do to prevent it." The network-use page says the same: "Rely upon it at your (and your customers') peril."

**3. It's slow and against the intended design.** Every page read and write would go over the network. The SQLite docs give this rule of thumb: avoid SQLite when the same database is "accessed directly… and simultaneously from many computers over a network."

**What to do instead** (in order of preference):

- **Use a client/server database, such as PostgreSQL.** At 20 writes per second from three servers, this is the standard answer, and it's what SQLite's docs recommend.
- **Keep SQLite on one host.** Put the database on one server's local disk and run WAL there. The other two servers send their reads and writes to a small service on that host instead of opening the file.
- **Use rollback mode over NFS only if you must.** The docs say this mode reduces the network problems, but it's untested by SQLite, allows only one writer at a time, and the corruption risk is still on you. I wouldn't use it for production data.

Since a corrupted shared database could take down all three servers, I'd go with PostgreSQL.

**Sources:**
- https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

**Two separate slowdowns add up, and your Linux colleagues have neither.**

**1. File I/O: `node_modules` on a bind mount.** On a Mac, bind mounts pass through a file-sharing layer (VirtioFS, or the older gRPC FUSE) into Docker's Linux VM. On Linux, the container uses the host disk directly. `npm install` writes tens of thousands of small files, so this is probably the larger cost. In one Apple Silicon test, `npm install` took 4–6 s natively, 17–22 s on a full bind mount, about 7 s with `node_modules` in a named volume, and 57 s on gRPC FUSE ([sparkfabrik#61](https://github.com/sparkfabrik/sparkdock/issues/61)). A 2025 measurement found VirtioFS about 3× slower than native ([engineered.at](https://engineered.at/articles/docker-on-macos-is-still-slow)).

**2. CPU: amd64 emulation.** A `linux/amd64` image on an M3 runs under emulation, which is much slower for compile-heavy work such as native module builds and bundling ([Docker](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/)). Docker's settings page lists Rosetta as **off** by default, which would mean the slower QEMU emulator. Some Docker sources disagree, so check Settings → General yourself ([settings](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/), [4.25 blog](https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/)). Docker VMM does not support Rosetta ([VMM](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/)).

**What to do, in order:**
1. Keep the source on a bind mount but put a **named volume over `node_modules`**, and run `npm install` inside the container ([VS Code guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance)). Confirm VirtioFS is selected.
2. Turn on **Rosetta** with the Apple Virtualization framework, not Docker VMM.
3. Best fix: **build the image as native arm64** and isolate the x86-only dependency, either in an amd64 sidecar or by finding an arm64 build. Rosetta lacks AVX and has caused hangs and 100% CPU with Vite/Next.js ([roadmap#384](https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384)). Node 20 amd64 images have also hung during `npm install` ([docker-node#1946](https://www.github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946)). Check whether your x86 binary needs AVX.
4. **Upgrade off Node 20**, which reached end of life on 2026-04-30, and update Docker Desktop.
5. Optional: Synchronized File Shares (4.27+, a paid plan according to Docker's blog, which claims 2–10× gains) ([docs](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/), [blog](https://www.docker.com/blog/announcing-synchronized-file-shares/)), or OrbStack ([vendor data](https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem)).

**Caveat:** No source measures how much of your 5–10× comes from each cause. Time `npm install` with bind mount vs. volume, and with Rosetta on vs. off, to find out which matters most for you.

I've used my search budget (11 fetches/searches), so here's my report.

## Findings: primary sources on the share of crates.io crates that use `unsafe`

**Number to cite:** About **19%** of crates with significant code use the `unsafe` keyword directly. About **34%** call directly into another crate that uses `unsafe`. Both figures date from May 2024.

**1. Rust Foundation, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild" (May 2024): the newest and most official source**
https://rustfoundation.org/news/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/
- About 145,000 crates in total, of which about 127,000 have "significant code".
- 24,362 crates use `unsafe`, which the post calls "19.11% of all crates". 24,362 is 19.1% of 127,000 but only 16.8% of 145,000. **An auditor will spot this mismatch.** Cite it as "19.1% of the ~127k crates with significant code" or give the range 17–19%. The post never defines "significant".
- 34.35% make a direct function call into a crate that uses `unsafe`. That counts direct calls only, not full transitive exposure.
- The data came from the Foundation's Painter tool: https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter. Its README lists these limits: it only includes crates that build locally, it doesn't resolve callee versions, it can miss calls because of inlining, dynamic dispatch or generics, and it doesn't document how it detects `unsafe`.

**2. Evans, Campbell & Soffa, ICSE 2020: corroborating source**
https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752
- Abstract: developers "use the keyword unsafe in less than 30% of Rust libraries". "More than half cannot be entirely statically checked" because of `unsafe` somewhere in the call chain.
- Secondary summaries say it covered about 15,000 buildable crates and that about 60% of the most-downloaded crates contain `unsafe`. I couldn't extract the PDF text, so those last two numbers are unverified.

**3. Astrauskas et al., OOPSLA 2020, "How Do Programmers Use Unsafe Rust?" (DOI 10.1145/3428204): corroborating source**
- About 31,000 crates (all of crates.io at the time). Reported as about 23.6% of crates using `unsafe`, with unsafe blocks in about 20% and unsafe function declarations in about 13%.
- **Not verified from the primary text.** The UBC PDF returned 404, ACM returned 403, and the Zenodo artifact page gives no figures. These numbers come only from secondary summaries (https://alastairreid.github.io/RelatedWork/papers/astrauskas:oopsla:2020) and need checking before citation.

## Confidence
- **High** that the direct-use share is somewhere around 17–30%. Three independent studies, using different methods and years, all land there.
- **Moderate** on the exact 19.11%. The base is unclear (127k vs 145k), the Foundation published a blog post rather than a peer-reviewed paper, it excludes crates that don't build, and it's already 2.5 years old.
- **Older and newer figures can't be compared directly.** The 2020 papers used crates.io snapshots about a fifth the size of today's, and each study defines "uses unsafe" differently.
- **Direct and transitive figures must be kept apart in the assessment.** Direct use is about 19–29%. Exposure through dependencies is 34% to more than 50%. For supply-chain risk, the transitive figure probably matters more.
- I found no peer-reviewed or official figure from after May 2024. A newer one may exist.

## Recommendation
Cite the Rust Foundation post as "19.1% of ~127,000 crates with significant code (May 2024)", with the ICSE 2020 "<30%" figure as corroboration. Also report the transitive figure: "34% directly call unsafe-using crates; >50% not fully statically checkable (2020)".

I'm done with this angle; the report is below. I used 12 searches and fetches. Two primary sources didn't load: the Astrauskas PDF returned a 404, and the Evans PDF came back as binary I couldn't read.

**Coordinator report: press, forums, issue trackers**

**Recommended figure:** cite **"about 19% (24,362 of ~127,000 crates with significant code), as of May 2024"**. It comes from the Rust Foundation post "Unsafe Rust in the Wild", published 21 May 2024 by "Rust Foundation Team" with no individual author: https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/
- It's the newest and largest-sample figure I found, and the press repeats it without contesting it.
- The same post says **34.35%** of crates make a direct call into another crate that uses `unsafe`. For supply-chain risk, that second figure arguably matters more.

**What an auditor will catch:**
- **The arithmetic doesn't match.** 24,362 / 127,000 = 19.18%, not 19.11%. Measured against all ~145,000 crates it would be ~16.8%. The 127k is evidently rounded and the exact denominator isn't stated.
- **"Significant code" is never defined.**
- **The method is thin.** It's a blog post, not peer-reviewed. The numbers come from the Foundation's "Painter" tool, which the post links to but doesn't describe. It doesn't say whether tests, macros, FFI bindings or generated code are counted.
- **The data is 2.5 years old.** I found no 2025 or 2026 update. An October 2025 crates.io analysis exists (https://00f.net/2025/10/17/state-of-the-rust-ecosystem/), but its search snippet doesn't mention unsafe; I didn't fetch it.

**Corroborating peer-reviewed figures (older, different methods):**
- **Evans, Campbell & Soffa, ICSE 2020** (https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752). The abstract says the `unsafe` keyword appears in "less than 30% of Rust libraries", and "more than half" have unsafe somewhere in their call chain. Secondary summaries give 29%, and ~60% for popular crates. I couldn't verify either from the full text.
- **Astrauskas et al., OOPSLA 2020**, DOI 10.1145/3428204, 31,867 crates. A secondary summary (https://alastairreid.github.io/RelatedWork/papers/astrauskas:oopsla:2020) says "75% of crates do not use unsafe". A widely repeated "29% → 23.6%" drop between the two studies is unverified; I couldn't reach the PDF.
- **Özdemir's Stanford blog** (https://cs.stanford.edu/~aozdemir/blog/unsafe-rust-syntax/): 1,048 of 3,638 crates, about 29%. Small sample, undated, not peer-reviewed.

**Press and community:**
- Coverage just repeats "~20%": Slashdot (https://developers.slashdot.org/story/24/05/25/2250236/rust-foundation-reports-20-of-rust-crates-use-unsafe-keyword), Fudzilla (https://www.fudzilla.com/news/59051-20-per-cent-of-rust-crates-have-unsafe-keyword), The New Stack (https://thenewstack.io/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild/).
- A July 2024 r/rust thread, "Unsafe Rust everywhere? Really?" (thread ID 1eaw93c), objects that counting keywords overstates risk. One commenter cites "72.5% of crates contain no unsafe code" and "94.6% of code on crates.io [by lines] is safe". I only saw this through search snippets; the mirror didn't load and I couldn't trace the original source.

**Confidence:** high that the true share of crates using `unsafe` directly falls between 19% and 30%. Three independent methods from 2020–2024 agree, and the trend points downward. Confidence is moderate on the precise 19.11%, because its method is opaque and its arithmetic slightly off. I'd present it as "≈19% (Rust Foundation, May 2024)" with the 2020 peer-reviewed ~24–29% as a cross-check. I'd also state plainly that the share with transitive exposure is much higher: 34% via direct calls, and over 50% per Evans.

**Still unverified:** the Evans full-text figures, Astrauskas's exact percentage, how Painter works, and any figure from after 2024.

**Report to coordinator: independent measurements, critiques and counter-evidence**

**Answer:** The figure to cite is **19.11% (24,362 of about 127,000 crates use the `unsafe` keyword)**, from the Rust Foundation, May 2024. Present it as a lower bound for direct use only. Two peer-reviewed studies from 2020 found higher shares, about 25–29%. Measured transitively, the exposure is much larger (over 50%). An auditor can trace the number to its source, but **the Foundation does not publish how it was measured, so confidence is moderate.**

**Findings**

1. **Rust Foundation, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild" (May 21, 2024).** About 145,000 crates, of which about 127,000 "contain significant code". 24,362 use `unsafe`, which is 19.11%. A further 34.35% "make a direct function call into another crate that uses the unsafe keyword". That is a direct-call measure, not a full transitive one. The numbers come from the Foundation's "Painter" tool. The post doesn't say how `unsafe` was detected, which crate versions were counted, or how macros and generated code were handled. https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/
2. **Evans, Campbell & Soffa, ICSE 2020 (peer-reviewed).** The abstract says engineers use `unsafe` in "less than 30% of Rust libraries", and more than half of libraries can't be fully checked by the compiler because of unsafe code in their dependencies. A secondary summary gives the breakdown: 29% of about 15,000 crates that still build, 38% with no direct `unsafe` but depending on crates that have it, and over 50% of the top ~500 downloaded crates. I couldn't extract text from the PDF to confirm these breakdown numbers myself. https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752 ; https://alastairreid.github.io/RelatedWork/papers/evans:icse:2020
3. **Astrauskas et al., OOPSLA 2020 (peer-reviewed, DOI 10.1145/3428204).** All of crates.io, over 31,000 crates. About 75% don't use `unsafe`, so roughly 25% do. Unsafe blocks appear in about 20% of crates and unsafe function declarations in about 13%. These numbers come from a secondary summary only, because the paper's PDF link returned 404 and ACM returned 403. https://alastairreid.github.io/RelatedWork/papers/astrauskas:oopsla:2020

**Critiques and caveats for the auditors**

- **The answer depends on the definition.** Counting the keyword (about 19–29%) says nothing about exploitability; the Foundation itself says most such code "is most likely not" exploitable. Counting transitive exposure (over 50%) is the measure that matters for supply-chain risk.
- **Shares are per crate, not weighted by downloads.** Popular crates use `unsafe` more often (over 50% in Evans), so the share in a real dependency tree is likely higher than 19%.
- **The share falls as the registry grows.** It went from about 25–29% (2020) to 19% (2024). That probably reflects growth in small, simple crates more than safer code. The 2024 data is now about 2.5 years old.

**What I'm unsure of**

- A search-engine summary said Evans reported "3,638 crates" and a drop "to 23.6%". I could not verify either, so don't use them.
- I didn't find a newer census (2025–2026) or any published critique of how Painter counts.
- The Astrauskas figures are second-hand. Get the paper itself, e.g. via ETH Research Collection or the Zenodo artefact (record 4085004), before citing it.

**Recommended wording:** "About 19% of crates on crates.io use `unsafe` directly (Rust Foundation, 2024). Peer-reviewed studies report 25–29% (2020), and over half of crates depend on unsafe code transitively (Evans et al., ICSE 2020)."

The slowdown comes from two causes that multiply. Your Linux colleagues have neither of them.

1. **CPU emulation.** A `linux/amd64` image can't run natively on an arm64 Mac. Docker emulates it with QEMU, which it says "can be much slower than native builds", or with Rosetta. That slows native-module builds in `npm install` and the bundler in the dev server. https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/
2. **`node_modules` on a bind mount.** On a Mac, every file access goes from macOS into Docker's Linux VM through VirtioFS or gRPC FUSE. On Linux the container reads the disk directly. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/ In one Apple Silicon test, `npm install` took 4–6 s natively, 17–22 s on a bind mount and about 7 s with `node_modules` in a named volume. https://github.com/sparkfabrik/sparkdock/issues/61

```text
Decision: Do now: put node_modules in a named volume (keep the source bind-mounted,
  run npm install in the container), confirm VirtioFS, and turn on Rosetta with the
  Apple Virtualization framework (not Docker VMM, which has no Rosetta).
  Later, if still slow: make the image arm64 and isolate the x86-only dependency
  in an amd64 sidecar.
Rests on: Docker's docs (both mechanisms apply to your setup as described) and
  third-party Mac measurements of the bind-mount cost.
Not verified: How much of your 5–10× each cause accounts for. Whether your install
  has Rosetta on (Docker's sources disagree on the default). Whether your x86
  binary runs under Rosetta (it lacks AVX).
Next check: After the volume change, time npm install with Rosetta on, then off.
```

**Notes:**
- **Named volume:** VS Code's guide covers the setup. If the container runs as a non-root user, `chown` the volume in `postCreateCommand`. https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance
- **Docker VMM:** it cancels the Rosetta fix. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/
- **Rosetta problems:** if you see hangs or CPU stuck at 100% under Rosetta, it is a known issue (no AVX, Vite/Next.js). Moving to arm64 is the fix. https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384
- **Node 20:** Node 20 has been end-of-life since April 2026. It also has a known `npm install` hang under amd64 emulation that people worked around with Node 22. Upgrading is worth it anyway. https://www.github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946
- **If file I/O is still slow:** Docker's Synchronized File Shares (4.27+, paid plan) keep files in a fast cache inside the VM. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/

I recommend citing **"about 19% (19.11%) of crates on crates.io directly use the `unsafe` keyword (Rust Foundation, May 2024)."** Present it as roughly one in five, not as a precise measurement, and state the date. Confidence is moderate: the figure is in the right range, but auditors will find weaknesses in how it was produced.

**The primary figure**
- The Rust Foundation post "Unsafe Rust in the Wild" (21 May 2024) says that of about 127,000 crates that "contain significant code" (out of about 145,000 in total), 24,362, or 19.11%, use `unsafe`. It also says 34.35% make a direct call into another crate that uses `unsafe`. https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/
- The numbers come from the Foundation's Painter tool: https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter

**Weaknesses auditors may raise**
1. The post is a blog, not peer-reviewed. "Significant code" is never defined, and 24,362 ÷ 127,000 gives 19.18%, not 19.11%, so the exact base is unclear.
2. I found no published dataset, so the figure can't be reproduced. Painter also only analyses crates that build locally.
3. The data is about 2.5 years old, and the registry has grown a lot since then. I found no newer census of `unsafe` use across crates.io.
4. It counts direct use only. For supply-chain risk, depending on crates that use `unsafe` matters more, and that share is higher (34%+).
5. Using `unsafe` doesn't mean the code is vulnerable. The Foundation says most uses are calls into C/C++ code.

**Supporting peer-reviewed study**
- Evans et al., ICSE 2020: developers use `unsafe` in "less than 30% of Rust libraries," and "more than half" can't be fully checked by the compiler because of `unsafe` somewhere in their dependencies. https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752
- I verified that wording from the abstract only. I couldn't read the PDF, so the commonly quoted 29% comes from secondary sources.
- Do not cite the "23.6%" figure often credited to Astrauskas et al. (OOPSLA 2020). I couldn't confirm which paper it comes from. https://doi.org/10.1145/3428204

**Suggested wording:** "Roughly 19–30% of crates directly contain `unsafe` code, depending on the dataset and method (Rust Foundation 2024: 19.11%; Evans et al. 2020: <30%). More than a third rely on `unsafe` code through their dependencies."

If you need a figure that can be fully defended, run Painter or a similar scanner on a current crates.io snapshot and record the method.

# Share of crates.io crates containing unsafe code: figure to cite

**Cite this:** *"About 19% of crates.io crates with significant code (24,362 of ~127,000) use the `unsafe` keyword directly, as of May 2024. A further 34.35% make a direct function call into a crate that uses `unsafe`."* The source is the Rust Foundation post "Unsafe Rust in the Wild" (21 May 2024): https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/. One researcher reached it under `/news/` instead of `/media/`, so check which URL is canonical before publishing.

**Corroboration:** Evans, Campbell & Soffa (ICSE 2020, peer-reviewed) is the only corroborating source we checked against the original text: https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752. The abstract says `unsafe` is used in "less than 30% of Rust libraries". It also says more than half of libraries "cannot be entirely statically checked" because of unsafe code in their call chain.

## Confidence

- **High** that direct use falls somewhere between about 19% and 30%. Independent studies from 2020 to 2024 agree on this range.
- **Moderate** on the exact figure. An auditor will raise these points:
  - **Arithmetic:** 24,362 / 127,000 is 19.18%, not the 19.11% the post states. Measured against all ~145,000 crates, the share would be ~16.8%. Write "≈19%" and name the denominator.
  - **Definitions:** "Significant code" is never defined.
  - **Method:** The post is not peer-reviewed. Its data comes from the Foundation's Painter tool (https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter), which only covers crates that build. Painter does not resolve callee versions and can miss calls made through generics or dynamic dispatch.
  - **Age:** The data is about 2.5 years old. We found no census from 2025 or 2026.

## How to frame it for a risk assessment

- **The 19% is a floor, not a measure of exposure.** It counts crates, not downloads, and popular crates use `unsafe` more often. Transitive exposure is above 50% according to Evans.
- **Keyword presence does not mean a vulnerability exists.** The Foundation itself says most of this unsafe code is likely not exploitable.

## Do not cite yet

- **Astrauskas et al., OOPSLA 2020** (https://doi.org/10.1145/3428204). Secondary summaries disagree, giving either ~23.6% or ~25%. None of us could open the paper itself.
- **Evans's detailed breakdowns** (29%, the share of popular crates, ~15k crates). These come only from secondary summaries.
- **The Reddit claim** that "72.5% contain no unsafe". We could not trace where it comes from.

If you obtain the Astrauskas paper, you could add a second peer-reviewed cross-check.

**Answer: no.** SQLite's own documentation rules this out. WAL mode in particular does not work when the processes are on different machines sharing one NFS mount.

**Findings (all from primary sources):**

1. **WAL does not work across machines.** The WAL docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem… processes on separate host machines obviously cannot share memory with each other." WAL coordinates through a shared-memory index: a `-shm` file next to the database that each process maps into memory and that is "never synced." Three servers can't share that memory, so the WAL plan fails at the design level, not just as a tuning issue. The only exception is EXCLUSIVE locking mode, which only works when a single process is the only one using the database. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

2. **SQLite explicitly advises against NFS.** The "SQLite Over a Network" page says: "Rely upon it at your (and your customers') peril." SQLite is "not tested in across-a-network scenarios." The exclusive locks used for writes "have been known to operate incorrectly for some network filesystems. This has led to database corruption." Its recommendations are: (a) use a client/server database (it names PostgreSQL); (b) keep WAL mode but run a proxy on the machine that holds the file and send all reads and writes through it; or (c) use rollback-journal mode, which allows several readers or one writer, never both at the same time. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html

3. **Corruption risk.** The "How To Corrupt" page says locking bugs are "especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular," and two processes accessing the database at once on such a filesystem "might result" in corruption. It also warns that every connection must use the same locking protocol. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html

4. **The rule of thumb fits your setup.** "Avoid using SQLite in situations where the same database will be accessed directly… and simultaneously from many computers over a network." And: "if the website is… so busy that it requires multiple servers, then consider using an enterprise-class client/server database engine." The same page notes that NFS locking bugs are "nothing SQLite can do to prevent." https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

5. **NFS makes no coherence promise.** The Linux nfs(5) man page says "The NFS protocol is not designed to support true cluster file system cache coherence" unless the application serializes access itself. It only promises consistency when a file is closed and reopened, plus file locks. It doesn't cover mmap coherence across clients. NFSv4 does build locking into the protocol, but nothing says that makes SQLite safe. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html

**What I'm unsure of:**
- I found no official benchmark or test for rollback mode on NFSv4. Whether that mode is corruption-free depends on your NFS server's lock implementation, and SQLite doesn't test this.
- On volume: whentouse.html says SQLite "will handle more write concurrency than many people suspect," so 20 writes/second is probably fine on local disk. Over NFS, latency and lock round-trips are untested, and I couldn't find official numbers.
- SQLite 3.51.0 (2025-11-04) added some defenses for multi-process WAL use. The docs say "they are not a cure-all" and they are about processes on the same host, so I don't believe they help here, but I haven't confirmed that.
- Replication tools such as LiteFS, rqlite and libSQL weren't part of my angle.

**Bottom line for the coordinator:** don't share the file over NFS. Either move to PostgreSQL, or put the SQLite file on a single host and have the other servers send their reads and writes to a service there (SQLite's own "proxy" option).

I found nothing in the press, forums, issue trackers or community write-ups that supports this setup, and the plan as proposed (WAL mode, writes from 3 hosts) is unsafe. WAL relies on shared memory, so it can't work across hosts on a network filesystem. Every source I read says to use a client/server database or put a single owner host in front of the SQLite file.

**Findings**

1. **WAL can't coordinate writers on different machines.** GoToSocial's docs quote SQLite: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." They also say SQLite on NFS is "neither recommended nor supported by the SQLite maintainers" and "puts you at risk of database corruption." https://docs.gotosocial.org/en/latest/advanced/sqlite-networked-storage/
2. **SQLite's own network-use page** (official, but the community cites it constantly) says network filesystems don't support simultaneous reads and writes. Its suggestions for multiple machines: a client/server database such as Postgres, a single host that runs SQLite in WAL mode and serves the others through a proxy, or rollback-journal mode (one writer at a time, at the user's risk). https://sqlite.org/useovernet.html
3. **Corruption can be silent.** A SQLite forum post explains that NFS can report a lock as taken when it isn't, so SQLite commits pages and "NFS lied, so now the database is corrupt in some way that might or might not manifest" later. A server outage, by contrast, fails loudly. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/02c1a784a2830a3d?raw
4. **NFSv4 has never been confirmed safe.** A 2021 forum thread asks exactly the v3-vs-v4 question and gets no reassurance (https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/49fe87db5387c757?raw). One mailing-list post argues SQLite's convention-based locking is "never safe" for read-write use on NFS, NFSv4 included (https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg31786.html). I saw that only as a search snippet and didn't read the full post.
5. **People report real failures.** On TrueNAS, a user got "disk I/O error" over NFS and the problem went away when the file was copied to local disk (https://www.truenas.com/community/threads/sqlite3-over-nfs-flock-issues-after-upgrade-to-12-0-u3.92635/latest). On Gluster mounted as NFS, a user got "database is locked" even on new database files (https://lists.gluster.org/pipermail/gluster-users/2011-September/008756.html). On python-diskcache, issue #345 reports "database disk image is malformed" with NFS as the suspected cause (https://gh.mise.run.place/grantjenks/python-diskcache/issues/345). I didn't confirm the root cause of #345.
6. **Performance is also poor.** An HN commenter says SQLite "performs very poorly on EFS," probably because every lock is a network round trip. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=31318708. A SQLite forum user found that adding cachefilesd didn't speed up queries. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/bdc0e2e2ae??t=c&hist
7. **Testing doesn't settle it.** A 2026 OneUptime guide says: "Do not place a cross-host SQLite database in WAL mode." If you must try anyway, it says to use rollback-journal mode and run cross-host lock and fault-injection tests. Passing those tests "reduces uncertainty but does not remove it." https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-09-08-detect-unsafe-nfs-smb-embedded-database-locking/markdown

**What I'm unsure of**

- I found no first-hand success story of several hosts writing over NFSv4 at around 20 writes/s. The only hint is a ServerFault question saying some companies run this with "fewer and less frequent issues," and that page now returns 410, so I couldn't read it.
- I didn't find a statement from Richard Hipp specifically about NFSv4.
- I couldn't load the Stack Overflow answer attributed to SQLite contributor Roger Binns ("you will eventually get corruption") because the mirror returned 401. That quote comes from a search summary only.
- Whether rollback-journal mode plus a well-configured NFSv4 server (e.g. Linux knfsd, hard mounts) holds up for this workload is still untested in anything I found.

I've finished the research and am writing up the findings.

**Short answer: no, not as planned.** WAL mode cannot work across hosts. Without WAL, rollback mode over NFSv4 locking might work, but only at your own risk, and I found no rigorous multi-host test that shows it is safe.

**What I found**

1. **WAL across hosts is unsupported.** SQLite's WAL docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." The reason is that the wal-index is shared memory (an mmapped `-shm` file), and processes on different machines can't share memory. Using WAL without shared memory is only allowed with `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, which means one process only. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
2. **NFS locking is a known cause of corruption.** SQLite says buggy locks are "especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular," and that corruption can follow when two or more processes access the file. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
3. **SQLite's network page says rollback mode can reduce the risk** "completely or to an acceptable degree." It also says "SQLite library is not tested in across-a-network scenarios" and that early test success shouldn't be trusted, because failures are "not frequent or repeatable." It recommends either a client/server database or a single-host proxy in front of a WAL database. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
4. **Independent case: a codebase whose docs say Linux hosts sharing NFS can corrupt WAL SQLite.** Its fix is to force DELETE (rollback) journal mode on NFS. https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/network-file-systems
5. **Red Hat's answer is "In most cases no"** for SQLite on NFS. It says NFSv4 locking is better than v3, but its recommendation is still to avoid it. https://access.redhat.com/solutions/120733
6. **Counter-evidence (it can work under contention):** an author tested SQLite on AWS EFS (NFSv4) from Lambda and saw no corruption. Concurrent writes failed often, though: 39 of 50 POSTs at concurrency 10 got "database is locked." https://zenn.dev/galette/articles/sqlite-on-efs-locking. Another EFS test measured about 140 ms per transaction versus 30–40 ms on local disk, with no concurrency testing. https://lambrospetrou-github-io.vercel.app/articles/aws-lambda-and-sqlite-over-efs
7. **Old cache-coherence caveat:** NFS caches file size separately from data, and fcntl locks only keep the data cache coherent. Mount options like `nocto` make this worse. https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg31765.html

**What this means for 20 writes/s:** rollback mode blocks all readers while a write happens. On top of that, every lock and fsync is a network round trip. Based on the EFS results, expect frequent SQLITE_BUSY errors and high latency, even if the data doesn't get corrupted.

**What I'm unsure of**
- I found no controlled study that measures how often corruption happens with rollback mode, multiple hosts and NFSv4. All the evidence is either documentation or small anecdotal tests. "Didn't corrupt in a short test" proves little, as SQLite itself warns.
- Results depend on your NFS server's lock implementation (Linux knfsd vs NetApp vs EFS), on mount options (`actimeo`, `nocto`, `lookupcache`), and on how the server recovers locks after a failover. I couldn't check any of these.
- I couldn't open the AWS re:Post thread on EFS lock failures (403) or the Server Fault thread on NFSv4 mount tuning (410).

**Recommendation from my angle:** use PostgreSQL or MySQL. If you want to keep SQLite, keep the file on local disk on one host and have the other servers write through that host, as SQLite's own proxy suggestion describes. Another option is a replication layer such as rqlite or LiteFS, though I didn't research those.

**Decision:** Cite **19.11%: 24,362 of about 127,000 crates "with significant code" use the `unsafe` keyword** (Rust Foundation, 21 May 2024). Next to it, cite **34.35%** of crates that make a direct call into a crate using `unsafe`, from the same post. For supply-chain risk, the second figure is the more relevant one.

**How to phrase it for auditors**
- Quote the denominator exactly as the source gives it: "crates with significant code," not "all crates." Against all ~145,000 crates the share would be ~16.8%. 19.11% implies about 127,480 crates, which matches the post's rounded "~127k."
- Label it as **direct keyword use, per crate, not download-weighted**. It does not measure exploitability.
- Note the limits: it is a blog post, not peer-reviewed; it was measured with the Foundation's Painter tool, whose method is not documented; it covers only crates that build; and the data is now about 2.5 years old.

**Corroboration you can cite safely** (verified from the abstract only):
- Evans, Campbell & Soffa, ICSE 2020 found `unsafe` in "less than 30% of Rust libraries," and "more than half" cannot be fully statically checked because of `unsafe` in their dependencies.

**Do not cite** these yet, because no one confirmed them from the primary text: the Astrauskas et al. (OOPSLA 2020) figures (~23.6%/~25%), Evans's 29%/38%/60% breakdowns, and the Reddit "72.5% / 94.6%" numbers.

**Confidence:** High that the figure is quoted correctly and can be traced to its source. All three researchers read the post directly. Moderate on how well it reflects today's registry. Studies from 2020 to 2024 consistently place direct use between ~19% and 30%.

```text
Decision: Cite 19.11% (of ~127k crates with significant code) plus 34.35% direct-call exposure, Rust Foundation, May 2024
Rests on: Figures read directly from the Foundation post by all three researchers
Not verified: Whether a post-2024 census supersedes it; Painter's detection method
Next check: Read the Oct 2025 crates.io analysis (00f.net, below) for a newer unsafe figure before finalising
```

**Sources**
- Rust Foundation, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild": https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/
- Painter tool: https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter
- Evans et al., ICSE 2020: https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752
- Unchecked possible update: https://00f.net/2025/10/17/state-of-the-rust-ecosystem/

# Should our SQLite database live on a shared NFS mount?

**No. The plan as described is unsafe, and the WAL part cannot work at all.**

## Why WAL fails across hosts

SQLite's WAL documentation says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." WAL coordinates writers through a shared-memory index (the `-shm` file). Processes on three different machines cannot share that memory, so this is a design limit, not something tuning can fix. The only exception is `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, which allows a single process only. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

## Why NFS is risky even without WAL

- **SQLite advises against it.** SQLite is "not tested in across-a-network scenarios." Locks on network filesystems "have been known to operate incorrectly… This has led to database corruption." The page says to use networked access "at your (and your customers') peril." https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- **NFS is singled out for locking bugs.** SQLite names "network filesystems and NFS in particular" as a source of broken locks. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- **NFS doesn't guarantee consistency between clients.** The Linux man page says NFS "is not designed to support true cluster file system cache coherence." https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html
- **Corruption can be silent.** NFS may report a lock as granted when it isn't. The damage then shows up later, not at the moment it happens. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/02c1a784a2830a3d?raw
- **Red Hat agrees.** Its answer is "In most cases no," even with NFSv4's improved locking. https://access.redhat.com/solutions/120733

## Rollback-journal mode as a fallback

Switching to rollback-journal mode removes the WAL problem, but it is still at your own risk. Writes block all readers, and every lock and fsync becomes a network round trip. In one test on AWS EFS (NFSv4), 39 of 50 concurrent writes failed with "database is locked." https://zenn.dev/galette/articles/sqlite-on-efs-locking

At 20 writes/s from three hosts, expect frequent `SQLITE_BUSY` errors. A short test without corruption also proves little, because these failures are rare and hard to reproduce.

## What to do instead

1. **Use PostgreSQL (or MySQL).** This is the standard answer for several app servers sharing one database, and SQLite's own docs recommend it: https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
2. **Keep SQLite on local disk on one host.** That host runs WAL and serves reads and writes to the other two through a small service. This is SQLite's own "proxy" suggestion (useovernet link above).
3. **Try a replication layer** such as rqlite or LiteFS. These are worth evaluating, but our research didn't cover them.

At your load, option 1 is the simplest robust choice. Option 2 works if you want to keep SQLite.

**Decision:** Don't put the database on the shared NFS mount. Run PostgreSQL (or MySQL). If you want to keep SQLite, keep the file on local disk on one server and have the other two send their reads and writes to a small service on that host. This is the proxy setup SQLite itself recommends.

**Rests on:** WAL mode can't work across machines. This is a design limit, not a tuning problem. WAL coordinates through a shared-memory index (the mmapped `-shm` file), and processes on three different hosts can't share memory. SQLite's documentation says so directly: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." The only exception is `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, which allows a single process, so it rules out three servers. All three researchers traced this to SQLite's own docs, and nothing in the reports points the other way.
- https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html

The fallback, rollback-journal mode over NFS, doesn't give you what you want either:
- **It's untested and not recommended.** SQLite isn't tested over networks. The SQLite docs warn that lock bugs on NFS have corrupted databases, sometimes silently and much later. Red Hat's answer to running SQLite on NFS is "in most cases no", even for NFSv4.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
  - https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
  - https://access.redhat.com/solutions/120733
- **It performs badly for multiple writers.** Rollback mode blocks readers during every write, and each lock and fsync becomes a network round trip. In one test on AWS EFS (NFSv4), 39 of 50 concurrent writes failed with "database is locked." Another EFS test measured about 140 ms per transaction, compared with 30–40 ms on local disk.
  - https://zenn.dev/galette/articles/sqlite-on-efs-locking
  - https://lambrospetrou-github-io.vercel.app/articles/aws-lambda-and-sqlite-over-efs

SQLite's own guidance for a site busy enough to need several servers is to use a client/server database. About 20 writes per second is easy for PostgreSQL, or for SQLite on local disk behind a single owner host.

**Not verified:** Nothing that would change the decision. No one tested your specific NFS server or mount options, but the WAL plan fails by design whatever the configuration.

**Next check:** None needed.

I found that the official investigations agree on the mechanism: overvoltage leading to a cascade. They don't agree on who is responsible, and no official investigation assigns blame. A caveat on sourcing: I couldn't read the ENTSO-E final report (the PDF is over the fetch size limit) or the Spanish government's report directly. Their findings below come from ENTSO-E's summary page and from trade press. Check figures and quotes against the PDFs before you cite them.

**Established cause (supported by every official report)**
- **No single cause.** The ENTSO-E expert panel's final report (20 March 2026) names many interacting factors. These include oscillations at 0.63 Hz and 0.2 Hz, gaps in voltage and reactive power control, differing voltage regulation practices, fast output cuts and generator disconnections in Spain, and uneven ability to damp oscillations. Together they caused a rapid voltage rise and cascading generation trips. Spain and Portugal lost synchronism with Europe at 12:33:19.
- **Specific findings reported from the ENTSO-E report:** several conventional units missed their reactive power setpoints; shunt reactors were switched by hand, which was too slow; renewables ran at a fixed power factor; some plants tripped below the regulatory voltage limits; and small rooftop solar disconnected. Lack of inertia was not a root cause.
- **Spanish government committee (17 June 2025):** overvoltage with several causes. Red Eléctrica (REE) did not schedule enough voltage-control generation the day before. Synchronous plants absorbed less reactive power than expected. Some disconnections were "apparently improper."
- **Ruled out:** a cyberattack, by the government report and by the National Court (Audiencia Nacional), which provisionally closed its case.
- **CNMC, the Spanish regulator (19 March 2026):** the tools and obligations to prevent the blackout already existed.

**Still contested**
- **Who is responsible.** REE says the ENTSO-E report finds no cause attributable to it, and blames generators: missed voltage-control obligations (operating procedure P.O. 7.4) and at least nine incorrect disconnections. The utilities' association Aelec (Iberdrola, Endesa, EDP) says "La operativa fue la que falló" ("it was the operation that failed"), and Iberdrola has sued REE for defamation. ENTSO-E and the CNMC both say they are not assigning liability.
- **CNMC sanction cases (April 2026):** about 20 cases opened against REE (as a possible "very serious" infringement), Iberdrola, Endesa, Naturgy, Repsol and the operator of the Ascó and Vandellós nuclear plants. The CNMC says opening them does not attribute the cause of the blackout. I haven't confirmed any outcomes after April 2026.
- **Gaps in the evidence:** the role of the oscillations is unclear, and missing data left the cause of some disconnections undetermined.
- **Role of renewables:** ENTSO-E's president said the problem was voltage control, not renewables. How much renewables contributed is still debated.

**Sources:**

- https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/03/23/entso-e-report-finds-systemic-failures-behind-2025-iberian-blackout/

- https://www.renewableenergymagazine.com/panorama/ree-no-fall--en-el-apag-20260320
- https://www.renewableenergymagazine.com/panorama/aelec-respalda-el-informe-de-la-cnmc-20260319

# Iberian blackout, 28 April 2025: cause and open disputes

**Caveat:** None of the researchers read the ENTSO-E final report PDF. The findings below come from its landing page and press summaries. Check the wording against the PDF before quoting it. The summaries disagree on details such as the page count (440–472) and the number of recommendations (21 or 22).

## Official findings

**ENTSO-E Expert Panel, final report (20 March 2026).** The panel found no single cause, and says the report is "not an attribution of liability." The interacting factors were:
- oscillations: a 0.63 Hz forced oscillation from converter-based generation and a 0.2 Hz inter-area mode, which set conditions but were not the direct trigger;
- gaps in voltage and reactive-power control;
- divergent voltage-regulation practices;
- rapid output cuts and generator disconnections in Spain.

Together these caused a fast overvoltage and cascading generation trips from about 12:32–12:33 CEST, followed by loss of synchronism.

Contributing details reported:
- Synchronous units missed reactive setpoints, with no penalty for doing so.
- Renewables ran at fixed power factor.
- Shunt reactors were switched by hand.
- Spain allows a wide voltage band (up to 435 kV).
- Protection settings were misaligned.
- Some trips remain unexplained because fault records are missing.

Sources: https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/ · https://www.powermag.com/anatomy-of-a-blackout-findings-from-the-spain-portugal-grid-collapse-final-report/

**ENTSO-E factual report (3 October 2025).** It sets out the timeline only, with no root-cause analysis. https://www.pv-tech.org/over-voltage-triggered-iberian-blackout-report/

**Spanish Government committee (17 June 2025).** It named three causes:
- insufficient voltage control (REE scheduled 10 synchronous units, one became unavailable, and some did not respond properly);
- oscillations;
- apparently improper disconnections.

It ruled out a cyberattack. https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/consejodeministros/resumenes/Documents/2025/Informe-no-confidencial-Comite-de-analisis-28A.pdf

**Audiencia Nacional (12 January 2026).** The court closed the sabotage case for lack of evidence. https://www.elindependiente.com/espana/2026/01/12/el-juez-archiva-la-investigacion-por-el-apagon-al-no-existir-un-minimo-indicio-de-sabotaje/

**CNMC (2026).** It made recommendations and opened sanction proceedings. The CNMC states these proceedings do not assign cause. Reports put the number at about 20 or up to 64, and no rulings were found. https://www.cnmc.es/prensa/informe-incidente-electrico-20260319

## Contested (mark as such)

- **Senate report (April 2026).** It blames REE, the government and the CNMC. It is a political document. https://www.vozpopuli.com/economia/energia/el-senado-senala-como-culpables-del-apagon-a-red-electrica-el-gobierno-y-la-cnmc-.html
- **Unresolved in the official findings.** Why units missed their setpoints, unexplained trips, and missing data for small and distributed generation.

No independent (non-industry) re-analysis of the PMU data was found.

**Decision:** Split. You can write the headline cause now, attributed to ENTSO-E and the Spanish Government. **Why the evidence is weak**

- **Origin of the 91%.** It came from a March 2024 conference poster (HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.20–3.03) that was promoted before peer review. https://www.heart.org/en/news/2024/03/18/time-restricted-eating-may-raise-cardiovascular-death-risk-in-the-long-term
- **Published version.** The peer-reviewed paper (2025) used a different comparison group and reported HR 2.35 (1.39–3.98). It found no rise in all-cause or cancer deaths, and the authors say residual confounding may explain the result. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/
- **It didn't measure what you do.** Eating windows came from two single-day food recalls. Nobody was asked whether they practised time-restricted eating. A short window on one recorded day is not a deliberate year-long 16:8 routine, and sick people often eat less. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- **Small, different group.** The poster's under-8-hour group was about 414 people (around 2% of the sample) with 31 cardiovascular deaths. That group had more smokers and more people with existing disease. A former AHA president said, "It wasn't their eating time… It was what they brought to the table." https://peterattiamd.com/time-restricted-eating-and-ascvd/
- **No independent replication.** A second analysis found a U-shaped curve, but it used the same NHANES dataset, so it doesn't count as confirmation (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40944446/). An independent UK cohort found no mortality link (https://www.nature.com/articles/s43856-025-01035-x). A large French cohort linked a longer overnight fast with lower stroke risk (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10721609/).
- **Trials show no harm.** Randomized trials are short and only measure risk markers such as blood pressure and cholesterol. They show no harm, and also no benefit beyond weight loss. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full

```text
Not verified: Nobody could read the full 2025 paper, so its final group size, death count
  and covariates are unchecked. None of these would turn a single-day recall into evidence
  about your routine.
Next check: none needed.
```

Overall, this is weak, hypothesis-generating evidence for harm. Neither harm nor benefit has been tested in trials that measure deaths.

**Decision: cite "about 19% of crates.io crates directly contain `unsafe` (Rust Foundation, May 2024)" as the headline figure, with Cui et al.'s 20.8% (January 2023 snapshot) as independent corroboration.** You can state "roughly one in five" with confidence. Do not claim precision beyond that.

**Primary source.** All three researchers read the Rust Foundation post, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild" (21 May 2024): https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/ (one researcher reached it at a `/news/` path; check which URL resolves before you publish). It reports 24,362 of about 127,000 crates "with significant code" (19.11%), measured with the Painter tool: https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter. For supply-chain exposure, the same post gives a better-suited figure: another 34.35% of crates directly call into a crate that uses `unsafe`.

**Corroboration.** Two researchers read this in the primary text: "21,506 crates use Unsafe Rust among the 103,516 crates on crates.io (3,614 are yanked)", snapshot 2023-01-30, which is 20.8%. It was published by Cui et al. at ICSE 2024: https://arxiv.org/html/2308.04785. A related preprint by the same group repeats the count: https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06251v1. Treat these as one data point, not two. Their method (regex over source) differs from the Foundation's, so the two figures agree only roughly.

**Caveats auditors will raise**
- 24,362 ÷ 127,000 = 19.18%, not 19.11%, so the published denominator is rounded.
- "Significant code" is never defined. About 18,000 of about 145,000 crates were excluded.
- No dataset is published, so the figure can be traced but not reproduced.
- The data is 2.5 years old. No researcher found a 2025–2026 registry-wide census.
- Using `unsafe` is not the same as being vulnerable. Much of it is FFI or SIMD.

**Do not cite yet:** the 2020 figures (Astrauskas et al. ~25%, Evans et al. ~29%, and ">50% of popular crates"). No researcher could open those PDFs, so these numbers come only from secondary summaries. An auditor checking them could find a mismatch.

**Decision:** Two stacked causes are likely: file I/O on the bind-mounted `node_modules`, and x86 emulation of the whole image. Fix the first now. Run one timing test before restructuring for the second.

1. **Do now:** keep the source bind-mounted, but put `node_modules` on a named volume and run `npm install` inside the container. VS Code documents this setup for devcontainers. In an independent test on an M4 Pro, `npm install` took 9.53s on a bind mount, 3.61s with a named volume and 3.37s on the host:
   - https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance
   - https://www.paolomainardi.com/posts/docker-performance-macos-2025/
2. **Check settings:** in Docker Desktop, set file sharing to VirtioFS (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/). Also look at "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation", which needs the Apple Virtualization framework VMM (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/). Sources disagree on whether Rosetta is on by default, so look at your machine. Without Rosetta, Docker falls back to QEMU, which is much slower (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/). Rosetta has known cases of Node builds hanging or pinning a CPU:
   - https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384
   - https://github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946
3. **Dev server:** remove `CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING` or `WATCHPACK_POLLING` if either is set, because polling a bind mount wastes CPU (https://github.com/docker/for-mac/issues/7274).
4. **Likely next step:** build the image as native arm64 and run only the x86-only dependency as a separate amd64 service. Also check whether that dependency now has an arm64 build.

```text

Rests on: An independent benchmark (Mainardi, M4 Pro, Docker Desktop 4.37) measured a ~2.8× bind-mount penalty for npm install that a named volume removes. Your amd64 image is emulated on an M3 by construction; the size of that penalty comes only from sysbench runs and anecdotes, 1.2–6× (https://vpsmac.com/en/blog/docker-on-m4-mac-linux-container-performance-analysis.html, https://github.com/orbstack/orbstack/issues/2744).
Not verified: How much of your 5–10× is emulation versus I/O. Whether your Docker uses Rosetta or QEMU. An unconfirmed report that amd64/Rosetta got slower on macOS 27 (orbstack #2744).
Next check: With node_modules on a named volume, time `npm ci` in an arm64 container and in your amd64 one. A large gap means the arm64 split is worth doing.
```

If your plan is paid, Docker's Synchronized file shares are another option (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/). Its "2–10× faster" figure is Docker's own marketing number, and the independent test above found it no faster than a named volume.

**Decision:** State the cause as the official investigations give it. It was an **overvoltage collapse with several causes**, not a single fault. Gaps in voltage and reactive power control, oscillations, the steps taken to damp them (which raised voltage), and generator disconnections combined into a voltage rise and a cascade of trips. A cyberattack was ruled out. Hold the detailed figures until someone checks them against the ENTSO-E report itself.

**Rests on:**
- **ENTSO-E Expert Panel final report, 20 Mar 2026.** It finds no single cause: "fast voltage increases and cascading generation disconnections." https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/ ; https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/
- **Spanish government committee, 17 Jun 2025.** It found too little dynamic voltage control scheduled (10 synchronous units). Some generators did not absorb reactive power. A 0.6 Hz oscillation at 12:03 was followed by a 0.2 Hz mode at 12:19. Trips came between 12:32:57 and 12:33:18, some apparently before the 380–435 kV limits were reached. No cyberattack. https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/consejodeministros/resumenes/Documents/2025/Informe-no-confidencial-Comite-de-analisis-28A.pdf
- **CNMC.** It also found a multifactorial overvoltage collapse. Its sanction cases (opened 17 and 24 Apr 2026) "do not by themselves" establish cause. https://www.cnmc.es/prensa/incoacion-incidente-electrico-28A-20260417 ; https://www.cnmc.es/prensa/incoaciones-incidente-electrico-28A-2
- **ERSE.** It calls this an "exceptional event" that started in Spain. https://www.erse.pt/communication/press-releases/erse-classifica-apagao-iberico-de-28-de-abril-de-2025-como-evento-excecional/

**Mark as contested:**
- **Responsibility.** REE blames generators for breaching the P.O. 7.4 voltage-control rules. Aelec's Compass Lexecon/INESC TEC study, which is partisan, blames REE's scheduling and line switching. CNMC cases are open, roughly 35 of them, including one "very serious" against REE. https://www.compasslexecon.com/insights/publications/analysis-of-events-leading-to-the-peninsular-blackout-of-april-28th
- **Source of the oscillation.** No official report names the plant. One blog's claim that it was Núñez de Balboa is disputed by Iberdrola. https://www.reversemode.com/2025/10/what-happened-at-iberdrolas-nunez-de.html
- **Reliability of the ENTSO-E report.** Endesa alleges gaps and a conflict of interest. https://www.energias-renovables.com/panorama/endesa-denuncia-carencias-en-el-informe-europeo-20260421
- **Unexplained trips.** Some disconnections are unexplained because of data gaps, including about 208 MW of distributed generation.

**Not verified:** No researcher opened the ENTSO-E report PDF. The following come only from trade press (https://www.powermag.com/anatomy-of-a-blackout-findings-from-the-spain-portugal-grid-collapse-final-report/ ; https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/03/23/entso-e-report-finds-systemic-failures-behind-2025-iberian-blackout/):
- the 0.63/0.64 Hz figure
- the "below 75% of reactive set points" finding
- the MW sequence: press accounts conflict, giving about 928 MW "within two seconds" in one and "2.5 GW in about 78 s" in another
- the statement that the oscillations "did not directly cause" the blackout
- the counts of recommendations (21 or 22) and pages (440–472)

Do not attribute these to ENTSO-E yet.

**Next check:** Read Chapters 4 and 9 of the ENTSO-E final report and replace the press-sourced figures with direct citations.

- CPython calls 3.13t experimental. Its docs warn of "some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit" of about 40%, and they list ways to crash it. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
- PEP 779 keeps 3.13 at the experimental stage. Free-threading becomes "supported but optional" only in 3.14. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ The 3.14 release notes put the single-thread penalty at about 5–10%. https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html
- pypa/manylinux removed cp313t from its build images on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch dropped 3.13t wheels as a result. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- The researchers read the PyPI file lists for the latest releases of all three of your dependencies. NumPy 2.5.4, pydantic-core 2.50.4 and lxml 6.1.3 each ship cp314t x86-64 wheels and none ship cp313t. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files, https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files, https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files
  - Some older releases did ship cp313t wheels, for example pydantic-core from 2.29.0. https://newreleases.io/project/pypi/pydantic-core/release/2.29.0
  - Pinning to those releases would leave you without security fixes. That matters most for lxml, which parses untrusted XML.

**Risks that remain on 3.14t**
- Free-threading support is still labelled experimental in all three libraries:
  - NumPy: https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/thread_safety.html
  - pydantic: https://pydantic.dev/articles/pydantic-v2-11-release
  - lxml 7.0.0a1: https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a1/
- NumPy arrays shared between threads need your own locking.
- lxml has published nothing on thread safety under free-threading.
- If any extension you import isn't marked free-thread-safe, the GIL silently turns back on. https://pyo3.rs/v0.23.2/free-threading

**Decision: No. Don't put the SQLite database on the shared NFS mount for all three servers, in WAL mode or any other mode.** Use one of these instead:

- **PostgreSQL or MySQL.** This is SQLite's own first recommendation when several machines need to write. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html, https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
- **One server owns the SQLite file** on its local disk, in WAL mode, and the other two send reads and writes to it through an API. 20 writes/s is easy for SQLite on a single host; the problem is the layout, not the load.
- **A tool built for shared SQLite**, such as LiteFS or rqlite. None of the researchers evaluated these.

**Rests on:** WAL keeps its coordination index in a memory-mapped `-shm` file, and processes on different machines cannot share that memory. SQLite's documentation says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html. Richard Hipp, SQLite's author, says a cross-host WAL setup that seems to work "just means you didn't test it enough." https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg108685.html. OpenAI's Codex documentation reports this exact failure: Linux hosts opening one WAL database over NFS corrupted it. Two researchers gave slightly different URLs for that page; this is one of them: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/network-file-systems. NFS version doesn't change any of this, because the problem is shared memory, not locking.

Switching to rollback-journal mode doesn't make it safe either. SQLite doesn't test it over a network, failures are rare and hard to reproduce, and NFS locking is a named cause of corruption. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html, https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html (Q5)

**Not verified:** Nothing that would change the decision. No one tested your NFSv4 server or mount options, and no published benchmark of rollback mode on NFSv4 exists. Those would only matter if you wanted to try rollback mode, which I advise against.

**Next check:** None needed for this decision. Separately, one report says the corruption page describes a "WAL-reset bug" affecting SQLite 3.7.0 through 3.51.2, even on a single host. If you go with the single-owner option, check your SQLite version against https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html.

**Short answer: no, this headline is not a reason to stop.** The evidence behind it is weak, and it doesn't describe someone like you.

**Where the 91% comes from.** It was a 2024 American Heart Association conference poster built on NHANES, a US survey of about 20,000 adults. People eating within a window of under 8 hours had a hazard ratio of 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03) for cardiovascular death, compared with 12–16 hours. There was no link with death from all causes or from cancer. The senior author said it does not show that time-restricted eating caused the deaths. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death

**Why it's weak**
- **Small group:** only 414 people (about 2%) were in it, with 31 cardiovascular deaths. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- **Thin measurement:** eating windows came from just two days of food recall.
- **A different group from you:** it had more smokers and higher BMI, and many likely ate briefly because of illness, work or poverty rather than by choice.
- **Expert criticism:** AHA cardiologists called it "not ready for prime-time," and 34 researchers objected to the press release. https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/
- **Later papers:** the peer-reviewed version reported HR 2.35, but we saw that figure only in news coverage, not in the paper. https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915 A second analysis of the same survey found a U-shaped curve. Coverage says its cardiovascular signal wasn't significant in younger adults after full adjustment. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40944446/ · https://www.news-medical.net/news/20250915/Daily-meal-timing-influences-longevity-risk-in-adults-study-reveals.aspx
- **Trials:** randomized trials show modest or neutral effects on risk factors. None measured deaths. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full

**What is worth asking yourself:** is 16:8 actually helping your weight? In one 16:8 trial it did no better than the control group, and much of the weight lost was muscle. Adequate protein and resistance training address that. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32986097/

```text
Decision: Keep doing 16:8 if it works for you; this study is no reason to stop.
Rests on: Self-reported 2-day windows, a small confounded group, and authors disclaiming causation. Read in the AHA release and TCTMD coverage.
Not verified: Neither journal paper was read in full. Nobody observed deliberate 16:8 eaters in healthy middle-aged people, which no available study could settle.
Next check: none needed
```

**Decision:** Don't stop 16:8 because of this headline. The study behind it doesn't measure what you are doing, and nothing in it shows that a deliberate eating window harms a healthy 45-year-old.

**How strong the evidence is: weak.**

- **Source:** The "91%" came from a March 2024 AHA conference abstract that had not been peer-reviewed. Its own senior author said it "does not mean that time-restricted eating caused cardiovascular death." https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death
- **Published version:** The full paper came out in 2025 using the same dataset. It reports a hazard ratio of 2.35 (95% CI 1.39–3.98) for cardiovascular death, comparing under 8 hours with 12–14 hours. It found no rise in deaths from all causes, and the authors say residual confounding may explain the result. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/
- **Small, different group:** Only 414 people (about 2%) were in the short-window group, with about 31 cardiovascular deaths. That group had more smokers and a higher BMI, and may have included shift workers or people with irregular eating forced on them. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- **Weak measurement:** Eating windows came from just two 24-hour food recalls at enrollment, then assumed to hold for years. Critics of the study, who are themselves time-restricted eating researchers and so not neutral, made the same point. https://www.nutritioninsight.com/news/scientists-dispute-study-linking-time-restricted-eating-to-poor-heart-health.html
- **Randomized trials:** These are short-term and measure risk factors only. They show neutral to modestly helpful effects, including lower blood pressure, and no harm signal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9644535/ ; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10630127/

```text
Decision: Continue 16:8 if it works for you; this study gives no
  reason to stop.
Rests on: The study's design, read in the AHA release and the paper's
  abstract: two-day recall, small confounded group, no all-cause signal,
  authors disclaim causation. It did not study deliberate 16:8 in
  healthy people.
Not verified: Long-term safety of deliberate 16:8. No trial has
  measured heart attacks or deaths, so a small real effect can't be
  ruled out either way. A U-shaped cohort result (lowest risk at 11–12 h)
  is reported but its details were not checked:
  https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12610411/
Next check: None needed. Keep your normal checkups (blood pressure,
  cholesterol) as for anyone your age.
```

If you'd rather hedge cheaply, widening your window to about 10 hours costs little. But this evidence doesn't require it.

**Decision: No. Do not put the SQLite database on the shared NFS mount for all three servers to write. Use PostgreSQL, or keep the SQLite file on local disk on one host and have the other two servers send their reads and writes to a service on that host.**

**Rests on:** WAL mode cannot work across machines. This is a limit of how WAL is built, not a tuning issue. WAL coordinates through a shared-memory index (the `-shm` file), and processes on different hosts cannot share memory. SQLite's docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem" (https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html). Two researchers read this page directly. Because the limit comes from the design, it applies to your three servers without anyone needing to test it on your setup. The same docs recommend the two alternatives above (https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html).

**Why rollback-journal mode isn't a good fallback:**
- **Corruption risk depends on NFS locking.** SQLite says locking bugs are "especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular" and lead to corruption (https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html). It also says it is "not tested in across-a-network scenarios" and warns that early test success proves little, because failures are infrequent and hard to reproduce (https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html).
- **NFS doesn't promise coherence.** NFS "is not designed to support true cluster file system cache coherence" (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html). Red Hat's answer for SQLite on NFS is "In most cases no," even for v4 (https://access.redhat.com/solutions/120733).
- **Expect poor performance at your load.** Rollback mode blocks readers during every write, and each lock and sync is a network round trip. In one EFS (NFSv4) test, 39 of 50 concurrent writes failed with "database is locked" (https://zenn.dev/galette/articles/sqlite-on-efs-locking). Another measured about 140 ms per transaction, compared with 30–40 ms on local disk (https://lambrospetrou-github-io.vercel.app/articles/aws-lambda-and-sqlite-over-efs).
- **SQLite's own guidance fits your case.** If a site "requires multiple servers," use a client/server database (https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html).

**Not verified:** Nobody tested rollback mode against your NFS server and mount options. That gap doesn't affect the decision, because the WAL plan fails by design and the fallback is risky and slow either way.

**Next check:** None needed. If you'd rather keep SQLite than move to PostgreSQL, the next step is to evaluate replication layers such as rqlite or LiteFS. None of the researchers covered those.

**Cause:** Two stacked slowdowns that your Linux colleagues don't have:

1. `node_modules` on a macOS bind mount, which crosses the slow file-sharing layer into Docker's VM.
2. CPU emulation of the amd64 image on your arm64 Mac.

The research found no measurement of how the 5–10× splits between them, and none was taken on your machine.

```text
Decision: Split. Make the cheap, reversible fixes now. Hold the arm64
  re-architecture until you've timed the result.
  Now:
  1. Keep the source on the bind mount, but put a named volume over
     /app/node_modules and run npm install inside the container.
     If the container runs as a non-root user, add chown in
     postCreateCommand.
  2. In Settings → General, confirm VirtioFS file sharing and
     "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation" with the Apple
     Virtualization framework. Not Docker VMM: it has no Rosetta
     support, so it falls back to slow emulation.
  3. Update Docker Desktop, and move from node:20 (end of life since
     April 2026) to node:22. Both fixed npm-install hangs under amd64
     emulation.
  Later, if still slow: build arm64 by default and isolate the
  x86-only dependency in an amd64 sidecar.
Rests on: File I/O: one Apple Silicon test measured npm install at
  17–22 s with a bind mount, ~7 s with a named volume and 4–6 s
  natively. Emulation: Docker's docs say amd64 on arm64 needs
  emulation and that QEMU can be much slower than native. All
  observed elsewhere, not on your Mac.
Not verified: Whether your install is on QEMU or Rosetta (Docker's
  pages disagree on the default). Whether your x86 dependency needs
  AVX, which Rosetta doesn't support. If it does, Rosetta fails and
  the arm64 split becomes necessary.
Next check: After step 1, time npm install and dev-server startup
  with Rosetta on and with it off. If it's still more than ~2× slower
  than Linux, or the x86 binary breaks under Rosetta, do the arm64
  split.
```
